div.p: godly.
CONTENT.
Not asking how or why, Before Thy will, 0 Father, let my heart Lie hushed and still! Why should I seek to know
Thou art all-wise; If Thou dost bid me go, _ _

Let that suffice. - If Thou dost bid me stay, Make me content In narrow bounds to dwell Till life be spent. If Thou dost seal the lips That fain would speak, Let me be still till Thou The seal shall break. If Thou dost make pale Pain Thy minister, Then let my patient heart Clasp hands with her. Or, if Thou sendest Joy To walk with me, My Father, let her lead Me nearer Thee! Teach me that Joy and Pain Alike are Thine, Teach me my life to leave In hands Divine.

THROUGH THE SNOW. The cutter stopped before the gate— Out sprang her highness lightly; Half co.y, half cool, this cruel Kate, And altogether sightly. In mock distress exclaimed she, " Oh ! How far we must have ridden! For under this fast falling snow The walk's entirely hidden !" Entirely hidden it was, and more, For, as the catch I lifted, Six inches deep from crate to door, I saw the snow had drifted. " Ugh!" shuddered she, "You lead the way l" Was her command next spoken, To hear, at once was to obey; And through the snow unbroken. I walked with steady, ample feet; With lifted skirts she followed, Daintily stepping, while her neat Footprints in mine were swallowed. 94 Back to her mirthful puzzling face I looked across my shoulder, And wondered if she'd smile with grace On me should I grow bolder. "Why may not you and I," I said. Through life thus walk together? I'd break the way with happy tread Through all life's snowy weather." She did not answer me a word But one sweet glance permitted, And then, before me, like a bird, Int.' the house she flitted. And through the snow and from the gloom Her fairy footprints drew me Into the cheerful, cosy room, Where love surrendered to me. Ah ! in our wedded life since then Snowstorms have broken o'er me; But always. into light again, 'Tis she has walked before ma

SIMPLICITY IN DRESS.—A Swiss lady, who has for some years lived a retired life in a country home, recently -.aye herself a holiday, and went to spend it Lausanne, ;here she was so much horrified at the style of dress worn by young people that she addressed a long letter to a popular journal, urging Swiss mothers to dress their daughters again in white frocks with coloured ribbons and neat straw hats. What struck her as being so very ridiculous was to see the girls dancing in costly silk or China crepe toilettes, with bonnets, hats, and gloves to correspond, and to listen to their careworn mothers seated in knots together and discoursing on the difficulty of making both ends meet. The country lady considers that the problem would be solved if the young people re- turned to the white frocks for Sundays and fete days. How she would have rejoiced over the plain white frocks of Princess Beatrice's bridesmaids! NEURALGIC HEADACHE OF WOMEN.—The increased, and apparently increasing, frequency of neuralgic head- ache among women must needs have a cause. There is one of singular simplicity and quite obvious which has been overlooked, and to which it is worth while to draw attention. The pain experienced is generally located in one or more of the branches of the second cervical nerve, very commonly those terminating in the scalp at the oc- cuput. As a matter of fact, the nerves of the scalp are irritated by the hair being drawn tightly back and put on the strain, not as a wale, in which case the strain would be spread over a large area of the'surface, but by small bundles of hair which are pulled back and held in place by hair-pins. Relief is often consciously experi- enced as a result of removing the hair-pins, but this has enly a temporary "and partial relief. The injury done is lasting, if not permanent, in its consequences. The pre-, sent style of dressing the hair should be discontinued, as it probably, in part, accounts for the extreme prevalence of a form of suffering which is both intractable and dis- tressing. FEMALE EMPLOYMENT.-Seven hundred women are employed at the Central Telegraph Office in London, and about 350 more at the different teleg-ravph and postal branch offices of the metropolis. At Liverpool, Glasgow, Manchester, and other provincial centres, a considerable number earn their living in this way, besides 900 simi- larly employed outside the civil service. It,is not diffi- cult for a girl to qualify herself for the post of a tele- graph clerk. Preliminary competitive examinations, open to all, are held twice a year, and girls between 114 and 18 years of age may be entered for the examination, the fee .for which is is. If she satisfies the examiner in dictation, handwriting, and easy sums, she enters the Post-office Telegraph School, where no charge is made fir the instruction. Three months generally qualify the learner for the lowest stage of the actual work in a tele- graph office, when she receives a weekly payment of 10s. The first month however, is considered probationary work, during whi y ch, if it is seen that a girl has not the necessary qualifications, the appointment is cancelled. This period of probation having been passed success- fully, the pay begins to rise by degrees to 275. per week. As a rule, women do not rise higher, which is attributed to the fact that women do not enter into the work with a thoroughly business-like spirit. "When a young man begins," said Mr. Fischer, the controller of the Central Telegraph Office, "he knows that his career lies before him, and that according to his exertions he will rise. Girls do not seem to see the work in that light. Some, however, form a laudable exception, and are promoted to higher classes, according to merit." A REMARKABLE DOG STORY.—His name was Tobv Trotter; Old Tobe he was generally called. , He was an old Virginian from Culpepper county. A sober, quiet fellow was old Tobe, and he did nothing but loaf around and tell big tales. Everybody liktd to hear him talk_ Tobe was not a bore; he was not always forcing you to hear one of his tales. He always waited far a nice chance to slip in a yarn. If you were sitting in a grocery and happened to be talking about dogs, Tobo would tell this story :—" Gentlemen,—l once owned the best dog that ever lived. That dog was a ratter, a regular ratter —a Scotch terrier imported from Dundee. Lord, gentle- men, what sense that dol.; had, ancl he seemed to know just what his mission in this world was. He seemed to know that Providence put him here to kill rats. 6entle- men, I saw that dog kill 1,257 rats in one hour, and when they were all gone he sat down and howled be- cause there were no more. It was a pitiful sight to see. One day I took him to the barn to kill rats; it was com- pletely undermined with holes, and I stationed him at a hole on one side, and I went to another place and punched them up. Well, the rats began to pour out, and he killed a hundred, and then they commenced coming too thick for him, :and he caught three in his mouth and got one ueder each foot, and then if he didn't back up and stick his tail in the hole to stop -em until he killed what he bad; after he killed those he had in durance vile he opened the hole and let 'em come again, but every little bit they would get too fast for him, and he would:back up and stop the hole. He did that 52 times and killed 2,4871 rats. Poor fellow! the strain on his mind was t.-)o much for him; he died next day of apoplexy." After he had finished, some one would ask him about the half of a rat, and he would say: "Oh, I can't just explain it, but I know the figgers are right; it occurred some way n averaging..

DISRAELI (Cog:Truss oP BEACONSFIELD).—No more interesting chapter could be added to Isaac D'lsraeli's gossip about the wives of groat men than an account of his own son's domestic happiness and the good influence of his wife upon his fortunes and career The literary and studious father held that few great men have flourished who, were they candid, would not ac- knowledge the vast advantage they have experienced in the earlier years of their career from the spirit and sym- pathy of women. From all one has heard of the late viscountess, she might come into the famous list of "un- lettered wives" who have done so much to foster and strengthen the genius of their husbands. "The Pro- fessor of the Breakfast-table" is eloquent upon this theme. "Many a blessed woman," he says, "who dies unsung and unremembered, has given out more of the real vital heat that keeps life in human souls, without a spark flitting through her humble chimney to tell the world about it, than would set a dozen theories smoking, or a hundred odes simmering in the houses of so many men of genius." Mrs. Disraeli had money. It was her fortune which enabled her husband to fight his way into the House of Commons. and kept him free from the worries of "working to live." She was a simple-minded, honest, earnest woman. She loved her husband, and was proud of him. He responded to her affection with a happy, personal devotion. She was not what north of England people call a "fine lady ;" she was not even "a woman of society." Every night, whatever the hour at which the House of Commons adjourned, she sat up for her husband. The Queen made a friend of her, and no one knew better titan her Majesty the peaceful, happy life which her illustilous subject led at home. Some clever journalistic pen, in a notice of her death, wrote : It is a pretty sight, that of the remorseless Parliament- ary gladiator, who neither gave quarter nor asked it, who fought with venomed weapons, although he struck fair, and shot barbed darts, which stung and rankled in the wounds—it was a pretty sight to see him in the sun- shine of domestic life, anticipating the wishes of his wife with feminine tenderness of consideration, and receiving her ministering with the evident enjoyment which is the most delicate flattery of all. The secret of the spell she held him by was a simple one. She loved him with her whole heart and soul; she believed in him above all other men • and he appreciated, at its real worth, that single- minded, self-sacrificing devotion." In his. latter days, after her death, he always did everything he could to get leisure to wander about the grounds atHughenden—to roam in the paths he and she had walked together; and it was no cynical remark that which he made on his de- defeat at a late election. "Ah, well, I shall be able for once to see the roses bud and bloom at Hughenden."— Joseph Hatton. How A WOMAN PUTS ON A BONNET.—Did you ever notice how a woman puts on a bonnet? No? Then you have missed the enjoyment of a most interesting performance. When man dons his head-piece he merely claps the cover over his brows, with as little con- sideration as one would drop an extinguisher over a candle. He simply puts his hat on, and that is all there is in the operation. Light or dark, it is all one to him. With a woman how-different? When she puts on her bonnet a poem is created, a picture is called into being, music is brought back to earth, and the atmosphere is saturated with sweet sounds. She brings forth a band- box, sets it upon 'a chair or table, removes the lid, and with a sweet smile reaches down into the cavernous-in- terior of that box, and draws forth very tenderly, a little, insignificant, heterogeneous affair that courtesy calls a bonnet. To the male eye it has neither beauty nor comeliness in its present condition; but wait a bit. Now sise advances towards the mirror, holding the delicate trifle before her after the manner in which the careful housewife carries a pan full to the brim of hot fat. Ar- rived at the looking-glass, she releases one ear of the bonnet, and with the disengaged hand deftly brushes her front hair; then her hand resumes its hold of the bonnet, and the fellow-hand in its turn pays attention to the clustering locks on its side of the house. Now. both hands have the bonnet in their gentle grasp. The fair creature looks into the glass, and remarks, apologetically, that her hair isn't fixed. She feels that it is her duty to exhibit that bonnet in the most favourable manner. She has no excuses to make for its shortcomings; it has. none. It is herself alone, and always her hair, that is responsible for anything short of absolute perfection when the nuptial knot shall be tied 'under the chin, and the bonnet and herself.shall be one glory. She raises the airy nothing aloft' her chin protrudes; her hand oscil- lates; she cranes her neck and hunches her shoulders, Fhile she adjusts the bonnet astride her pug, and settles it down carefully upon its hirsute couch. It is now exactly where it should be. There is no guess work about it. Square, level, and plumb could not be more precise in results. Up goes her round chin, the strings are tied without the slightest wrinkling of the ribbon, the ends are brushed out withoa delicate sleight-of- hand, the bows are picked out flat and square—not too flat nor too square—and a long, slender pin is thrust re- morselessly through the bow, its point, naked and un- guarded, protruding from the thither side, a warning to all whom it may concern that no trespassers are al- lowed upon the premises.—The Ilouseuqe. Dean, Barnes. and Clarke. forwards. Referee. Mr. E. Trevor Smith. WEST LANCASHIRE AND BORDER TOWNS UNION V. WEST CUMBERLAND. In very enfavourable weather this fixture was played if on the Warrington ground at Wilderspool Causeway, en Saturday afternoon. A body of men had been engaged by the Committee of the Warrineton Football Club to clear away the snow from the field, and in this way the progress of the game was assisted. It was also a great convenience to the spectators, who as- sembled, to the number of about 4.000, from all parts of the country. The West Lancashire team was as follows:— J. Buxton (Warringson), back; H. C. Speakman (Runcorn), W. Lind (Southport Olympic), and J. Roberts (Aspnlll, thrte-quarters backs; H. Hughes (Runcorn) and J. E. War- ren, captain (Warrington), half-backs; L. Whittle (Wigan), F. Turner (Warringtois), H. Wilcock (Waverfr.e), W. Wright (Runcorn), W. Hughes (Runcorn), H. Ash- ton (Warrington), S. Rimmer (Newton), A. Borthwick (St. Helens), and W. Haydock (Aapull), forwards. The umpires were Mr. T. Barnes (Warrington) and Mr Lewthwaite (C;ockermouth), and the referee Mr. A. T. Kemble (Liverpool). The ball was started by West Cum- berland, playing from the Wilderspool goal against the wind. Speakman got the ball, made a dash up the field, and passed to Roberts, who punted the ball well up the field, the leather eventually being kicked into touch. From the scrimmage which resulted from the line out, Warren gained possession, and, on being tackled. passed to Speak- man, who immediately re-passed to Lund, but, tit e ball being thrown forward, was called back and a scrimmage formed in the middle of the ground. From a throw out afterwards, Turner dribbled the ball to the Cumberland goal line, but was smartly tackled by Lauriston. On a scrimmage being formed, the Cumberland forwards took the game into the enemy's quarters. From the loose play re.ultine from the line out, Wilcock dribided in grand stile up the field, finally gaining the ti-v. The try was attempted by Turner, but he failed in gaining the point. The game was re-started from the 25-yard flag, and the leather was smartly returned by Warren and bounded out of play. On the line up being formed Wiloock again showed to the front, dribbling the ball finely up the field. For the next few minutes, play was confined within the West Cumberland quarters. From a tight scrimmage in front of the Cumberland goal post, the sphere was kicked across into touch near the half-way flag. The next five minutes were spent in loose play. A. scrimmage was now formed, which resulted in Cumber- land haying to save. On a recommencement, loose play was the order of the day. Another scrimmage was formed, and Warren succeeded in getting possession, dashed off, but was tackled, when he passed to Roberts, who, however, be- ing off side, was called back, when the whistle was blown for half-time. On the game being resumed Warren kicked off, and a loose scrimmage was formed, the ball being even- tually kicked to the Cumberland three-quarter Lack (Bell), who was tackled by the 25-yards flag. Tne Cumberland team being pressed on their own goal line, their forwards managed by combined play to carry the oval grandly ue the field. On the ball being thrown out a scrimmage resul- ted, when the Lancashire forwards turned the tables by a piece of the combined play. The ball was now carried all round the field by a series of loose scrimmages, at last set- tling in front of the Cumb.srland goal posts. The ball was now caned out of danger by the Cumberland forwards to the other end of the field. From a scrimmage in front of the Lancashire goal post the ball was played to the hair- way flag, when Warren secured it, and passed it to 11)berts, but, some dispute occurring, it was called back. Here Buxton made a dodgy run, the result being that the ball was carried into the Cumberland quar- ters, where a scrimmage was again formed. On the leather again emerging Warren obtained possession and passed to Roberts, who was unable to make much headway, owing to the close following up of the Cumberland forwards, play ulti- mately landing in the middle of the field. The Cumberland forwards now began to press their opponents back, and the ball was carried dangerously near the Lancashire goal line. A scrimmage was formed in front of the Lancashire goal post, Cumberland claiming a free kick, from which, how- ever, nothing resulted. From a line up the ball was again carried by Cumberland within dangerous proximity of the Lancashire goal post, where a series of tight scrimmages ensued. The Lancashire forwards carried the ball out of danger, and a scrimmage resulted outside the 25-yards flag, the ball on 'emerging being taken by Roberts across the field, where another scrimmage was formed, the leather be- in e taken from one side of the field to the other without either side seeming to gain advantage, Warren being notice- baTabhll lee ofvo re r htihs e d Cumberlanda as h ir infe ago rswrhuai rnr eds sg,aonabdl y coo opc dka ds frl oei bryb lhge t et aidnr rrgii be dbal i try amidst amidst great excitement. Bell was deputed to try the shot at goal, being assisted by Ridley, and the hall was kicked within a few inches of the posts. "No side " was Lame- aiately proclaimed, leaving the result—West Lancashire one try and two touchdowns to Cumberland one try.

NOTES BY THE WAY. The heavy fall of snow last week compelled many clubs to reluctantly forego their engagements, only a few matches being played, where the snow bad been removed at consider- able expense to the clubs thus engaged. The most important fixture of the day was that played on the Warrington ground, between the West Lancashire and Border Towns Union and West Cumberland, which was witnessed by something like 3,000 people To within ten minutes of time the Lancashire men had by far the best of the play (thanks to the half-backs), as they led by one try; but the Cumberland men, by sheer down-right bard work, managed to equalise the score, a most pleasantly contested game ending in a draw, slightly in favour of West Lanca- shire by one try and two minors to one try. Swinton went over to Oldham to play off their fixture with that club. The Lion having a very narrow shave of baying his tail trod on, as the result at call of time, was a draw slightly in favour of Oldham by three minors to two. THE LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT CHA.LLENOII CUT.—The committee of the Liverpool and District Football Associa- tion met at the Neptune Hotel, Liverpool, on Monday even- ing, to draw the fourth round of ties in connection with the present season's competition, the result being as follows : Earlestown (holders) v. Stanley, High Pak (Southport) v. Everton, Warrington v. Haydock, Earleatown Wanderers v. Bootle. The first-named club in each case haa the choice of ground, and the round mast be played oft on or before the 27th of February next. BRYN HALL BLUES V. SANKEY REFINERS (Etteteeigrowei). The first teams of these clubs met on Saturday, at Bryn Gate. The visitors arrived shortly after two o'clock, but it was 3-30 before the ball was kicked off. The home captain winning the toss chose to play downhill. The visitors' cap- tain started the ball, and passed to the right wing, but Jones took it down to the visitors' quarters, and Kynaston sent in a beauty, which Thavne failed to stop, thus scoring the first goal for the home team in one minute from the ' , start. The bell wandered from end to end uutil half-time, I when the score was one goal each. W6en the whistle blew for the call of time the home teem, after a hard fought game were victorious by four goals to one. Tan GOLBORNB V. STANLBy DlSPUTlL—Amtingst other matters which the committee of the Lancashire Football , Association had under notice at their last meeting was the j recent unfortunate fracas during a Liverooel Cup tie in I which the Golborne and Stanley clubs were engaged, which led to the expulsion of the former club by the Liverpool Association. The Lancashire committee, however, found that the Golborne Club had taken all reasonable precautions lagainst disturbance, but John Culkin, of Stanley Club, and J. Clough, of the Golborne Club, were each suspended for two months. The question was again considered at a meet- ing of the committee of the Liverpool and District Football Association on Monday evening, when some discussion took , place with reference to the suspension of Culkin, of the I Stanley Club, by the Lancashire Association. It was decided Ito send a deputation of three to meet a similar number of the Lancashire Association to debate the subject, as the action of the Lancashire Committee will cause a good deal of confusion.

FOO'S. Everybody's a foo' at sumulat ; but my owd rib says, "If -t4ey're foe's at one thing, they'll be foo's at another." I say boo's wrung theare ; but boo sticks to it hoo's reet, an' ut it's me ut's wrung. I know it's no use tryin' to con- vert her; so I'll see if I con talk to someb'dy else. I say everybody's a foe' at sumrnat. Tiler never wur a , yead put on a pair o' shoothers but, if yo' wur to feel it o'er, yo'd find a crack or a soft place somewhere. It met no' be a crack as wide as a church dur, nor a place as soft as a turf-clod; but soft or shaken for o that. An' heaw we becoen one another for th' bits of leatheryeadishness ut we conno' help but show! An' haaw we gotten eaursels up on o hee peearch, an' praiohen deawa to thooee ut we thinken ha' no' sense to look up, an' try to get at us! We damn' ealkilate, at th' same time, ut someb'dy may be talkin' deawa to us, for bein' sich feo's as to think we'n more sense nor other folk. Torneyism, to tlf very chapter an' verse; bat we oonno' see it.

Someb'dy says—th' wo'ld's kept on by foo's, an' ut ther'd be poor doin's for some folk witheant 'em. Rogues would ha' to look eaut for fresh pastas' wheere folks' wits hadno' bin put to th' grindleetone ; an' thoose ut liven by rogues aa' foo'e met follow. Newspappers ud ha' little to say; lawyers ud ha' nowt to do nobbut scrat their wigs; doctors ad ha' to swallow ther Own physic, an' pa'sons ud I ha' moors time to beelatch one another, a job ut some on 'em liken better than pointin' thar finger board another wo'id, an' tryin' to mak' us rest i' this. What must become ov eaur red-jackets I dunno' know; for ther'd be no moore thumpin' upo' the owd war-tub (drum); no moore makkin' holes i' one anothees stomachs; no moose trailin' o'th' owd striped rag abeaut, an' denim' anybody to touch it. Some good howsome puucite would be o at ad be wanted when we geet a bit cranky, an' very little o' that ud satisfy us. One could find very nee as ruony sorts o' foo's as faces; so it ad taie a bit o' time for to reckon 'etn up an' sort 'em. I I nobbut meean to tackle one or two partikilar sorts ut I have abeaut me. Somitime thoose folk ut partend to be th' lamest (the most cunning) are th' biggest vorneys ov o, an they're th' plagueyest sort we han to diesel wi'. But I'll just put one o' theme upo' th' table, so tat yo' con see what he's like. For th' fast thing he's as stupid as a jackass, an' it's a pity his ears are no' th' length they should be. Yo' could- ao' mak' him to believe ut anybody's any sense beside hissel if ye' wax to talk to him wi' a hommer, an' let him feel what yo' had to say; an' I'm sure Pat ne'er try. It's no use him roadie any books; he knows o ther is in 'em, an' a good dessal moose ut ther should ha' bin. He never goes to !loather church nor chapel, becose he could taich th' pa'son moore than he knows; an' as for religion makkin' him a better mon—he's quite good enoogh for Cs' weld he's in, or any nes waitin' for him. Trier's anlue summat gooin' wrung for him—i' Lunnon fowt speshly. He'd manage thing: i' that shop better than o th' wiseakers ut ever threw ther wynt awayat a sleepy parlyarienL Owd Ned Crummell wur stun-drink to him, an' that he'd let 'em see, if they'd nobbut put th' guiders o'th' owd state waggle in his hont. He'd show 'em heaw to cleean th' war score (national debt) off, an' male orerythin' an' everybody look as breet as a summer Sunday wi' a new suit o' doom! on. It's a pity nob'dy con see him as ~,;eel as he con see hiseel, an' ut we should be gropin' through th Blotch dark, an' knockin' th' owd waggin to pieces wi' bad droivin' when this wiesaker could male it goo like a railroad, an' hang as mony lanterns abeaut it as usl lest t' reaund th' corner o'th' wold. But it wur aulus so. Nob'dy knows what a gowdera kernel tbees shut up i' his nut; an' shey'll never find it eaut, becose th' shell's too thick to g,t at it; so we may grope, an' tumble abeaut eenday. Knock him off th' table, an' punce him for tumblin'. Oe a vary common sort o' leatheryead is yor good natured too', at says brass (money) wur made reaund so it could rowl abeaut, an' maks this into an excuse for spenclin' o he sots, an' happen a bit o' summat moors than he con co his own. I' some oases we find this yorney is summat beside a fee'; for sometimes, when he's fund th' bottom or his poc- ket before he's tired o' yerrin folk praise him for bein' "a rare good son," he goes whoarn, an' puts th' wife's e'en i' nsournin', becose boo conno' put him a supper under his nose at ud be good enoogh for a strawberry-faced justice.

- Generally spakin', this foo's heause isno' quite a palace. Th' windows are no' very promisin' for a start. Th' heause window bu a short curtain made o' faded print, an poo'd so right as a drum for t' mak' it raich across; an' it's fifty to nowt ut one or moore o'th' quarrels (squares) are broken Gaut int' a ragged sore, or docthered wi' a ;tapper plaister. chamber window is screened off, like th' front ov a gal- lanty show, wi' an owd petchwork bedcover, hanged upo' two nails. Goo into th' heapse. Ther'll be no d tnger on yo' breakin' yor shins agen th' mahogany. Ther's nowt nob- but three cheears an' a Moo'. If I mast chase, I'd rayther sit me deawn upo' th' stoo' for safety, becose cheears are like owd "Berm Joe,"—knock-a-knee'd o' one side, an' bow-legged o'th tother, and th' bottoms are like crowneests, ut had wintered badly. Th' table—there's nobbut one—has three or four flirty spoons on it, an' happen as many knives ut han been made widows through th' childer using forks for gardenin' i' their way. Ther s a dirty basin or two, an' a brokken pitcher ut looks as If it had bin cryin' till churn- milk tears had run down th' sides. If it's th' weshin'-daY, ther' a line stretched across th' fire-place, wi' a two-thri (few) hauve-wesht rags hanged on it. Th' hoeshole's full o' hess (ashes), an' th' fender's plashed o'er suds an' milk. Th' childer are like th' heause— bare an' dirty. One on 'em's makkin a ship eaut ov a piece o'th' table-top. That's tb janious (Ali' family, an'll come to surmnat some day. At any rate his feythur says so when he's swaggerin' i'th' alehouse nook abeaut his heause an' his childer, as if ther nowt like 'em nowhere for bein' forrad an' smart. Another o' this preshns lot should be minim , (nursing) th' little un ; but hoo sits o'th' end o'th' fender leetin papper at th' fire, an' wonderin' if thoose are th' best OY her days, what hoot be like when ho' e a woman. Th' child's laid upo' th luarthstorie, nussin itsel'—dauhfd up to th' e'en wi' porritch an' traycle, an' 'min' cinders as a sort ov a relish after dinner. Th' mother's dabbln away at surd- mat in a crackt mug; neow an' then sea wsin th' childer wi' west hoed, an' sheautin' like a mad-cap at 'ern, an' tellin' Nun hooll knock ther yeds off ther shoothers, or writhe 91.. r tle neVkS reaond, as soon as hoo's done weshin'. This is summat like a good natured foo's heause, becose I know mony a one o'th' sort; an' when I come for t' calkilate haw ninny scamps it tak's for t' keep one o' these leather- yeads conceit wi' Mattel, I break out in a cord swat, an' cue th' whul wo'ld for lettin"em ran loose. Another port o' foo's—aa' a rare kennelful en 'eoa ther is —are thoose at ran starin' after women, as if ther nowt Nil' wo'ld beside ut wur fit to be looked at, an' ut wine() stop at nowt short of a rope or a razzor, as if soul an' body warno' wo'th keepin' t'gether beant a pratty wench war grinnia' at 'em, an' lookin' feaw at everybody beside. I'm no' quite sure whether these are no' th' biggest leatheryeds ov o. They're what one may co wappers, at any rate. I dunno think so raich at a great hobblin' lad at's just begun o' gropin' abeaut his chin for th' smo end ov a beeart, starin' his e'en *sant ov his yead at a saucy begone ut's ening lookin' at hersel', as if her own e'en wur made for nowt else; but when a grey-yeaded sinner at con hardly get his shoon-heels off th' greaund, puts his e's windows on, an' goes blinkin' at some faded duchess wi' tight stays, an' a blue nose, an' talks at her same as if they'm tooath on 'era eighteen, an' won- derin' if they'd ever be twenty—l think that ther's a soft place somewheere ut his hat would hardly cover. Ther's one o' these lives neighbour to me neaw ; an' he's abeaut as good a sample ov a woman-mad yorney as ever soikt under a chamber window. He'd once as dacent a woman for a wife as any i' Hazelw'oth, or any other pleck. 1300 kept booath hersel' an' him as straight as a new pin; an' th' heause floor yo' met ha' etten yor dinner off, it wur aulus so clean. But th' foo' didno' seem for t' think hoo're ' any better nor her neighbours, becose boo didao' mak' a show ov hersel', an' goo a gaddin' abeaut fro' place to place, puttin' fine fithers on, an' scandihnongerin', an' Bich like. Hoo minded her heause, an' her own bizness, an' that's sayin' a good deeal. My owd rib says if women muss mind nob'dy's biznrss beside ther own, ther'd be no danger on 'em thin' till they're owd folk. They'd fret thersels to deearth afore ther teeth had done grooin. Well, this couple war middlin' west to do, as things went. Th' husbant geet plenty o' brass, an' th' wife took care on it for him. They put a heause or two up eaat o' what they'd saved, as a sort ov umbrell for a rainy day. Then th' wife took it int' her yead for t' doe, an' boo did dee, as mony a gradelv body does, afore eer time had getters heavy on her 'Mothers.

800 hadno' bis buried mony week afore th' husbant be- gan o' pattin' a better polish upo' his hat than he're used to do, an' gooin i' younger company than hissel. He began o' ' shavin' twice a week, an' puttinf a dicky on ov a Thursday. We could yer on him hanging abeaut a certain heauee, too, wheere ther a woman lived ut had bin browt up to th' boardin' skoo, an' nowt else, an' had waited for a fine has- bant till hoo're as pilthert as an owd apple ut's bin • tumbled abeaut in a drawer a year or two. He're one neat seen rappin' at th' window, an' peepin' under th' curtain; an' then we could yet on him stondin' wi' one shoother in at th' dur, talkin' to sonaeb'dy ut wurso' far off. The next news we yerd, he're seen walkin' eaut wi' this owd-fashint piece o' boardin' skoo fur- nitur' donned up in his Sunday best, an' tryin' t' talk as fine as a manty'-makker. He'd his hat cocked o' one side, an' a little fancy stick in his hont—though what he carried th' stick for I never could mak' eaut ; an' I've axt mony a just as wise as me abeaut it. It wur jackasses fro' corain' a lickin' him, same happen one sin', f o an n t, they'reke ep as they dun when they meeten one another. He bowt her as mony rings as ud a wed a whul parish, an' a litt'e una- brell for t' keep th' sun fro' tannin' her face, though it wur as breawn as !ulna leather at th' Same time. He looked as preaud as a dog wi' a tin tail when he met anybody; an' it wurno' lung afore a jury o' owd women, wi' "owd Mally-at- th'-rain-tub" for th' forewoman, browt it in ut ther'd be a ' weddin' made up i' less time than it tuk some folk for t' ax th' question. A vreddis' wur made up, an' th' foo' had a coach for t' tale em' to tlefchurch, 83 if their Makker hadno' done enoogh for 'em wi' givin' em' legs, bat owt to ha' put wheels ,to 'em i'th' bargain. Tla' woman tried to luk as yank an' pratty as a pot shepherdess; but geet on badly wi' it, an' afore they went into th' church, hoo stood o'er th' tother wife's grave an' whimpert a bit—though at th' same time, if hood thowt ther any chance on her comin' to life again, , hoo'd a' had th' coffin lid nailed down wi' tenpenny nails, an' a looad or two o' weightstones tenad upo' th' grave beside. When th' weddin' war o'er, an' that gowden bant, as they con it, teed as fast as it could be, they set off to Blackport, or Southpool, I've forgotten which, becose I'm no quality chap, an' tarried theere a fortnit, though th' fast wife never as mich as zee th' sae, nor thowit o' such a thing, bin' a dacent woman. They coom back like a lord, an' a lady; but th' day after, one on 'em had to go to his work, an' th' [other to lin heaase-keepin, if boo knew owt abeaut it. Ho

A farmer in Georgia, U.S., has a team of mules wits which he has put in 23 successive crops, and they were " aged " when he bought them. A veterinary surgeon of Totnes, when making a post- mortem examination of a large cart-horse, belonging te a local firm of millers, foundin the)animal's stomach a triangular-shaped stone, which weighed just over 3lbs. While Henry Meyers was skinning a horse that had been killed'on his place at Monroe Village, N.Y., the other day, he found two silver 10-cent piezes buried under the skin, one on each shoulder-blade. One coin bore the date of 1847. The date was worn off the other coin. Why, when or by whom the coins were placed where they were found is not known. CIIESHIRB CIIRESI4 MARBET.—There were about 30 or 40 tons of cheese on offer on Wednesday. With a good attendance of buyers there was a marked improvement in the demand, and an increase of ss. per cwt. in the quotations, which were as follow :—Medium cheese, 30s. to 40s. per cwt.; good Cheshire, 555. to 655. per cwt. All the dairies were sold before noon.

"Cheese Factor," in a letter to the Standard, gives an example of the manner ix which the home trade is han- dicapped for the advantage of foreigners. Cheese shipped at either Jersey or Guernsey, he says, is deli- vered in Somersetshire at 20s. per ton, inclusive of cost of unloading and re-loading, at Weymouth; while :the same article put on rail at Weymouth only is not deli- vered in Somersetshire under 255. per ton.

LORD ABERDEEN AND His TENANTS.—The Emil of Aberdeen has sent to his tenants, in reply to a deputa- tion which recently waited upon him with reference to aF,ricultural depression, a letter in which he fully recog- ruses that depression exists. With regard to the methods of alleviation suggested by the deputation, hig lordship proposes that a ipneral meeting of the tenants should be held, and states his willingness to attend if the tenants desire, as he does, to encourage communication between landlord and tenants as to all applications for revaluation of farms, and to deal with them according to circumstances.

Lososyrrr OF HORSES.-With moderate core and good usage a horse's life may be prolonged to 25, 35, or 40 years. An English gentleman had three horses, which died in his possession at the ages of 35, 37, and 39 years respectively. The oldest was in a carriage the very day he died, strong and vigorous, but was carried off by a spasmodic colic, to which he was subject. A horse in use in a riding school in Woolwich lived to be 40 years old, and a barge horse of the Mersey and Irwell Naviga- tion Company is declared to have been in his 62nd year when he died.

BOTCOTTMG BY BUTCHZIRS.—Many of the butchers at- tending Dorchester market have boycotted all stock sent in for sale by Mr. G. Wood Homer, of Athelhampton Hall. near Dorchester. The butchers have taken offence because Mr. Homer, with other farmers in the district, took it upon themselves during the recent severe depres- sion to slaughter their own stock and sell it to the resi- dents of the districts where they are living. This is looked upon by the butchers as an.interference with their business, and they are showing their resentment by resolutely declining to purchase any of Mr. Homer's stock when offered for sale. In consequence of this step Mr. Homer is now slaughtering large quantities of both cattle and sheep—the experiments being very encourag- ing

-ADULTERATION.— TRH EXPERIENCE OF THREE FURS.— A very telling story, illustrative of the generality of adulteration, is told in the lowa Dairy and Farm Journal. Three house flies, travelling in company, found their way into a certain dining-room. On looking round they espied sitting upon the table the sugar bowl, the cream pitcher, and a plate of fly poison. The first fly rushed for the sugar bowl, and after eating for a moment, fell into a spasm and died from the effects of the alum and nitric acid contained in the sugar.- The second fly began to sip from the cream pitcher. It, too, soon died from contraction of the stomach, caused by the lime- water in the milk. The other fly, in despair at the death of its fellows, concluded that the sooner it died the sooner it would be at rest, so it took to the plate of poison, but that, too, was so adulterated that it not only did not die, but lived and grew fat fat in eating it,

THE FRONT GAHDEN.—WaIk Edgings: Thrift (Armoria Vulgaris) should be ml)re extensively used for this pur- pose, as it gives so little trouble, and its very beautiful rose or red-coloured flowers, whichever is selected, is another recommendation. There are also tolerably good white and pole lilac varieties. Assuming that the ground has been prepared as previously directed, planting will be only a simple matter. After the line is laid down, the ground should be cut away from it about four inches deep to receive the plants. For this purpose it is neces- sary to procure a few clumps and pull them in small pieces and lay them against the cut part, and place soil al the same time over their roots ;to prevent thew, moving and, before placing the remainder of the soil over the roots, it is as well to perform the whole of the work, when the operator will be better able to detect any faults which at that stage, may be easily rectified, and one most likely will be that of having some plants higher than others. In finishing placing the soil, it should be slighly beaten with the back of the spade and left sloping slightly from the plants, so as to give them soil to grow in, on the walk side of which they would have but little if left perpendicular. THE GRHEINHOUSIL—The fall of snow reminded us of the dangers the cottager's greenhouse is subject to when it suddenly thaws and the snow from roofs of adjoining buildings slides in frozen masses on to the greenhouse. At such times it is advisable to provide some protection for the glass, such as a few thin boards laid on the top, with spaces between to admit light. Snow should at all times be quickly moved from the roofs of green- houses, so as to admit light and prevent drip, which is most undesirable for plants at all times, and more es- pecially when the water is nearly at freezing point. The first to suffer ill this way are the Chinese Primulas, and not only will the flowers decay in a few hours, but the whole plant is liable to go off almost as suddenly. They fare better if elevated on a shelf near the glass where there is a constant current of air passing over them, to dry up the moisture. These, with Cyclamens and Cine- rarias, are the only plants the cottager can expect to have in 'flower at this season of the year. The latter, unlike the Primula, delights in a cool, moist atmosphere, and should be placed in that part of the house most likely to supply these conditions.

All men are prophets in their own country; and M. Meissonier, the great French artist, is no exception to the rule. Once, when his little granddaughter had re- ceived a beautiful white satin fan, he offered to paint a little picture on it. The ten year old maiden was highly indignait. "I am inclined to think .you won't do any such thing, grandpa!" she exclaimed. "I don't want my nice fan dirtied with your old paints." " ThuS," said the great artist, "the child has scorned what an empress would have prized. Which is right, I wonder— the child or the empress r_

hadno' bin used to weetin' her fingers for owt beside weshin' her face, so by th' week end ther as mony dirty pots lee abeaut as would ha' filled a wheelbarrow. Th' honeymoon (trayele moon, I co it) wur getten i'th' last quarter, an' a very thin bit, too, it war. It tad soon be dark o'th' moon th' rate it war gooin' on at. Hoo gan cant her weshin'. Bake hoo coaldnno', an' when hoo should ha' mended th' husbant's shirt, hoo gan it to th' ragmon, an' said it wurno' fit for wearin' any langer. Hoo turned cant to be as big a sloven as ever "Black Sam's" wife war, an' no dog i' Hazelwo'th would ha' passed her beaut givin' her a shake, as if it had mistakken her for a mop. Hoo sowd her rings for gin, if he'd let her ha' no brass' ad' hoo' sluthert abeaut in a pair o' clogs made eaut o' top-boots, aa' wi' a yead as roogh as a haycock, an' her clams same as if they'd bin tossed on her back wi' a pikel (pitchfork). Th' other side o'th' bargain wur as Isaiah gone i'th' vaeaut (moult) as hoo wur; an' neaw ther isno' sich a pair o' carnboggarts o ' Hazelwo'th as they are. Th' jackass met ha' known ut a woman ut wur aulus donned up, an' did aowt nobbut read po'try an' books abeaut young lads an' wenches runnin' off wi' one another gettin' wed, ud never do for a wife for him. Hoo wanted throe or four sarvants, an' a carriage, an' someb'dy t' dondle abeaut her, an' tak her to th' play-heause, an' Kersey Moor races, an' doancin' shops; an' then for t' be a little poorly toard midsummer, so ut hoo could go to th' saeside, an' strollop abeaut theere for a month or two, as If folk now-a-days conldno' go on beaut bein' blown a bit wi' Owd Daf Jones's ballis. Hoo'd popt into th' wrung shop; an' when a woman find's it cant ut boo's made a mistake o' that sort, it's wo-up wi' her, an' thoose abeaut her, too, for as atich o' this life as they han to live t'gether. If hoo' s bin aimin' at fiyin' o' her young days, an' has never bin able to raise her feet off th' greaund, an' neaw, PAH gettin' a lift, gate a seause—boo tumbles i'th' gutter, an' tarries theere till boo's ready for cartin' off to th' church- yard. Hoe's bin as big a too' as anybody. Get th' tongs, ac' lift 'em boo4th off th' table. If ther are women-,mad too's, there are foo's quite o'th' tother side hedge—foo's at believen if a mon spices to a woman, it's same as puttin' his foot in a rotten-trap, or his neck in a noose—he's to be hobshackled for life. These beleng to th' clever sort o' yorneys, an' a pretty kittle on' 'ens ther is, as far as my exparience take me. I con tell one as soon as ever I clap my e'en on him. If he's a young un, ut hasno' gang o'er bein' marred wi' his mother, he'll ha' plenty o' brass in his pocket, an' isno' partikilar abeaut folk knowin' it. He walks abeaut by hissel o'th' edge o' dark; an' if he yors a pair.' }amens beheend him, or seeds a red cloak afore him, he looks abeaut for a gap et he con dart through, an' get cant o'th' road. Whenever yo' meetia' him he'll be sure to have his bonds in his pockets, an' owder he gets an' deeper he thrutches 'em. He'll be walkin' abeaut th' rate ov a snail ut's ta'en to crutches, an' mooastly wi' his chin nar his clogs than it should be for a chicken. If he says owt, he's sure to talk aheaut things ut are no' nil' common way; an' he'll bother yo' as ill as a boat-hose wi' some eranklety notion ut 's bin hatchia.' in his yead for happen a hay-time or two. It's seldom he puts his best clooas on ov a Sunday, 4o ut he'll groo owd i'th' same hat, an' same cooat ut he had male when his great grommother war buried. Yo' may know him when he's getten into years by that, for he'll look like an owd brid P young fithers. Bat this foo' never gets owd in his own e'en. He fixes upo' a hobbyhoss when he's in his yard-wide days. or what " Owd-Pee" would co th' beginnin' ov his puppyhood, an' rides it till he con howd no !anger. He'll happen keep pigeons, or hens, or ducks, or dogs, or brids=an' it's a wonder to him I:maw anybody 'll gie these up for th' sake ov a woman. His rnother praises him for- bein' th' beat lad o' England, an' I da'say wi' some reeason, for, though a foo' he may no' be th' wo'st son ever marred, an' a mother 'll soon put th' tother to. He eonno' go wrung for her chase what he does, if he'll keep hissel to hissel. Hoo aulus has his shirt th' whitest ov anybody's, an' keeps him o'th' hearthstone as snug as an owd tabby cat, till he's fit for bein' nowheere else. But when boo's gone, an' he ands a twe-thri gray yourss in his whiskers, an' a dry gutter or two abeaut his een, an' his sisters han o getten wed, an' ther's nob'dy nobbut him an' his feyther laft, ho begins o' lookin' sicha pictur' o' misery as eouno' be loikened to nowt ut goes upo' two legs. Ther one o' these lives i' eau: fowt now, ut we coat "Slogger," an' he's fairly a seet to be seen. He's as ragged an as ever owd " Mungo " wur, an' so bad tempered tat, if tie childer meeten him anywheer they scuttern away, like a. lot o' chickens when ther's a dog abeaut. He's aalus lived unuer th' same thatch, an' he doesno' know ut he could live under any other. It's th' thatch ut his feyther an' mother ' dee'd under, an' sin' then he's lived theer by hisser. Twenty year sin' (heaw time slips o'er!) he're quite a swipper young chap. Nowt very grand abeaut him; but he're aulus cleean, an' his clooas, if they wurno' as fine as some folk's, wur kept good fettle. But he set so lest o' women tat I felt sure he'd never be wed as lunges he lived, an' so far I've been a fortin-teller. (If any woman nd have him neaw, hoo'd no' be ov a very partikilar sort). When I towd him I're gooin' t' be wed, he used o sorts o' gam o' me, an kept, shakin' a leg at me, for t' let me see it wur lose, an showm me a hontful o' brass, an' sayin' I should never be plagued wi' havin' holes i' my pockets when a wife had getten howd on me.

Well, I geet wed, like a foo', as Slogger thowt, an' in a while after, ther a young "Ab " chipped his shell, an' chellupt i'th' kayther (cradle) like a young throetle ut's ne'er tried it's wings. Eaur "Joe" followed, an' then eaur "Dick" said it wur is turn ; an' ever sin' then th' kayther has hardly ever gan o'er rockin'. We geet as throng as a little skoo, au' welly as noisy. Every year we had to buy a new porritch dish, an' every time it had to be a size bigger. It war hard scr,ettia' for 'sal, I con tell yo'; wi' wark chop, an' atin-stuff dear. But when Seturday fleet coom, an' we'd raised a bakin', th' heause looked as brisk as a wakes. Th' ckilder would ha' bin 'amain' abeaut wi' a mouffin apiece, th' size ov a trencher—beawlin"em across th' floor, ate stiskin' her angers through th' middle, an' makkin pin- wheels an 'em.

Slogger would ha' come in Hi' thrung ov o this, an' at me if I could do wi' a a week's fuddle, or a rant absaut th' country. He knew emir Sal ad fly at him like a cat; but he did it for t' plague me with, as he thowt, an' he'd a run grinnin' eaut o'th' heause, an' when he'd getten to dur, he'd ha' rickled a hontful o' braes, for t' show heaw mich better off he wur than me. Well, at th' same time Pro as content as a king—if ever a king is content—as poor as I wur ; an' I duuno think ther ever a crust fund th' road eaut o' eaur heause but war grip- pen as tight as a hommer as lung as it lasted. It wur gradely spooart when flyin'-up time coom—weshin' th' childer—eaur Sal one mug an' me another—pooin"em cant o' ther bits o' clooas like skinnin' meaudiwarts—an' lettin' 'em do a bit o' natur' reannd th' heause a time or two afore they went into th mug. " Owd Ryder races" war nowt at th' side o' these. Off they'd goo--eaur Jib th' fast, an' th' tothers after him, alopin' deawn like a pair o' stairs, till it coom to th' leeast, ut could hardly stride o'er th' nick ov a flag. Slogger used to say I'd getten mysel' in a nice mesa; but when he see'd what fun we'rn havin', an' heaw eaur Sal's face shoint as hoo watched her bits o' chickens flusterin' an toddlin' abeaut her, he'd ha' bitten his lip, an' gone straight an' getten drunken. •

IC Sett:ll.day neet wur a grand time, so wur Sunday mornin'. Every youngster had a carrit apiece saved for him, an' that ut geet up th' fast had th' biggest. As soon as dayleet had oppent it's e'en, ther'd ha' bin Bich tumblin' deawn th' stairs as yo' never yerd, for o th' lot on 'em ud ha' bin as wakken as hummabees--ewarmin after th' carrits. Th' youngest ud ha' gone, too. I could ha' yerd it bumpin' npo' th' steps for abeaut ten minutes after th' tothers had londed; an' when I'd getten ud mysel', I could ha' fund it croodlin' upo' th' hearthstone, an' wrostlin' a carrit th' size ov a leg—as happy as a young bird ut's just fund th' use ov its wings. If Slogger had seen that pictur', he'd ha' wanted th' strait jacket soon after. Well, things" Wl' me kept gettin' brisker every year. I'd summat else to do than fret abeaut bare livin' an' hard scrattin' ; so eaur Sal an' me sung an' wortched, an' wortched an' sung, till time flew past as if it wur runnin' a raca. Wi' Slogger it wur different. He began o' mopin' abeaut like a hen i'th' meant, an' his clone wur gettin' sadly too big for him. If anybody had spoken to him, he'd ha' set his teeth, as if for bithe, an' he'd ha' growlt like a bear wi' a sore ear. He wur seldom seen eaut o'th' heanse, an' one week we thowt we'd missed him o together. I began o' feelin unyeasy abeaut him, tbinkin' summat had I happened him, till one neat, as we'rn havin' a blow cant o' blackpullin's an' breawis, he oppent tit' dur an' walked in. He wanted to know if I could spare him a spoon, for his feyther had cleared th' buttery o' what bit ther wur in it, an' that wurno' mich. I could 'see he looked very slack abeaut th' waistcoat, so I towd him for t' sit him deawn at th' table, an' delve in amung th' rook. He did so, an' played a good stick at what ther wur, an' when he'd finished, he shaked his yead, an' said—" Ab, theau'rt noane sich a foo' as I took thee t' be. It's me ut's bin th' foo." Tak' him off the table gently—poor leatheryead !—Ben Brierley.

CONSTAIs-TINOPLE, SAT-lIRDAY.—The Porte has given much censideration this week to the attitude of Gleece, and it is believed that a Turkish ironclad squadron will he orderect to cruise in the neghbeurheoci of Prevesa and Salonica. Sup' Plies of war meterial continue to arrive at Salonica arid pedegatch. The relations between Prince Alexander and the Porte are not of a satisfactory character. Sir William White continues to counsel the Porte to come to an understanding with Bulgaria, and is stated to have represented that Russia would have no objection to a direct understanding between the Sultan and Prince Alexander. ATHENS. SUNDAY.—Yesterday Sir Horace umbold, the English Minister, informed M. Delyannis th t the British Government was prepared to send a fleet into Greek waters Should the Hellenic Government persist in its refusal to Ttiey t lierskrlninyorder to prevent the poesibility of an attack upon sea. M. .Delyanais replied to-day, stating that the Government declined to give way. The Greek fleet put 10 sea sea at daybreak with sealed orders. Its destination is unknown. Tsanoff, the Bulgarian atinister for Foreign Affairs, Fife making favourable pro- gress. Intelligence has been received -here that three Greek vessels have left for Crete. Viamea, MONDA.Y.—AS I am informed, the action of the British Government was taken without concert with any of the Powers except Germany. All the Powers have been seUnded as to their willingness to undertake a naval demon- • Stration against Greece, but France held back. M. de Frey- einet even thought it seemly to choose this moment for ex- decorations with M. Delyannis. The latter sent the Grand Cross of the Redeemer to the Minister of the Re- • llilblic, and M. Freycinet repaid the compliment by getting M. Delyannis appointed Grand Cross of the Legion of Hen- Our. Meanwhile intelligence reached the. British Govern- ' re ent that the Cabinet of Athens, in view of a naval war with Turkey, intended to issue letters of marque to priva- teers and this rendered some immediate action necessary, arld Greece had been allowed to issue commissions te count- i ' :ess naval adventures.' The shipping of every country hay- , tng trade in the East would have suffered heavily. and Eng- -- shipping of course most of all.—Times. BERLIN. MONDA.Y.—The semi-offiial North German wtzette says that the action of England with regard to Greece ' Must be vigorously supported. Germany and the other ._Great Powers, it ;ads, could not suffer the peace of Europe '0 be placed in jeopardy by the fire-brand policy of one of the smallest States. BELGRADE, MUNDAY.—An order of the Minister of War directs that only the cadres of the different regiments of • the reserves are to join the colours, the me being kept in readiness to march with three days' provisions. This delay ' ja the eeneral mobilisation of the army is due to diplomatic representations. Transyneera., Mosna.Y.—Of 2,000 hones ordered for the Army • port Service. 550 have been shipped during the pre- ,,.t week. Fifteen hundred reserve men have also been re- sent in small detachments to Salonica. CONcTANTINOP, E' .NIONDA.Y.—The Great Powers have In- form Servia that the negotiations for the conclusion of Peace exclusively concern Bulgaria, and have nothing to do With the Eastern Roumelian question. SERVIA. AND GREECE. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY.—The understanding between M. Delyannis and the Servian Government determining the LesPective interests of Greece and Servia was arrived at a Year ago, but its terms have only now transpired. They Provide for a considerable extension ef the Greek frontier to the north, whereby the line starting from Melnik would pro- Zeed in a south-westerley direction so as to include Nosere- "el) and Strumnitoa to Bit:Aia, proceeding from the latter MR. GLADSTONE AND THE GREEK QUESTION. The following is the translation of a telegram received - by Mr. Gladstone from Athens:— "The people of Athens are full of their recollections of Vtl,and of confidence in the noble sentiments which you We always expressed in defence of the liberties of nations. We therefore place in your hands the Hellenic . Cause, with the firm hope that it will find in you a generous champion." The following is Mr. Gladstone's reply : „ "To the Dernarch of Athens,—l have had the honour to receive your appeal. and I now answer it as one profoundly anxious for the welfare of the Hellenic race as well as for the peace of the East. Considering the authority which at- taches to the action of the Powers both on general grounds, and by reason of the intervention in the formation of the .Greek Kingdom, and at various periods in the concerns of use Ottoman Empire, and especially of the Balkan Penin- : 804, I earnestly hope that Greece will pause before placing herself on this occasion in conflict with their deliberate and Ilrlited recommendation. (Signed) Jtnuary 26th." SUBaIISSION OF GREECE TO THE POWERS.
W. E. GLADSTONE."

- THIIRSDAY.-9. telegram published here from Athens, of to-day's date, sates that a sudden change appears IP., have supervened yesterday evening in the views of the "rreek Cabinet. The Ministers are represented to have de- that Greece will defer to the wishes of Europe. ENGLAND AND BURMAIL CALCUTTA, SIINDA.Y.—The disturbances in Lower Eurmah are being gradually suppressed, and the main bodies of Shans 4nd dacoits seem to have broken up, although some small Potties remain vich are being actively followed. Namer- '3llB arrests have been made. The native Burmese officials tild Policemen, with few exceptions, have shown a decided want of courage and capacity .during the recent troubles, many Persons knowing Burmah will assert that these , otibles were largely due to Mr. Bernard's system of plac- ing yoxng incompetent natives in pssitions of great trust and responsibility. THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY COMMISSION.

VIE-res-A,-11-lON-D-tY.—According to a telegram received here trom St. Petersburg the Afghan Boundary Commission have eft) compelled to suspend their operations in consequence of an expected rising of Kara Turcomans. THE BRITISH FORCE IN EGYPT. - -

.--T-liIIRSDA.Y.-Sir Charles Warren arrived here to-day and proceeded to Cairo. The let battalion of the Dublin Fusiliers has received orders to embark for Kingstown at the beginning of nest month. FRANCE.

PARIS, MONDAY.—The Chamber of Deputies to-day re- solved to postpone the discussion of a bill, the effect of Which woulc: be to exclude fortAgn workmen from markets controlled by the State. M. Debarly, deputy for the l‘lcrcl pointed out that the proposal raised grave economic luestions, and tended to interfere with the freedom of la- bour.
GREAT FIRE IN SPAIN.

MADRID, SEND AS.—A great fire occurred to-night in the Roods sheds adjoining the Northern Railway Station, the 3beds and storehouses, with a large quantity of property and Leveral trucks and vans, being burnt. The cause of the fire unknown. URNING OF A POOR-HOUSE IN AMERICA.— FORTY PEOPLE ROASTED TO DEATH. The fire 11011 e. out in the kitchen, and the whele of the interior of , "" building was quickly destroyed. No fire-extinguishing ,4Ppliances were available, and the reservoirs were empty. I,4au Poor-house was situate at about six miles from the `" ,wri Forty of the. inmates, five of them insane, blind, or 'tear and dumb pauper,,, were literally roasted to death. The ethers rushed out half naked in the snow, and several, it is feared, will die from the effects of the exposure. The sur- -7boors have been brouzlit into Jackson, where they will he properly cared for: RUSSIA IN ASIA. ST.
