1 HuUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY. The L Ch:neellor toek his seat shortly after 4-0. Sevel al oeers te,k the (Atli and subscribed the roll. THE IRISH VICEROYALTY. Lord KII•431 /REY moved, “ That, in the opinion of this House, the time has now ceme Iwhen the post of Lord Lieutenant of Ireland may be alp- liabed." He wished to have in Ireland, instead of a Vice- roy, a Royal Prince, and rec)mmencled that the Duke of ' Concaught should be sent over to take up his residence in the country, so that the Irish people might have a Prince whom they could call their own.—Lord COWPER, having tilled the office of Lord Lieutenant, was desirous of express- ing his concurrence in the motion.—Lord HOWTH supported the motion.—Lord FourrEscrE was-in favour of abolishing the Viceroyalty ; but Lord FITZGERALD thought the tines was not opportune for the proposition before the House.— Lord SALISBURY agreed with Lord Fitzgerald. lie regarded the Vicero,alty as a survival. The arguments in favour of the motion were not so overwhelming that the Government could accede to it without a dereliction of their duty.—Lord KIMBERLEY, while on the whole in favour of the abolition of the Viceroyalty, pointed out that there were difficulties of arrangement which would have to be provided for.—The motion was withdrawn. LEGISLATION FOR IRELAND.—Lord WATENEY moved— " That the Ministerial plan of the government of Ireland be introduced forthwith and tike precedence of all public business up to report."—The Marquis of SALISBURY said the Government would shortly be able to make an announce- ment to Parliament, and to explain the steps they intended to take to remedy the terrible and scandalous state of things. (Hear, hear.) He hoped they would be able to do this in 24 or 48 hours.—The Earl of KIMBERLEY was lost in astonishment, at their method, and could only suggest that they had been able to gain information by a species of second sight on the part of Mr. Smith after 48 hours' resi- dence in Ireland.—The motion was then withdrawn. LAND REGISTRATION.—The LORD CHANCELLOR intro- duced the Land Registry Bill, which was read a first time. Their lordships adjourned at 1-10. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. _ _ _

1 _ _ i The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. THE 'NATIONAL LEA.GrE. Sir Ti. Tyler gave notice, as 1 t an amendment to the Address, to move—" Humbly to repre- sent to her Majesty that, in the opinion of this House the ; condition of Ireland, as appears from the statement of her Majesty's Ministers, and from other concurrent testimony, !requires immediate action, and that this House is prepared to assure her Majesty's Government of its support in pro- claiming the National League—(ironical Irish cheers)—and in bringing forward such measures as may appear to them to be necessary for the true interests of Ireland for the pro- tection of life and liberty against terrorisna and kiycotting, and aenerally for the restoration of law and order in that country." (Ironical cheers.) THE limn LAND QuEsrtotr.—Mr. JACKSON, in replying to Mr. Marorn, said it was his intention to move, on behalf of the Government, for leave to bring in a bill to consolidate and amend the Acts for facilitating the improvement of landed property in Ireland. ITALIAN SHIPPING.—Mr. STANTIOPE, at the instance of Mr. Tomlinson, offered to produce a translation of the Act lately passed by the Parliament of Italy giving a bounty to Italian ships. MARTIAL LA.77 IN BIIRMA.II.—In reply to Sir G. Camp- bell, Mr. 0. Morgan, and others, Lord RA.NDOLPH CHURCH- -1 ILL gave some explanations about the administration of ) civil and military jurisdiction in Upper Burma. ENGLAND AND GREECE.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN asked what truth there was in the statement that the threat of a naval demonstration by England had been addressed to GTeece, and Mr. BotraKE replied that, at the instance of her Majes- ty's Government, the six Powars had presented a Collective Note to Grcece informing her that a naval attack on Tar- kep would not b., permitted. THE AD DRESS.—BU amAH.

Mr. Hr-N-rEn moved an amendment expressing regret that the revenues of India have been applied to defray the expenses of the military operations in Burmah without the. consent of Parliament, as required by the Government of India Act, 15S Mr. CONYBEARE seconded the amendment. The ATTORNEY.GENERAL denied Mr. Hunter's view of the statute, and maintained that its proviAons'would be fulfilled if the assent of Parliament were subsflucntly given. Mr. GLADSTONE, while complimenting the mover of the amendment, deprecated a division on it, as the House was not at present in a position to form any judgement, and a more favourable opportunity would occur when Lord R. Churchill came to move the statutory r,solution sanctioning the expenditure out of the Indian revenue. If the Minister then showed that there was a sudden and urgent necessity, be need not fall back on the high doctrine of the Attorney- Gm.-.eral, from which he personally entirely differed, con- tending that the object of the statute was to secure the prior control of Parliament. (Hear, hear.) Lord R. CHURCHILL remarked that Mr. Hunter could not have sufficiently studied the Burmah Blue Book, and en- dorsed the Attorney-General's interpretation of the Govern- ment of India Act, which, he contended, had not been viola- ted. He denied that ttie course taken by the Government deprived the House of Commons of all control over the em- ployment of Indian troops. Even now it was within the power of the House, if it thought fit, to replace King Thee- baw on the throne of Bunnah. At the same time he pointed out that it had always been customary to seek the sanction of Parliament for the employment of Indian troops out of India after such employment had been determined upon and the initial expense incurred, and he denied that it was es- sential to apply for such sanction before the troops were employed. Mr. Hunter then withdrew his amendment. THE DEPRESSION IN AGRICULTURE.

Mr. BARCLAY moved an amendment representing "the pressing necessity for securing without delay to the cultiva- tors of the soil such conditions of tenure as will aid and en- courage them to meet the new and trying circumstances in which the agriculture of the country is placed." After alluding to the great depression of the agricultural industry, he pointed out that the British farmer was fettered with all sorte of conditions as regarded the growing of crops, and that if he developed the resources of the soil he had no real security for the capital he invested. The hon. gentle- man thaneed the Tory party for their action in familiarising the agricultural labourers with the idea of the possession of three acres and a cow, assured them that it dil not seem so absurd to the labourers as it did to hon. gentlemen op- posite. Sir GEORGE BALFOUR formally seconded the amend- ment. Mr. STEWART contended that it was unfair to taunt the landlords with taking as much out ef the land as they could get, and maintained that the question could be settled by hard and fast rules. Colenel BROOKFIELD advocated a revision of the system of local taxation as a means of remedying the present de- pression of agriculture; and Lord GRIMESTONE, having pointed out the inutility of leases. disapproved of special legislation for landlords and tenants, who, with the labour- ers, he contended, must stand or fall together. Mr. J. ELeas, speaking also for the first time, informed the House that at one time he wag a tenant farmer for four- teen years under a yearly tenancy, and that at the end of that time he received six months' notice to quit, improvements of the value of £BOO or £l,OOO being con- fiscated. Sir G. Balfour and Mr. Esslemont having joined in the discuesion. The LORD ADVOCATE twitted the Opposition with having boycotted the commission appointed last session to ascertain the causes of trade depression. Mr. DUCKRATI criticised the Agricultural HolAiugs Act, and called for further security to the tenant for capital and freedom of cultivation.—After some further discussion, Mr. KIMIER made some observations, and moved the adjourn- ment of the debate.—The House was cleared for a division, hut when the question was put a second time there were no " Ayes' " and the motion was negatived.—At 12-30 the House divided, with the following result For Mr. Barclay's Amendment 173 Against

Majority for the Government ... 28 The announcement was received with Ministerial cheers. —Mr. JESSE COLLINGS moved the adjournment of the de- bate, and the motion was aFreed to. MISCELLANEOrS.—Dr. Cameron obtained leave to bring in a bill amending the law relating to the vacating of seats in the House of Commons; and Mr. King a bill to amend the Merchant Shipping Act, 1854. These bills were intro- duced and read a first time. The House adjourned at 12.45. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIJESDAY. The House met at 4-15. Lord Elphinstone, introduced by the Earl of Kintore and Lord Colville of Culrosse took the oath and sub- scribed the roll on his elevation to the peerage of the Unite.d Kingdom. LAND REGISTRATION —The LORD CHANCELLOR moved the second reading of the Land Registry Bill, and explained that its purpose was to make temporary provision for the discharge of the duties of chief registrar, which office was now vacant owinK to the death of Mr. Spencer Fellitt. Considering the dissatisfaction with the amount of business and the public expenditure involved, it had neen thought inexpedient to fill the office until Parliament had had an opportunity of dealing with the whole subject. The ques- tion of land transfer would, he hoped, shortly be brought before their Lordehips.—The second reading was agreed to. The committee stage was negatived, and, the Standing Orders having been suspended, the bill was read a third time and passed. On the motion of the Marquis of SAusnrnY, the Hosse adjourned at 4-35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TrESDAY.
The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. Several new members took the oath and their seats. EXCITEMENT IN THE HOUSE. _

_ Upon the assembling of the House f Commons there were unmistakeable signs of an expectation of some impor- tant Ministerial statement. The demand for seats WrIS large, and the gallery of the Peels was unusually crowded. At the close of an extremely brief sitting of the House of Lords the Lord Chancellor himself sought a place in that already well-filled gallery, and the late Lord Lieutenant of Ireland was also semi on the verge of the obviously expectant crowd. A dispute concerning the composition of the Com- mittee of Selection, and a long list of notices, delayed the intimation for which their Lordships were waiting, but presently the explosion came. The Chancellor of the Exchequer rose immediately before questions, and, reading from a paper in his hand, gave notice, on bekalf of the Chief

Secretary for Ireland, of a Bill to be introduced on Thurs- day next for the purpose of "suppressing the National League and other dangerous associations." This annoence ment evoaei vociferous cheers from the afinisterial 'amches. in tho intervals of which mockintr lauehter and ironic 41 counter cheers from the Parnellites were heard. Some cries of "Shame!" were also audible amid the din. This demonstration over, the Chancellor of the Exchequer was able to continue the statement of the object of nis measure,l which he described as being also "for the prevention of in- timidation, and for the protection of life, property, and public order in Ireland." There was a renewal of laughter among the Parnellites, followed by Ministerial cheers, at the further intimation that if the debate on the Address were not tnen concluded, the postponement of that order of the day would be moved on Thursday to allow Mr. Smith to move for leave to bring in his Bill. Similar demonstra- tions greeted the deciarations that precedence would be asked for the new coercive measure on every day for which it might be put down, and that the bill would be followed by a project lor dealing with the land question, following " in a more extensive sense" the policy of the Land Purchase Act of last session. The excitement occasioned by these notices threw somewhat into the shade other subjects of in- terest which were touched upon in the coestions ; but it was noted that the Leader. of the House declined further to meddle with Mr. Bradlaugh at present, and that Mr. Bourke met Mr. Chamberlain's interrogation regarding Greece with a curiously and ambiguously worded disavowal. At the end of the questions on the paper, Mr. Chamberlain returned to the charge with a carefully prepared inquiry, designed to I ascertain positively whether there had been no conditional threat to send the British fleet into Greek waters. Mr. Bourke again pleaded that to answer a question of such im- portance notice must be given him. Mr. Chamberlain re- newed the notice, but added that in consequence of the un- satisfactory nature of the answers he had received, he would call attention to the subject on the Report of the Address. if the House ever got to that stage. Mr. Mitchell Henry revived an old grievance. He accused his fellow members of bringing down bats that were not their own, or at all events not their wearing hats, and placing them on the benches to secure seats. " Even wideawakes' "he declared, were need for this unhallowed purpose. He prayed the Speaker for some authoritative ruling on this vexed sub- ject. It was thereupon gravely laid down from the Chair that the seat-securing head-dress must "undoubtedly be the bona fide ordinary hat in daily use," and that its owner must be in the precincts of the House. The Speaker coun- selled the settlement of this matter by the courteous con- sideration of one member for another, but hinted that if necessary recourse might be had to a standing order prevent- ing the appropriation of any seat before the hour of prayers. Mr. Woodall having received from the Chancellor of the Exchequer an assurance that the debate on the Ad- dress would not be proceeded with to-day in view of the hon. member's wish to proceed with his Woman's Suffrage Bill, some question arose as to the date of resumption of the business at present before the House. In this the Par- nellites became warmly interested. Opportunity for protest being given upon the formal motion for giving the debate precedence of the ordinary Tuesday night's motions Mr. Parnell was ready with an amendment that precedence should be at once taken for all days on which it was set down. He accused Ministers of seeking by various strata- gems to avoid discussing the interests of land tenants, and likened them to drowning men clutching straws. In the course of the conversation much amusement WAS occasioned by the premature appearance in the speech of Mr. Finch- Hatton of the probable election-cry of the "integrity of the Empire." Sir Michael Hicks-Beach repudiated any desire to stave off agricultural questions, but insisted on the necessity of proceeding without delay to the eon- I sideratien of the measures reluctantly resolved upon by the Government. On sugestions from the front Opposition bench the immediate question at issue was decided by Mr. Parnell withdrawing his amendment in favour of a pro- posal simply giving precedence for the debate on the Ad- dress. This arrangement, facilitated by Mr. Wood-all's relinquishment of his hope of taking his Bil next day, was only arrived at on the nodded as- sent of the Chancellor of the Exchequer and Lord R. Churchill to Mr. Parnell's stipulation that a division on Mr. Collings's amendment should take place at that sitting.
DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.
DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.

It was nearly seven o'clock before Mr. Collings intro- duced his amendment to the Address by the insertion of the following words, "hut this House humbly expresses its re- gret that no measures are announced by Her Majesty for the present relief of these classes, and especially for affording facilities to the agricultural labourers and others in the rural districts to obtain allotments and small holdings on equitable terms as to rent and security of tenure." Mr. Cnaplin recognised this amendment as practically a motion of censure, offered to the House with the voice of Jesse, though the band was the hand of Joseph. He declared the willingness of the Government to encourage and facilitate , the extension of allotments, and pointed to the proposed measure respecting glebe lands as likely to result in benefits to the labourers. The Government, however, were opposed to sanctioning purchase of lands by compulsion. He warned those who intended to vote against the Ministers to prepare for the enjoyment of the heritage the Government had re- ceived from their predecessors, and had only retained so long from a sense of duty. Mr. Gladstone, rising in the dinner hour and addressieg a House, which notwithstanding the hour of the evening rapidly filled, opened with ironical comment en the strain of the Chancellor of the Duchy's peroration, and presumed that members of that House were always prepared to take the consequences of their votes. Dealing with the general matter of Mr. Chaplin's speech, he said that to speak of dealing with glebe lands as a general remedy for the condition of the agricultural labourer was preposterous. If Mr. Colling's proposition was socialism, it was socialism of a very old date, as proved by an existing , Act of Parliament. As to compulsion for public objects, it was recognised already in principle; and he would not con- sent to shut it out from consideration should that become necessary. The case of his hon. friend had been stated with moderation and fairness, and be hoped his motion would be carried by a vast majority. Later in the evening Mr Joseph Arch made his maiden speech, eloquently advo- cating the claim of the labourer to be restored to the land. "We do not ask the land to be given us," he says,' and we have no desire to steal it. But I ask you whether you do I not think the time has come when thousands of industrious and willing workers should no longer be shut out from the soil." Between ten and eleven o'clock Mr. Goschen put the Ministerialists into the highest spirits by a speech of vigor- ous protest against the identification of the Liberal party with the amendment. He sarcastically congratulated Mr. Chamberlain on having apparently succeeded in transferring a serious item to "the unauthorised programme" to the "authorised programme" of the Liberal party. For him- self he protested that it was not possible for him to be con- verted in three days. Compulsory allotments appeared to him to be calculated to arrest spontaneous developments of the allotment system, and to involve local authorities in serious expenditure. He passionately maintained that the question was one upon which every member of the Liberal party was entitled to vote as he chose. Mr. Brad- laugh announced his intention to vote for the amendment. Mr. A. Balfour, while representing the true issue in this debate as, not allotments, but Ireland, declared that the Government had always intended to deal with the allot- ments question in their -local government scheme. Where- upon Mr. Chamberlain rose, and said that as Mr. Goschen congratulated him, he in turn respectfully condoled with the right hon. gentleman, who, after promising to vote for Ministers under the influence of disappointment with his own leader, had discovered, that the other side were also heretical upon this question. The Chancellor of the Ex- chequer followed to represent that the amendment was a party move to turn out the Government, the success of which would not only defeat Ministers, but the policy they believed it to be their duty to pursue with reference to Ireland. The debate was concluded by Lord Hertington, who, while dissociating himself from his friends in the sup- port of this amendment, indicated his desire to continue giv- ing the party his general support. The House divided at ten minutes to one, the Liberals, I with the eiception of Lord Hartingten, Mr. Goschen, and Mr. Courtney, apparently voting solid for Mr. Collings' amendment. A quarter of an hour later the clerk handed the tellers' report to Mr. Collings amid frantic cheers from I the Irish members. Cry was heard, " Don't forget coercion I on Thursday." The numbers were then declared— For Mr. Colling's amendment 329 Against

Majority against the Government 79 The appearance of the tellers at the table was greeted with loud cheers from the [ahem). and Irish benches, and on the announcement of the figures the cheers were renewed ' agaiti and again, and were answered with cheers from the Ministerial side. The CHANCELLOR of the ESCHEWER, who was loudly cheered from the benches behind him, then rose, a cry of " Boycott him" being heard from an Irish member. The right hon. baronet said : Mr. Speaker, of course, Sir. we I quite appreciate the nature of the vqte at which the House has arrived, and I think that, remembering the early hour at which the House vtould meet to-morrow, the proper chum will be for me to move that the House, at its rising, do adjourn till Thursday next. (Cheers, and an Irish member; excitedly, " Don't forget coercion on Thursday !") The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, rising again after a communication from the Speaker, said—l beg to move the adjournment of the debate en the Address. This having been agreea to, The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said—l am afraid, Sir, the fault was mine. I intended to move the immediate adjournment of the House. I now move that the House do adjourn till Thursday. ("No, no," from the Irish mem- bers.) Mr. HEALY hoped the right hon. gentleman the Chan- cellor of the Exchequer would not put them to the trouble of beating them again on this motion of adjournment. Mr. GLADSTONE : It appears to me that the course taken by the Chancellor of the Exchequer is in accordance with usage. (Hear. blear.) Wheuever her Majesty's Govern- ment consider a crisis has arisen which makes it desirable for them to examiee their position and their duty, it is the uniform custom of the House to suspend the immediate prosecution of business, and I think the adoption of any other course would probably lead to much confusion. (Hear, hear.) The motion for the adjournment of the House was then agreed to, at ten minutes past one o'clock, the Irish members as they took their departure indulging in cheers and cries of " Coercion." HOUSE OF LORDS.—TEmetspea. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock.

NEW BOOKS. Sze "Just the Very Thing for Newspaper Readers" Messrs. Diprose and Bateman, L eldon) is precisely what it purports to be. It is designed ro ine:it the wants of the reader of every-day news; telle all about the birth and growth of newspapers; their mottoes and their meanings; gives explanations of familiar phrases; and a long list of foreign phrases in general use, with the pronunciation. The volume, which is published at Is only, is exce.eclingly readable as well as informing. "Famous Centenarians " is a record issued by the same firm of " Two hundred persons who have lived to be 100 years and upwards!' It begins with Henry Jenkins, Who died in 1670 at the reputed age of 169 years, and comes down to centenarians who died last year. The work is from the pen of Mr. J, Redding Ware, and has been carefully compiled. The" Magnet Telegraph Code" is another useful little work from the press of Messrs. Bateman and Diprose. It is constructed for the use of business men who avail themselves largely of the sixpenny inland telegrams. The key is easily learned, and it is so comprehensive as to cover everything that relates to buying or selling. "Words of Wisdom," a new volume which is ad- vertised in another column, is admirable in its way. It is a collection of quotations from ancient and modern authors, along with proverbs of many.nations. The collection and compilation is the work of Mr. George Wilson, who formerly resided in Warrington, and was an occasional contributor to our colomns. The sayings are under numerous heads, such as " hope," "virtue," " reason," "nature ;" and there is besides-a copious index which makes reference very easy. As the work is beautifully printed and neatly , bound, it will form an excellent gift book. We con- gratulate Mr. Wilson on the capital way in which he has accomplished his task. A publication of somewhat similar kind, though on a much smaller scale, is issued by Messrs. Percy Lund and Co., of The County Press, Ilkley. It is entitled, "Wise Sayings," and contains a selection of short, pithy extracts from the writings of great men. These selections are left without the authors' names, and a prize of three guineas is offered to any one assigning correct authorship to the largest number of quotations. Messrs. Ward and Lock's Technical Journal and Industrial Self-instiuctor has reached part 15. It continues to ,be profusely, illustraied with full-page plates. The current issue contains articles of special interest to the sanitary architect, the steaw-engine user, the house planner, the grazier and cattle breeder, and there are technical facts and figures for every- body. Messrs. Cassell and Co. have commenced an extra- ordinary venture by the publication, weekly, of a series of reprints of good literature at the ridiculously low sum of threepence each. The first volume ia Lord Macaulay's "Warren Hasting," and comprises 192 pages of clear type on good paper. Cassell's National Library is the title of the series, which is being edited by Professor Henry Morley. The same firm are now in another way meeting the wants of the million by publishing in monthly parts (7cl) the Rev. Dr. Farrar's Life of Christ. This popu- lar edition of the celebrated work will be completed in ten parts. It is printed in clear type and on good paper, and is sure to have a large sale. Cassell's" Magazine of Art" for January is per- haps less conspicuous than usual for striking illustra- tions; but there is no lack of interest in the number. People in this part of the country'will turn to the illus- trated article in Chester. It makes one more than ever proud of the ancient city. 'rho views of interiors of Buckingham Palace are also very fine. Mr. J. R. Tait furnishes a sympathetic account of David Neal, , and there is too a portrait of the clever American artist. " The Romance of Art," is continued, and there is " Vlore about Abysinnia " • and a short but powerful paper on "The Art of Sketching." Following on Wordsworth, Longfellow, in two volumes, has been issued in the "Miniature Library of the Poets." Those who have commenced with these dainty shilling volumes by Messrs. Cassell are sure to keep on with them. " Little Folks" begins a neve series with the new year, It abounds in fresh features, among the best of which may be mentioned the four pages of pictures with the stories printed in large type for the especial benefit of very little folks. There is a bright new cover from a design by Alice Havers, and a pretty coloured frontispiece with the title of" The New Pet." "Cassell's Magazine" for January gets well into the new serial stories, "A Wilful Young Woman,' and "Lyndon of High Cliffe " ; and there are as usual several highly interesting complete tales, besides such illustrated papers as "London for Londoners," "The Impressions of a Noticing Eye," Sec. The "Family Doctor" diseourses on "Ailments one gets little pity for" ; and "The Gatherer" has plenty to offer. "The Quiver" commences the year well. Mr. George Weatherly contributes a poem, "White as , Snow," which is charmingly illustrated. "The Opening of the Year," by the late Dean of Chester, will be read with especial interest under the sad cir- cumstances of the dean's recent death. Dr. Blackio has an article on "How Some Northern Fishermen Built Their Houses " ; and there are other interesting papers by eminent writers. Cassell's "Gleanings From Popular Authors" pre. serves the good start it made. Selections, illustra- tions, and printing are all first-class. The complete series will make one of the most readable works it is possible to conceive. Part 24 closes the second vol- ume of "The Encyclopedic Dictionary" and leaves the reader, who cannot follow this work without hun- gering for more, in the midst of words beginning with "D."

We have also to hand, from Messrs. Cassell and Co., the current issues of the fine art edition of Longfel- low's works, Popular Gardening, the Book of Health, and British Battles on Land and Sea, by James Grant.

THE REPLY TO THE ADDRESS. The E.trl Of MOUNT- ! EDGCUMBE (Lord Steward of the Household): I am com- manded by the Queen to deliver to this House the gr..cioals answer which she has been pleased to send by me in re- sponse to the loyal Address unanimously pass,Kl by your Lordships ia acknowledgment of Her Majesty's Speech from the Throne. The message is as follows : "I thank you sincerely for your loyal and dutiful address. I rely with confidence upon your hearty co-operation and assist- ance in my endeavours to advance the best int.rests of my , empire, and promote the happiness and proeperity of •ell classes of my people." I have to move that this gracious Address of Her Majesty be printed and circulated among your lordships. t The motion was agreed to. THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS.—Lord CRANEROOK : My Lords, in the absence of my noble friend Lord Salisbury, I have to inform you Lordships that in consequence of what has happened elsewhere, communications have been made by Her Majesty's Government to Her Majesty, and Lord Salisbury has now gone down to Osb gne, and has requested me to move that this House adjourn until Monday. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty-five minutes afte four until Monday.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THURSDAY.
The SpeAker took the chair at four o'clock. There was a crowded attendance of nienabers.—Mr. Sid- ney Herbert, who was received with cheers, took the oath and his seat for Croydon.
NOTICES.—Lord William Compton gave notice of a bill to amend the Ground Game Act. Sir Julian Goldsmid gave notice of a bill to amend Vie law relating to the registration of lodgers.

PET—ITION.—Mr. GLADSTONE, who was received with £l. cheer, presented a petition from noblemen, justices of the pe.ice, and commissioners of stapply of the county of Edin- burgh, complaining of the charges of returning officers in Scotland not being registered as they were in England under the 68 and 39 Vic., chap. 84.

div.head: THE- MINISTERIAL CRISIS.
div.p: THE- MINISTERIAL CRISIS.

The CIANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, who was received with Ministerial cheers, rising at half-past four, said : I have to inform the House that in consequence of the vote at which this House arrived at on Tuesday, Her Majesty's Ministers deemed it their duty, at their meeting yesterday, to address a communication to Her Majesty, of the precise nature of which it is not at present proper for me to inform the House. As the result of that communication Lord Salis- bury has received Her Majesty's commands to attend at Osborne, and has gone there to-day. It is not possible for me at present to make any more definite announcement, and it is not likely to be possible for me to do so to- morrow, therefore I shall conclude with the motion that this House at its rising do adjourn till Monday. Of courpe under circumstances such as these it has been the invariable custom that ordinary business should not be proceeded with. It will be obvious to the House that we are not at present in a position either to be responsible in the conduct of that business, or to have any satisfactory or sufficient answers to questions that may be asked as to the views and intentions of the Government, and therefore, al- though this is a matter for the consideration and determina- tion of the House, yet if the House should accept the motion I have made I should also propose that the House should immediately adjourn. The motion for the adjournment of the House till Mon- day was agreed to, and the House at once adjourned.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF
div.p: WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF
COMMERCE.

The anual meeting of this Chamber was held at the office in Bewserstreet, on Monday. The president, Mr. Wm. Long, took the chair, and there were also present Messrs. Wm. Pierpoint, John 1 airolough, and the hon. secretaries, Alderman J. Davies and ...4. J. L. Tunstall. ' THE ANNUAL REPORT.—Mr. TUNSTA.LL read the ninth annual reportl of the Council, which was as follows : "Several important matters have engaged the attention of the Chamber during the past year 4 and the following sub- jects have had special attention :—Royal Commission on the Depression of Trade: Communicatioes were obtained from I several manufacturers and duly forwarded to the commis- sioners. Associated Chambers: The president and Mr. IBleckly attended the annual meeting in London. Congress of the Chambers of Commerce of the Empire (1886) : This Chamber has been invited to nominate a representative to attend the proposed congress. Liverpool Exhibition (1836) : Your council has jointly, with some exhibitors from War- rington, acted as a local committee, and will continue to promote the success of this exhibition and interests of the exhibitors from Warrington and the neighbourhood. Regis- tration of Telegraphic Addresses: A memorial has been sent Ito the Postmaster-General praying that the cost of regis- tered telegraphic addresses should be reduced from £1 is to ss, and his reply received, intimating that the matter is under consideration. Extension of Indian Railways: A communication has recently been sent to the Indian Secre- tary, urging the desirability of constructing a railway to the Siamese frontier, in order to extend British commerce in India and China. The annual statement of accounts showed a balance in hand of £l2 17s 10d.—The CHAIRMAN, in pro- posing the confirmation of the report and balance sheet, ex- pressed his regret that there was not a better attendance. He I supooeed that they might to some extent lay the blame upon the weather, but it seemed to him that the manufacturers of Warrington would find it very mach to their advantage if they would sutiport such an institetion as that, which, if it was not supported as it should be, could not accomplish the work that it was qualified to do. He did not know that there WAS much in the report calling for remark, but he might mention—it was not mentioned in the report—that 1 they had got a valuable addition to their working staff by Mr. Tunstall having accepted the joint secretaryship, with theittothor secretary (Alderman Davies), who had always done se well for the Chamber, and without whose help it would perhaps not have been now in existence. Inquiries had been issued by the Royal Commission into the depres- sion of trade which, through the medium of the Chamber, were circulated amongst manufacturers, but they were not very enthusiastically responded to. Such answers as were received were, he believed, sent up to London. It was not thought that the Chamber should take any further part than that of being the medium of communication. The Liverpool Exhibition was a matter in Which the Chamber i had taken an active interest, and one which it had brought as prominently as possible before the mannfacturer s of War- rington. They had every hope that the Warrington exhibits would be a credit to the town and they believed that the Liverpool promoters would be rewarded by a very interest- ing and lucrative exhibition.—Alderman DAVISS seconded the motion. The communications, he said, that were sent up from London with regard to the Royal Commission into the depression of trade were duly forwarded by the Chamber to the manufacturers. Those belonging to the wire trade formed themselves into a sort of local committee and for- warded their especial views to the commission. They had done considerable work in promoting the interests of local exhibitors at the forthcoming Liverpool Exhibition, and the council of the Chamber would be only too happy to con- tinue to do so and to forward the general interests of the exhibition, so that it might be beneficial to both Liverpool and the surrounding districts.—The proposition was then put and carried. ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COUNCIL.—The CHAIRMAN proposed that Mr. Frederick Monks be elected president for the ensuing year. This was seconded by Mr. W. PIER• POINT, and carried.—On the motlon of Alderman DAyfEs, seconded by the CHAIRMAN, and supported by Mr. W. PIERPOINT, Mr. John Fairclough was elected vice-president. —Mr. Dun was re-appointed hon. treasurer on the motion of Alderman DAVIES, seconded by Mr. JOHN FAIRCLOUGH ; and on the proposition of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. FAIRCLOUGH, Alderman Davies and Mr. J. L. Tunstall were re-elected hon. secretaries.—Mr. Ziba Armitage and Mr. T. Tunstall were re-elected auditors on the motion of Mr. PIM/- POINT, seconded by Mr. FAIRCLOUGH.—The following gentleman were elected on the council :—The Mayor of Warrington ( Alderman Harrison) and Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., 'M.P., ex-officio ; Colonel George McCorquodale, J.P., and Messrs. John Fairclough, J.P., John Dun, Thomas Jol- ley, Sylvanus Reynolds' J.P., R. A. Naylor, John Rylands,l J.P, William Pierpoint, Joseph Davies, J.P., Henry Bleckly, , J.P., Charles Broadbent, J.P. This was all the business.

div.head: ALLEGED GAME TRESPASS AT
div.p: ALLEGED GAME TRESPASS AT
BOLD.

Before Messrs. T. Pilkingtou and J. C. Gamble, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, Joseph Pownall and Matthew Pownall. of Great Sankey, were jointly summoned for trespassing on land in the occupation of Mr.T.ipping,Bold, in pursuit of game, and the last-named defendant was further charged with using a dog and getn to take game.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, prosecuted, and the defendants were represented by Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington.—Mr. Swift remarked that the case was a peculiar one; because as a matter of fact only one of the defendants was on Mr. Tip- ping's land when the offence was committed. The defen- dant Matthew Pownall was on his own land in the township of Sankey. On the 2nd inst. John Redhead, a gamekeeper employed by Mr. Tipping, was sent to the extremity of Mr. TiPping's land to a cover known as the Within Wood, and ' which ram along side fields in the occupation of the defen- dant Matthew Pownall. The gamekeeper, who concealed himself, saw the defendants and another man left Matthew Pownall's house, and they made direct towards the cover. The defendant Matthew Pownall, who carried a double-barrelled gun, entered the ,:over, and had with him a brown retriever dog, which he urged to enter the cover. The defendant followed to fire at anything that might rise, and the other man, whom they had not been able to identify, bad a stick in his hand with which he was beating Mr. Tipping's hedge. Mr. Swift said he thought the case was one calling for a substantial penalty, as it seemed to be the worst kind of poaching for adjoining farmers to enter the preserves of another landowner.—Eyidence to the foregoing effect was given by John Redhead, gamekeeper, after which Mr. Davies addressed the Bench at considerable length. He maintained that the defendant Matthew Pownall left the house quarter of an hour before his brother with a " bill- ! hook " in his possession and without a gun, for the purpose I of mending hedges on the farm while Joseph Pownall and a friend from eheeld were walking round the farm. It was denied that the defendants were trespassing on Tipping 's land in pursuit of game.—George Anders, a farmer at Burtonwood, who was at the defendant Matthew Pewnall's on the day in question, was called as a witness.—The Bench considered the case proved, and inflicted a fine of 40s and costs upon each defendant

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

The Lord Chancellor, the Attorney-General, and Mr. W. H Smith, the new Chief Secretary, arrived in Dublin on Sunday morning from London. The Kildare County Infirmary is amongst the latest vic- tims of boycotting. The cesspayers at the Naas Presentment Sessions refusing to vote the half-yearly sum of £6OO for the maintenance of their hospital, conse- quently the governors of the institution have resolved that the Infirmary shall be closed as soon as their funds are e±- hausted.

A Tralee telegram reports that at Finks Chapel, on Sun- day. the Curtin family were taunted as murderers, and but for the presence of forty policemen, would have suffered violence. The resident magistrate ordered the mob to be dispersed, and the police obeyed the order. The mob, how- ever,afterwarde entered the chapel, and broke the Curtin and ether family seats.

THRHATENED FAXINE IN ARIUN.—The Rev. M. O'Dono- hoe, parish priest of Arran, has made an urgent appeal through the Freeman's Journal for subscriptions for the relief of the distress, almost amounting to famine, which prevails irt\ the Arran Islands. He says that owing to the failure of the potato crop there are a hundred fami- lies on the north island alone who are living on what they can beg or borrow from their neighbours. The bois- terous weather has prevented the fishermen from pursuing their only industry, in the absence of proper boats and gear.

THE NATIONAL LEAGUE.—A Dublin correspondent says that Mr. Harrington, M.P., secretary to the National League, has been in Dublin since Saturday, and his absence from Parliament at so critical a moment, taken in connection with the action of the Government, bears out the announce- ment that the central machinery of the National League is to be transferred from Ireland to England, or to Paris ! case Parliament should extend the provisions of the bill to Great Britain. It is said that the bead-quarters of the League will be removed immediately to Manchester or Liverpool. A LANDLORD IN DISTRESS.—At the last meeting of the Dungarvin Board of Guardians a letter was received froni well-known local landlord, Mr. Price O'Brien, of Finithill, applying for outdoor relief, stating that otherwise he would be reduced to want. He had no means of living until diffi- culties concerning his property were settled. Be added that he bad paid thousands of pounds in rates out of his property. A Guardian remarked that they did not care if all the land- lords in Ireland were applying for relief. The application I was favourably received, but no decision as to amount of relief was arrived at. STRENGTHENING MR. PARNELL'S HANDS.—On Sunday night in Saintfield, county Down, a meeting convened by public advertisement was held "to take into consideration the grievances under which the leaseholders have been labouring for the last five years, with a view to have the grievances brought before Parliament." The attendance was not large. One of the resolutions passed was as fol- lows :—"That in the meantime we, the farmers and our friends of this part of county Down, in public meeting as- dembled, pledge ourselves to support the hands of Mr. Par- nell in the English House of Commons with all our stiength in his demand tor Home Rule for Ireland in the broadest sense of the term, and that we impress upon him to accept of no reform for the south and west of Ireland, in which Ulster is not included. Seeing that landlords, as a rule, have utterly repudiated any and every prayer of the tenants for a reduction of intolerable rents it is imperative that some person should come forward without delay and say to Irish landlords, "Restore !' " Resolutions on emigration and other subjects were passed, and a great many addresses were I delivered.

INCREASED BOYCOTTING.—The usual meeting of the Executive Committee of the Cork Defence Union has been held, Sir A. Warren presiding. A. number of applications for relief from boycstted farmers was read, the general pur- port of which showed that intimidation and boycotting were in almost all districts very prevalent, and the holding of

ILeAtte courts largely on the increase. In several eases labourers were supplied to boycett-d persons for the carry- ing on of :he work. The union having continual yon their hioks a lit of labourers who are bov'cot,ed thernstive. they have not found it necessary up to the present to avail themselves of tbe resources of the Emergency Association for the help required. A statetneut was made that to n.nv parts of the country the League were enforcing a rule that no labourers' cottages should be passed by the Poor Law Beards unless for those who were members of the League and regalar attendants at the meetings; also that a House League system was in force in many villages, persons be- ing obliged to reduce the rents of houses, and labourers and others not being permitted to enter into possession of a house until the local National Leafgue was fully satisfied that the former occupant was prepared of his Owol free will to leave. 1

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

Sir Wilfrid Lawson, on the advice of his physician, will, it is stated, go at once to Egypt. A man from the gallery of a Birmingham theatre into the pit on Saturday night, but received no serious injury. The Duke of Sutherland has intimated a reduction of 10 per cent, on the rents of his sheep farms on his Suthei- landshire estates. READ R. THOMPSON (30:11 SPECIAL CIidISTAIAS OFFER column of page 6.—Adrt. A goods train, from Berwick for Edinburgh, left the rails at Peaselye on Tuesday morning. Several trucks were smashed, and the line was blocked. Notices of a reduction of 2,1 per cent in wages have been posted up by the cod owners at all the ceilieries throughout the Rhondda Valley. The reduction is caused by the continued depression in the Welsh coal trade. Donations of £l,OOO each have been received from the Duke of Devonshire and the Duke of Buccleuch. in aid of the restoration of the ancient p Lrish church of Daton-in- Furnees. The Duke of Devonshire had previously given £2,500 in aid of the same object. • On Tuesday morning at Dublin Mr. W. H. Smith was i sworn in Chief Secretary for Ireland before the Privy Coun- cil. The Lord Lieutenant was present for a short time. Several resident ma(eistrates and Ceetle officials had inter- views with the Chief Secretary, who left Dublin oa Tues- day evening for London. CoAGuLlNE,—Cement for Broken Articles, 6d. is, 2s; postage 2nd. -Id everywhere. Kay. Bros., Stockport.—Advt. TERRIBLE Dar.—Oa Monday morning-, as William Reberts, aged seventeen, Handley, was engaged at Berry Hill Colliery, hooking on waggons, one of them, gathering too great velocity, overcome his strength, and fell from the spot were Roberts was working to the bottom of the pit shaft, a distance of over forty yards. Roberts was dragged with it in its fall, and was terribly mangled. Death was instant tneone. VALUE or' FARM LAND.—Messrs. Gerrod, Turner. and Son, of Ipswich, write that in no case where they have offered estates during the past year, by direction of the mortgagees, have the mortgages been realisaele. A faille of seventy-five acres, mortgaged for £4.500, commanded an offer of only £2 500. A farm in a district of known fer- tility cost upwards of £5O per acre a few years ago, and was recently sold for £23. SERIOUS- RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—As a train from Tyne- mouth was entering the Central Station, Newcastle, on Monday morning, at the usual rate of speed, the brakes, owing to the slippery state of the rails, did not act, and the carriages, before they could ha stopped, Caine into collision with the buffers at the end of the platform. The woodwork was broken, and some stones were torn up, while ten per- sons received cuts and bruises. RAY'S COMPOUND OF LINSEED, Aniseed. Senega, Son ill, Toln. &c . with Cbl^todyre. 9f-i„ 1-3.lfd, 23 9,1, of Chemists, —Advt. SHOCKING DrvinTros.—Ai an inquest held on Satur- day, near Mansfield, on the body of a collier who had been fatally injured, it was stated that the house in which the deceased bad lived was destitute of furniture and bedding, and that the woman with whom he had lived, and several little children, had slept close to the comae for three n'ghts without clothing. The coroner remarked that during the course of his experience he never met with such a shocking state of things. SENSATIONAL SUICIDE OP A YOUTH.—A youth narnal Walker, aged sixteen, employed as a clerk in the audit office of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, Victoria Station, Manchester, committed suicide on Saturday. He arrived at the office at the usual time, and nothing in his demeanour seemed unnatural. Suddenly his fellow clerks, working in the same room, were startled by a loud report, followed by Walker falling from his stool. He had shot himself through the temple, and died immediately. GREAT FIRE IN BIRMINGHAM,—A fire, broke out OR Sat- urday morning in Colmorelow, Birmingham, in the music warehouse of Messrs. Sabin and Ntockley. Before the arri- val of the fire engines the great block of buildings was in a blaze, and, in pouring water on the fire, the firemen did great damage to the valuable contents of the premises. Three firemen were severely injured. In addition to the damage done to the music warehouse, about twenty sets of offices were burned out. The loss is estimated at £lO,OOO.

Caution :—Condy's Fluid bears the name of Condy and Mitchell at f sot of every label. ,Beware of worfa less c'dourable imitations.—Adrt. IM. CHILDERS ON NATIONAL EXPENDITURE AND IRE- LAND.—Speaking in Edinburgh, on Saturday night, in pur- suance of his candidature Mr. Childers denied that the annual expenditure of the late Liberal Government ex- seeded that of their prececessors by nine millions sterling. There was an average yearly excess of nearly six millions, but the Liberals bad to pay off a deficit to provide large sums for education, and further amounts for the increase in the postal system. The real excess was £1,100,000 a year, and that included the expenditure on Egypt and the Soudan. ALLEGED FRAUD Olf THE ROYAL LIVER FRIENDLY Soctrrv.—Tor some weeks an officer of the Royal Liver Friendly Society has been investigating the accounts of Edwin Williams, Superintendent of the Society at Barn- staple. A few days ago he absconded. and subsequently, it is alleged, forged certificates of death were discovered ex- tending over a considerable period, the people on whose be- half death money bad been obtained being still alive. It is stated that nearly 20 cases have been discovered, amounting to several hundred pounds. On Saturday Williams was ar- rested at Plymouth. SHOCKING AFFAIR AT BOOTLE. On Monday morning Mr. A. G. Hutchinson. Stanley, archit,ct and builder, and inspector of works for the Lancashire Railway Company in connection with the improvements at Bootle, was killed at Bootle Railway Station. He had travelled from Stanley to Baliol-road station on the London and North-Western Rail- way, and on alighting at the latter station he attempted to cross the line of the adjoining station of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway with the intention of proceeding to Waterloo. While crossing, the ten o'clock train from Tithebarn-street approached, knocked him down, and killed him. BEETHAM it SON, Chemists, Cheltenham.—Adet, FATE OF EUROPEAN RESIDENTS IN BURMAlL—Authentic news has come to hand of the European assistants of the Bombay Burmah Trading Corporation, who were said to have been massacred by the Burmans on the outbreak of the war. These assistants divided themselves into two par- ties. One party got to the frontier near Meimipore, where they received protection. The other party, consisting of Messrs. Allen, Montenr, and Roberts, remained in their steam launches and tried to escape down the Chindwin. The launch, however, was boarded by Burmans, who sur- rounded all three. Menteur and Roberts jumped into the river and were drowned; Allen was cut across the neck and fell apparently dead, and the Burmans then proceeded to loot the launch. On Allen showing signs cf life they attacked him again with bars and spears as he lay on the deck of the launch, piercing him through the stomach in a most brutal manner until he died. The massacre is authen- tically reported to have been at the instigation of the Queen and the Sinedah. THE MINERS' CONFERENCE.— The Miners' National Conference at Birmingham was concluded on Saturday. In the absence of Mr. T. Burt, M.P., the president, the chair was taken by Mr. B. Pickard. A discussion took place on the law relating to confiscation. An opinion was generally expressed that an alteration was desirable, avid it was re- solved, " That the subject of confiscation be relegated to the Central Board of the Miners' National Union, and the com- mittee about to meet on general questions." The next ques- tion was a proposal in favour of the examination for sub- inspectors being lowered, so as to give working-men a better chance of passing such examination and being ap- pointed sub-inspectors. A long and animated discussion took place. Several delegates expressed the opinion that they should hesitate before recommending a lowering of the standard for this important office. It was unanimously re- solved, "That this Conference deems it desirable that prac- tical miners should be appointed as sub-inspectors, hut ttfat no such person should be appointed unless he holds a mines managers' certificate, or is prepared to pass an exami- nation qualifying him for one." On the motion of Mr. M'Kay (Ashton), seconded by Mr. Curling (Durham), it was agreed "that the relatives of deceased persons be repreeented in coroners' courts."—A discussion arose on the fatal colliery accident in June last at the Clifton Hall Colliery. Mr. Ashton (Lancashire) proposed—" That this Conference is of opinion that a new and more searching inquiry should be made into the cause of the explosion at the Clifton Mall Colliery, Pendlebury, which occured on the 18th of June, 1885, and caused the death of 179 persons; and therefore requests the president of this Conference, Mr. T. Burt, M.P., to question the Home Secretary on this matter as early as possible." Mr. Woods (Lancashire) seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried—The Conference con- cluded with a hearty vote of thanks to the chairanan and vice-chairman. THE PLOPOSED PRESENTATION TO COL. IticOORQUODALE. A proposal having been made that Colonel Geo. McCor.. quodale, J.P.. of Newton, the Liberal canlidate for the suf- frages of the electors in the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire at the last general election, should receive a tangible recegnition of his gallant fight against the return of Sirßichsrd Aesheton Cross, the Liberals of the division 'hare manifested a keen and earnest desire to carry it into effect at the earliest possible moment. The value of Col. McCorquadale's past and present services to the Liberal party of South-West Lancashire are incalculable, and his many acts of kindness and consistent advocacy of the prin.- cipies of "peace, retrenchment, and reform" are everywnere Ncogiml. Though he was defeated by his opponent at the last election, it was held on every- hand, and admitted even by his opponents, thet he made a praiseworthy attempt to wrest the- seat from the Tories. As a mark of the respect in which he is held by the Liberals of the division, it has been decided to have a suitable presentation, and a formal meeting to con- sider the question was held at the iselettOSiel gra Distticts„. Liberal Club, Fairclongt-street, Earlestown, onTu,sLir evening. There was a large attendance, and Mr. Charles Pilkington, J.P., presided. Among those pree.ent were Messrs. G. W. Rawlins (Liainhill), G. F. Aveline (Earles- town), W. Urquhart (Nee-ton), M. Birkhead, John Clarke, W. D. Burdis, John Prescott, &c.—The Chairman explained that the meeting was called to decide what shape the pro- posed testimonial to Colonel ltdcCorquodale was to take, and to receive the amounts collected in the various districts for the testimonial fond, it having been decided to close the subscription list that night.—Mr. G. W. Rawlins, treasurer (Rainhill), reported that, notwithstanding the adverse times, the appeal had been satisfactorily responded to, and that the committee were now assured of the amount they fixed as being required to carry oat their worthy object. (Applause.) The meeting afterwards decided that the presentation should consist of a handsome illuminated framed address, and the chairman submitted a draft of a proposed address. It as- sured Colonel 11IcCorquodale that he is held in the highest esteem by the entire Liberal electors throughout the divi- sion, and spoke in the highest nraise of the gallant and almost successful fight he made during the recent election against so strong a candidate as Sir R. Cross, who had pre- viously represented the district for seventeen years. Allu- 'sion was also made to the very great regret with which the entire Liberal voters received Colonel McCorquodale's de- cision not to again enter the contest—.e decision they were compelled to accept, remembering that he only entered the fight when severely pressed and from a sense ef duty to the Liberal party. They, however, rejoiced to know that in Colonel McCorquodale they would have an influential and active supporter in future contests. (Applause.)—A com- mittee was formed to select an artist to execute the address and carry out the arrangements for the presentation.—A cordial vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: MAKERFIELD PLOUGHING SOCIETY.
div.p: MAKERFIELD PLOUGHING SOCIETY.

ANNUAL CONTESTS. The 30th annual meeting of the Makerfield Ploughing Society was held on Thursday, when the ploughing contests were held at Newton Hall Farm, near Newton Bridge Sta- tion, on land in tee occupation of Mr. R. H. Wright. The proceedings shoald have taken place on the previous Thurs- day. but were postponed on account of the frost and snow. Though rain had fallen heavily on the previous day, the land-of a light sandy nature-was in good condition. Out of 50 entries received 40 competed in Lie various contests, which were witnessed by a considerable number of specta- tors. The prizes amounted in value to £6O. Ploughing commenced at half-past nine and concluded about three o'clock. The judges for ploughing were Messrs. Agnew (Rainford), Ledson (Fazackerley, near Liverpool), Turton (Hale, near Liverpool), Dean (Upholland). W. B. Kerfoot (Great Sankey), and Carswell (Lyme, near Stockport.) Tne prizes for turnouts were awarded by Messrs. Edwards (Nes- ton, Cheshire), and Jervis (Liverpool). The following were the awards :-Singe Furrow Fong hs : -Ist class : Ist, £B, S. Norcross (Ashton); 2nd, £5, John Banks (Buracough); 3rd, £3, Thos. Blackburne (Skelrners- dale) ; and 4th, £2, Wm. Ferguson (ploughman to Lord Gerard, Garswood.) Second-class (for men who have not within four years won a prize of the value of a for ploughing) : Ist, £6, Richard Naylor, Burton- wood (ploughman, Samuel Hoare) ; ' 2nd, £5, James Roe- bottom, tiainford (ploughman, Samuel Rosbottom) ; 3rd, £4, John Brown, Ashley (ploughman, John Brown) ; 4th. £3, William Balharrv, Haydock (ploughman, William Woodward); sth, £2, Richard Eckersley, Lowton (plough- man, Robert Eckersley) ; and 6th, £1 10s, Joseph Evans, J.P., Haydock (ploughman, William Nixon). Third-class (for youths under 19 years of age) : Ist, £3, Joseph Pimb- lett, Ashton (ploughman, Henry Pimblett) ; 2nd, £2, Joha Rigby, Kenyon ; 3rd, £l, Mks. Miller. Park House (plough- man, Lockland Miller). Extra Prizes :-A silver cup, value £5, presented by the CT. arswood Hunt to competitors whose land was in the hunt district, was won by William Ferguson, ploughman for Lord Gerard; and a silver cop. • value £5, presented by the Hon. W. Gerard, master of toe Garswoocl Hunt, to competitors in the bunt district, mainly dependent on farmiag, was awarded to Richard Eckersley, of Lowton. D. Harks won the society's silver medal as the exhibitor of the best and most reasonably priced single furrow plough; Messrs. Ransome, Sims, and Head got the society's medal as the exhibitors of an improved implement of tillage ; and W. Matthison (ploughman to Mr. Joseph Evans, J.P., Haydock) won the society's silver medal as the owner of the best team of horses completing the work allotted among competitors mainly depent.lent on farming. and a similar prize to other competitors was carried off by Robert Eckersley (ploughman to Richd. Eckersley Lowton). Tursouts :-Prizes to competiters- not dependent on farming were awarded as follows :-Ist, Walla n Matthison ; 2nd, William Putter ; 3rd, W. Car- ter ; and 4th, Joseph Nixbn (all ploughmen for Mr. Jos. Evans, J.P., Hayelock). The prizes to competitors depend- ent on farming were awarded-let, James Hall (ploughman for Mr. Richard Hunt,Newton); 2nd, Lockland Miller (Park House); 3rd, J. W. Pennington (Woecihead) ; and 4th, Robert Eckereley (Lowton). The annual dinner was field at the Pied Bull Hotel, New- ton, in the evening. A large number of persons were present, and Mr. T. D. Grinike, who presided, was supported by Messrs. C. Pilkington, J.P., R. H. Wright, H. Wright, W. Balharry, George Clarke, Dodson, Edwards, Jet eis„ Ledson, F. A. Frest (secretary), and others. The usual toasts were enthusiastically honoured, and the officials of the society ware highly complimented on the success wh;ch bad attended the contests and the gathering. Ti. proceedings were pleasantly interspersed with a selection of songs. •

div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 30, 1386.

1 THE Government have been defeated by the large majority of 79 on an important I amendment to the Address. , They refused to recognise their weakness, And have paid the penalty in a bad fall. If they had had ! the guiding hand of Lord BEACONSFIELD, ' they would have accepted with something of grace the verdict of the nation when it went against them. But there have been divisions in the councils of the Government, with the 1 result that the only semblance Of a policy upon which they could agree was to cling to the seals of offize until they were wrested from their grasp. Judging from the QUEEN'S 11 Speech which was laid before Parliament last week, the Government seem to have thought it possible that, by doing nothing until they were compell,A, they could play off their Coercionist followers against their Home Rule supporters. But this sort of flounder- ing pleased neither one nor the other, and i between the two stools they have, in less than a week, come to tlie ground. Sir M. HICKS-BEACH during the debate on the ! opening of Parlament sought to conciliate the Parnellites by arguing that it might not be necessary, after all, to ask for exceptional , powers, He laboured hard to prove that there was no alarming increase of serious crime, and that so far as he knew there was not a single Instance in which there had been a failure of justice through common juries refusing to convict. But this sort of reasoning, well-founded though it appears to have been, did not satisfy the landlords of ! Ireland who were clamouring for coercion. I Lord SALISBURY was besieged with demands for something stronger than milk and water; and, to gain time, he bade his impatient supporters "wait for Mr. SMITH"—Mr. W. H. SMITH, who had become Chief Secretary for Ireland, and was about to report on the situation. But they would not "wait for Mr. ' Sum' • " and so ford SALISBURY on Mon- day night—regardless of the argument used by his colleague in the House of Commons on the Thursday—was constrained to say that the state of things in Ireland was 'terrible and scandalous," and that, within forty-eight hours, steps would be taken to provide a remedy. This 'meant that coercion had been resolved upon—coercion which on Thursday had been relegated to " the dim and distant future." Could anything be more scandalous than that the Government should thus turn its back upon itself in less , than a week? That there might be no mis- take about it, Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH came down to the House of Commons on Tuesday night and gave notice, amid the exul- tant cheers of the Tories, that, on Thursday, a bill would be brought in " for the purpose

div.p: By Mr. THOMAS TUAYSTALL.

of suppressing the National League and other dangerous associations." It is stated that this announcement was received with yells and cries of " shame" by the Irish members, and we can well understand their indignation on learning that this was to be the reward for having asked their fellow - countrymen to vote Tory at the last election. It is not for us to say that under no circum- stances would Lord SALISBURY'S Government have been justified in resorting to coercion, but we do say that it is monstrous to argue on a Thursday that there is no case for coercion, and on the Tuesday following to' announce coercion in its worst form. On the face of it, this is madness, but there is this much of method in the madness--that the Government, finding that they must be beaten ere long, had suddenly made up their minds that they would rather be beaten on the Irish Question than on any other. Having degraded themselves by going into the office with " No Coercion '.' as their policy, they would be avenged by going to the country with the cry of "Down with .the National League." They therefore jumped Jim Crow, but they didn't jump quick enough, and have come to grief. The Government, failing in their manceuvres, have been forced to resign, not on their Irish policy, but on the question of providing allot- ments for agricultural labourers. Mr. JESSE COLLINGS, true to his pledges, moved, on Tuesday night, an amendment to the Address, expressing regret that no measures were announced " for affording facilities to the agricultural labourers and others in the rural districts to obtain allotments and small holdings on equitable terms as to rent and security of tenure." The Tories opposed this, for, although they pose as the farmer's friend, they cannot yet bring themselves to claiming to be the friend of the labourer. Mr. CHAPLIN, on behalf of the Govelmment, made the question one of confl- dence ; and Mr. GLADSTONE, taking up the challenge, delivered a vigorous speech in. support of the amendm at. He showed that it involved nothing that was new or revolu- tionary ; that the Government had nothing to offer that was satisfactory; and conclud- ing by expressing the hope that Mr. COL- LINGS' motion would be carried by a large majority. Mr. JOSEPH ARCH, in the Course of the debate, made an effective and eloquent appeal on behalf of the class he so worthily represents. Referring to the" three acres ' and a cow" theory, he said :—" The amend- ment of the hon. member for Ipswich meant that they did not ask for borrowed funds, they did not ask for land to be given them, and they had no desire to steal it. What he asked was whether the time had not come when these thousands of industrious willing workers should no longer be shut out from the soil, but should have an opportunity of gaining a fair livelihood, and of producing food for themselves and their families." The answer ; to that question, so far as the House of , Commons is concerned, is emphatically in the affirmative; for when the amendment was put to the vote the Government were de- feated ; it was carried in spite of their op'. position by a majority of 79. They would have preferred to meet their fate on another field; but it was not to be; they have flouted and, jibed and geered at that cow of the three acres, and now they are done to death by it.

LORD WOLSELEY, responding at a banquet on Saturday evening to the toast of "The United Service," asserted that our forces were "not so strong as they ought to be, regard being had to the duties which they had to perform in all parts of the world" This is to repeat, in a mild form, what military men are in the habit of saying, and may have been suggested by reflections on the annexation of Burmah. As "the man in charge," he is entitled to urge that if we increase our responsibilities we must add to the army and navy. He seems to think a bad time is in store for us, and that we ought to have the forethought and wisdom to prepare. "Last year," he said, "4.0 000 men were recruited, but notwithstanding this large number we are below our proper standard, and unless these ranks are properly aug- mented our military machinery will stop working altogether." If this is not merely a figure of speech, it certainly behoves us to mind what we are about: but we may take comfort in considering that it is "the way they have in the army" to make observa- tions of this kind. rhey are always asking for more, and when we come to look at the expenditure it is not too much to say that they are always getting more. Fifty years ago, the annual cost of the army and navy was from twelve to thirteen millions; it was considered high when it reached fifteen millions. To-day it is over thirty millions; it has averaged over twenty-nine millions for the last half a dozen years—that is to say our military expenditure is more than double that of fifty years ago. But this is not all; in addition to this burden of thirty millions a year for warlike objects, we have a burden of interest upon debt—the National Debt— for past wars amounting annually to over twenty-eight millions. Between the two, the nation is being taxed this year to the tune of , Sixty Millions ; while the total cost of civil government is Twenty-nine Millions—that is less that one-half the sum annually entailed for war in the past and preparation for war in the future. Looking at the disproportion in expenditure in the Civil as contrasted with what may be called the War Depart- ment, we cannot 'cut think that we are, at any rate, spending enough. Whether we are getting as much for our money as we ought to have is ano snt-r matter, and it is one which ought to be looked into. Perhaps if Lord WOLSELEY would turn his penetrating eyes in the direction ot economy—cutting down excessive expenditure in high places— he might be able to spare the long-suffering taxpayer, and have a large margin for addi- tions to the strength of "The 'United Ser- vice." The German army is ge.nerally re- garded as a model of efficiency; and it is certainly a model of economy. The annual cost per combatant to Germany is £49 per year; but the cost to Great Britain of each flailing man is .e i 3. Granted that the com- pulsory qstem is cht-ape.r. the difference be- tween .£49 and Li 13 is not to be explained by the difference of the two syst ms. Excepting the United States, where there is a small army —and all colonels, it is said—the cost of our army, in proportion to numbers, is nearly double that of every other fizhting Power in the world! Granted that England is rich, that is no reason why she should not spend her money wisely and well. If we look at the question from another point of view—in rela- tion to expenditure per inhabitant, we still find that the British army, small though it may be as to numbers, is not small as to cost. The average annual cost for keeping tIP 1 up the armies and navies of what is called the ! civi!ised world is eight shillings and sixpenc.e per inhabitant. The cost to Great Britain Is

sixteen shillings per inhabitant—that is very early double. This is surely sufficient to give us pause" The problem for "our only General "—and it is a problem which he ought to be able to solve—is to increase OUT fighting force without conscription, and Without increasing the cost to the nation.

THE proceedings at the presentation of the address to Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, On Wednesday evening, were characterised by an amount of enthusiasm which showed that the compliment was not of a formal kind, and that the Liberal party in Warrington are neither disheartened nor discouraged by their defeat at the last election. So far from being' afraid of the enemy from what has happened. they are looking forward resolutely and eagerly to the next conflict as a means of removing what they feel to be a discredit to the borough. If Mr. CROSFIELD had any re- Itaining doubt as to whether the battle had been lost through any fault on his part, it must have been removed On Wednesday evening by the unanim expression of approval of the manner in which he had acquitted himself during the campaign.' It was truly said of the Liberal Candidate, by more than one speaker, that the More those who worked with him saw of him and the better they liked him. He wears ?well ; he has always something in reserve— for he is not like the class of tradesmen who have most of their goods in the shop window. His speeches throughout the campaign re- ,veal him as a thorough-going Liberal, who 'Olds fast to the principles of his faith ; a,",d who, while earnest in expounding them. ''Splays an honest repugnance to playing last and loose in order to catch a few votes. Whenever he goes to Parliament, there need be no fear, either that he will for- tget how he votes, or that he will be unable !, a sound reason for any course he may ,Ti'e• He has done honour to himself and to .1 "le constituency by contesting the borourzh, tlcl we hope yet to see him returned to the °use of Commons as member for War- rington.

On Wednesday the deceased, who was about 40 years of age, was at the Old Quay, Runcorn. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that Holt died through " 'he visitation of God." LARCENY AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Abraham Hitchin, an elderly man, was chareed with stealing a pair of boots, worth 13s 61, the property of Samuel Tomlinson, assistent to Mr. George Hayes, at the Bridge Hotel. Tomlinson lodges at the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms in Church-street, where the prisoner w.s on Saturday morning, the 9th inst. Shortly after the pri- soner's departure the boots were missed, and it was subse- quently discovered that the prisoner had pawned them with Mr. Craddock for 4s 31.—The prisoner, who was received into custody. by P.-Clerk Wallace at Middlesborough on Saturday, pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol for a month. GOOD TEMPLARY AT WIDNES —On Tuesday evening a large and representative gathering of Good Tempters from the four lodges assembled at t',.e Science arri Art Building, MajonCross street. The chair was taken by Bro. Robert D.C.T. of South-West Lancashire, and there were else present Bros. Lamb, D.C., and J. W. Hell, D.M. Ad- dreeses upon " unity " were delivered by the above-named brethren, and were full of practical suggestions and advice. A discussion subsequently took place on the "Good of the Order," the outceme of which was a resolution to form a Convention, to be called "The Widnes Convention," and a committee was appointed with a view to furthering the above object. A FALLEN MASTER SADDLER AT WIDNES.—A respect- able looking man named William Ferrer was charged at Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday with stealing a saw, value 2s, the property of James Tilley, of the Norton Arms, Lugsdale. On Wednesday night Richard Rogerson, a clerk living at 44, Gladstone-street, was using the saw at Mr. Tilley's house. When he hung it up the prisoner was there. aubsequently it was missed, ant it was discovered that the prisoner had pawned the saw for Is to Mrs Jami- sota—The prisoner said he took the saw in order to get money for lodgings.—lnspector Wood said the prisoner was formerly a master saddler in Widnes. He had been away for some years, and all the police knew about him was that he was a drunkard when in business.—The prisoner was committed to gaol for a month. DEFRAT.IDING THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Patrick Burns, who did not appear, was summoned for travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from Liverpool to Widnes without a ticket. Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department. Lime-street, prosecuted. Miss Atkinson der posed that on the 4th inst she travelled by the 6-5 p.m. trait) from Lime-street to Widnes. As the train left Lime- street two boys entered the carriage, and from their conver- sation she gathered that they had no tickets. On arrival at Whines Alfred Rodgers, a porter. found Burns behind the board fencing outside the station after the train had depar- ted. He stated he aiael been waiting for his sister who had not come by traie. A youth named Marray was also found hiding on the platform. Burns was fined 10s, and costs Ms or n days. A WARNING TO RECRUITS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Jun. Kinsella, 17 years of age, was charged that he being a recruit of the 3rd Lancashire Mili- tia, made a false declaration. Froth the evidence of Hobert Wingfield and Colour-Sergeant James Dibbs it appeared that on the 16th of January the prisoner enlisted, and was re- jected by the doctor. On the 22nd he enlisted again with Wingfield, and then stated before the magistrate that he had never been rejected as unfit for service. Colonel Thack- w ell ordered these proceedings to be taken. The prisoner said he was only rejected for being short of weight. He was sentenced to two months' hard labour.

WIDNES POLICE COURT, YESTERDAY.—AIIeyed Theft of Eggs.—Eliza Roberts, a married woman, was charged wan stealing five eggs, valued at 6d., the property of Jos. Rout- ledge. shopkeeper, Mersev-road, Widnes.—Police-constable Holbrooke said on the previous evening he observed the pris- oner go in the shop and put something under her apron. S.ie came out of the shop, and went into John-street. He went into the shop, and asked Mrs. Routledge if she had sold the prisoner anything. She said she had net. Wit- flees went to the prisoner's house, and found the eggs on the kitchen table. He took her into custody, and on the way to the police station she admitted taking the eggs.— She was remanded until Monday.— Vagraney.—Petar Nolen was sent to prison for seven days for sleeping in Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works.—The Stone Throwing 2Vui- sance.—Michael Carr was brought up on remand for wound- ing John Hike-, of Midwood-street, at the Widnes Alkali Works.—Dr. M'Cambridge observed that Riley was still in a dangerous state, and would not recover for some time. Indeed he did not know whether Riley would ever recover. A remand was grantcd until Thursday. ALLEGED MURDEROUS ASSAULT BY A WOMAN AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. Jon. Brock, Mary E. Devine was charged with unlawfully wounding Elizabeth Burns. Burnt; lives with her parents at 21, Railway-street, Widnes, and the prisoner had lodged at the house for some time. About half-past one on Sunday morning the 17th inst., the pris- oner entered the house "the worse for drink," and made a disturbance because there was no fire in the kitchen. The prosecutrix and her sister Ellen went into a neighbour's house, and whilst there heard a noi,e in the house. Re- turning, they saw the prisoner had hold of their mother by the hair. The prosecutrix said the prisoner ought to be ashamed of treatiegaan old woman like that, and struck her on. the face with her open hand. The prisoner seized the poker and struck prosecutrix on • the head, inflicting a serious wound. Dr. M'Cambridge informed the Bench that the wound, which was in a bad state, was an inch-and-a-half long, and it would be a week before the woman could at- tend court.—The prisoner said the wound had been made touch worse by the presecutrix attending a " wake " and getting the frost into it.
