SACRED AND SECULAR CONCERT' AT PARNWORTH. —On Thursday evening the Farnworth-in-Widnes Church Choir gave their second annual concert in aid of a fund towards buying a new organ for the Parish Church. There was an excellent attendance. A long programme had been drawn up, and it con- tained many beautiful sacrcd and secular pieces by some of the old masters. The part songs and choruses were rendered in a finished manner by the choir. Mrs. Catherine Bradley had been engaged for the evening, and delighted the audience by her singing. Mr. Joseph Bradley was the accompanist. lie also skilfully played several pianoforte selec- tions. At the conclusion of the concert a vote of thanks was accorded to the singers and to Mr. W. A. Watts, who so ably conducted, on the motion of the Rev. George Bond, seconded by Hr. Ware-

mg. FATAL RESULT OF A FOOTBALL MATCH.—On Wednesday night Nathan Pilling, aged. 19 years, son of Adam Pilling, Vine-steeet, Widnes, died from what is supposed to be the effects of a football acci- dent during a match some weeks 'since at Penketh. The deceased was kicked in the stomach, and was carried off the ground in an insensible state. After a short time he recovered, and went back upon the field, bnt had to retire, when he again became un- conscious, and had to be taken home. He continued ill, and on Monday night last he:went to bed about seven o'clock. He had been in bed a short time when he shouted for his mother, who on going up- stairs found the deceased in a fit. Since Monday he has had a succession of fits,and during one of these on Wednesday night he died. He was a member of the Sunday school at Appleton, and was much esteemed by a large circle of friends. He was to have been married shortly. The facts have been reported to the coroner. Great sympathy has been expressed for the family. SwINI: FEVER.— A special supplement of the London Gazette published on Saturday evening con- tained a Privy Council order, cited as the Temporary Swine Fever Slaughter Order of February, 1886, which empowers-local authorities in England, Wales, and Scotland to slaughter, within two days after the existence of the infection is known to them, all swine affected with swine fever, and also swine in the same pigsty, shed, or field with any swine so affected. They may also, during the month of Feb- raary, slaughter any suspected animal. The rates of compensation are to be as follows :—For aninials infected, half their value, but not to exceed 405., and in other cases the full value of the pigs, not exceed- iing£4. A further Order, cited as the Temporary !Swine Fever Districts Order of February, 1886, which ,commences to take effect after the 31st inst., land !Teases to have effect :after the *2Bth February,•sets . forth the conditions and regulations for the holding of public or private sales or exhibitions of swine in the following, amongst other, districts :—County of Lancaster: The boroughs of St. Helens, Warrington, ' and Wigan. Cornaty of Chester: The bproughs of Chester, Congleton, Crewe, Thyde, MaccleSfield, and , Stockport. THE CAPITAL OF THE SEEP CANAL COMPANY. —Mr. Adamson ~(chairman) presided on Monday evening at the annual meeting of the Newton Moor Cotton Spinning Company, Limited, and introduced the question of 'taking up shares in the Manchester Ship Canal. He remarked that the Newton Moor Spinning Company was saving £l5O per annum by the reduction Of railway rates since the canal scheme was brought before the public, and he expressed the belief that when the canal was made it would save Newton Moor at least £l,OOO a year. He stated that between £700,000 and .EBOO,OOO had been already taken in shares, and he had arranged with Messrs. Rothschild to find the remainder at 4 per cent interest and 1 per cent commission. It was proposed to raise £1,000,000 by shilling contribu- tions of working-men, by a syndicate of labour re- presentatives, of whom Mr. Joseph Arch, M.P., Mr. Thomas Burt, M.P., and -others were leaders; and he expressed the hope that everyone would help forward the greatest national and commercial un- dertaking of the 19th century. It appeared that Newton Moor had already contributed £lOO to the scheme, and the meeting decided .to give discre- tionary power to the Board to invest not less than £6OO nor more than £l,OOO in the undertaking, as they might think best. THE NEW DEAN OF CHESTER.—The Queen has been pleased to appoint the Venerable Archdeacon Darby to the vacant deanery of Chester. The new dean is a graduate of Trinity College, Dublin, where he received his divinity testimonnun in 1855, and proceeded to his M.A. degree ten years later. He was ordained in 1856 by Dr. Graham, Bishop of Chester, to the curacy of Winwick, near Warring- ton, receiving priest's orders in the following year. He remained at Winwick, under Canon Hopwood, until 1858, when he accepted a similiar position at Neils, Somersetsh ire, from which he Was preferred in the following year to the vicarage ef Newburgh, near Wigan, on the nomination of the late Earl of Derby. He has since filled the position of Inspec- tor of Traintng Colleges in Religious Knowledge, and was in 1875 appointed to the rectory of St. Bridget 's with St. Martin's, Chester, which he still retains, In 1877, on the elevation of Archdeacon Johnson, rector of Northenden, to the Bishopric of Calcutta, he was appointed his successor as Arch- deacon of Chester, and he has for the last two years acted as examining chaplain to Dr. Stubbs, bishop of Chester, who, last year conferred upon him the canonry of Chester Cathedral, worth £5OO per an- num, in succession to Canon Blonafield, since de- ceased. DR. COOPER CENSURTD.

The recent death of an aged CV701;a7.1-rT:med Dewhurst, of Widoes, in Whisfon Workhouse, under circumstances repor- ted in the Examiner a fortnight ago, formed the subject of an inquiry by the Prescot Board of Gruatdiaas, who held a special meeting for that purpose, in the boardroom at the A'orkhouse, on Monay afternoon. In the ab-ence of Mr. G. Leatherbarrow (chairman) who attenoei during the meeting, the chair was occupied by Mr J. Lowe. Tnere were also present—Messrs. Hill, Fisher, D bell, Hall, Bir- chall, Newswire, Ellison, P. Longton, swift. Griffiths. and H. S. Hartley (clerk.)—Phe Clerk alluded ta the eh cum- stances attending the death of the deceased woman, and pointed out the discrepancies in the statements made to them by Dr. Cooper, the medical officer for the Widnes destrict, and Mr. John Scannell (relieving officer), and those given at the coroner's inquest. The following witnesses were then called : ' P.C. Savoury stated that he found the woman on the footpath in Gossage-street, Widnes, at 3-30 am. on the 30th November. She said she had been down to Widnes to buy some articles, aid she had sprained her ankle, and could not walk. He carried her home—about 500 yards. She was not drunk, but she had had a qaantity of rum. She told him that she had been rambling about for a long time.

Sarah Welsh, living near the late residence of the de- ceased, said she remembered Dewhurst being brought to her house on a Monday morning, a month or three weeks before Christmas. She did not see the constable, but she saw the woman at half-past seven the following morning. She said she had fallen and broken her leg. She was not perfectly sober when she wut out on Sunoay evening. She was in receipt of parish relief. A young woman gave the deceased some money, und her brother sent her £4, And with that money she turned out to pay her rent and coal bill. Her mother fetched the doctor on the same morning. The leg was bandaged by Dr. Cooper two. or three times. Her mother went for the doctor About hal f-p ist tem on Monday morning. She took the bandages off About a week before she went to the workhouse. Dr. Pattlnson then bandaged it after that. The relieving officer sent her some beef, sugar, butter, bread, meat, and tea. The officer first visited ner about a week after the accident, and she heard him say that Dr. Cooper had not told him. She saw her every day unti she was removed to the Workhouse. She was frequently "muddled." The doctor attended her the first time on the Monday morning, and several times after that The Clerk remarked that Dr. Cooper said he first attended the deceased on the 2nd Dc.cember.

Elizebeth Welsh, mother of the Previous witness, said de- ceased was drunk en ihe Sunday evening previous to the accident. • She went for Dr. Cooper about ten o'clock, but her daughter had gone before that, but he was not up. The doctor ordered her to pet some cold water bandages on tier leg for two or three days. He said be could not bandage it because the scelling was too bal. The doctor visited the house each day Bendages were were not put on or a week, and her leg was loose all the week. She did not complain much of pains. He did not put the splints on for about ' nine or ten days. He undid the splints every day. The relieving officer did not visit Dewhirret until after the splints .vere put on. A neighbour brought the rtlitt eereoey for her during, that ti rut Dewhurst. had drink h;otlet bet every tiay !ag. iig roe netiee. When her money was done she pledged articles. She bad lived alone in the house for about seven or eight weeks, n d before that another old woman lived with her. The bed was in a most fearful condition. The landlord did not say he would turn her our, in her hearing. The woman said she would go to the Workhouse. The case was then rneetioned to Mr. Scat:- nell. See repeated her desire to come to the Workhouse about a week before the time she went. She rambled a good deal in her talk. When the woman was taken to the Workhouse the splints had been taken elf by Dr. Cooper. It was then bandaged in a trough. She remember-6d Dewhurst taking the bandages off. Her daughter stayed with her mostly at 1,4bt4 and she looked ;kite, her chiefly at thy time. The doctor was not present when the welleen was taken to the Workhouee, but the relieving officer w.—Dr. Cooper, the medicel officer, was then called. He said he had his report book with him. lie saw deceased about ten o'clock on the morning of the 30th. The 29th was the day entered in the hook as the dav of the first visit, hut that was wronr, as it ought to have been the 30b.—Mr. Debeli asked how they were to understand what was correct and what was not. The beok was valueless if the. entries were not correct.—The evidence given by Dr. Cooper was con- sidered unsatisfactory by the Guardians, who spoke strongly on the matter. —Dr. Hall said when the woman arrived at the Workhouse she was as ill as she could be, and the journey, nu doubt, had a very bed effect upon her.—Mr. John Scannell, the relieving officer, ettted that he knew nothing of the occurrence until the 9th of December. When he visited the woman on the 10th she was under the in- thence of drink. On two occastons he supplied her with beef, sugar, bread, meal, etc., as he saw no food in the house.— After a lengthy discussion, Mr. Hill moved that Dr. Cooper should be called in, and the feeling of the Board with refer- ence to his treatment of the case should be placed before him as strongly as possible, and also that Mr. Scannell be instructed to exercise greater care in the future.—Mr. Dolled seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. birched, and carried.—Ou Dr. Cooper being called into the room' the Chairman said the committee were of opinion that there had been great neglect on his part, and it the deceased woman had been properly treated end the drink kept from her she, would have been alive at the present.—Dr. Ceoper admitted having made several errors ; and prornieed that they ehould not occur again.—Tbe Chairman informed Mr. Scanoeil that the Guardians thought he had neglected a Dart of his duty in not staking the entry and reporting the case on the 10th ult., and they wished hint to he more tare- fill in such mattets in the future. He thought that when paupers did not go personally for' their money he ought not so give it to ethers, but to see for himself the reason why the recipients did not go for it themselves.—The proceed- ings then terminated.

div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Thursday morning for the purpose of considering a certain bill now pending in Parliament. and intituled :—"A bill to authorise the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire sit- way Company, the Sheffield and Midland Railway Com- panies Committee, the Cheshire Lines Committee, and the Wigan Junction Railways Company respectively, to con- , struct new railwave and other works, and to confer farthee powers upon those Companies and Committees in connec- tion with their respective undertakings, and Kor other pur- poses," and, if considered expedient, of passing a resulc- tion or resolutions to oppose the said bill in rarliament, and to apply the general district rate, or otker. the oublic funds or rates under the -control of the said Local Board, to the payment,ef the costs and expeuses attend".ng such opposi- tion. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, B. Dutton, W. T. husband. H. Gaskell. ju.nr., S. Sadler, J. Taylor, Z. T. Allen (clerk), W. higginsoir (surveyor.) OncOSITION T 9 CHESIITRE LINES Rt.ILWAY BILL. Mr. Carey moverra resolution empowering the Board to appose the bill in Parliament and that Messrs. Oppereheim •and Malkin. solicitors, St. Helens, be euthorised to take the necessrery steps for the due protection and interests of the district, and that the costs and charges incurred and to be incurred be'peid out of the general-district rate or other funds applicable to the purpose. Mr. Carey explained that the Cheshire Lines in the course of the .construction of their railway stop up a bridle road and footpath to Ditton, and the Local Board had called upon them either to restore this road and path or to give them some other which would he equally convenient. The company proposed to follow the latter,courae and had suggested a road and footpath, and the Highway Committee was satisfied with the arrenge- ments if they could be carried out, and if the Local Board had no liability to repair Ditton-road. It was necessary, however, to carry out these arrangements that the form of oppoeing the bill should be gone through.---Mr. S. Sadler seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. THE PROPOSED COUNTY COURT. Mr. Husband said he had great pleasure in moving that the cl,,..airman and the clerk be authorised to put the seal of the Board to a petition which had been got up in Widnes, asking for the establishment of a County Court in that town. He proposed to add a memorandum to the petition to the effect that at a special meeting of the Boar& it was resolved unanimously that the Board support the petition in favour of a county court being held monthly in Whines. Mr. Hasband narrated the steps which had previously been taken, unsuccessfully, for the establishment of a cart, and remarked upon the great convenience and saying to poor people the proposed court would bring. Mr. Sadler seconded the motion, because he felt that the Board would be carrying out the wishes of the vast ma- jority of the ratepayers of Widnes by supporting the peti- tion. He was sure the court would be a great boon. The resolution was carried unanimously. THE COLONIAL ExnunTroN: INTERESTING SUGGESTION.

A liner dated the 19th inst., from the Royal Commission for the Colonial and Indian Exhibition, South Kensinaton, London, S.W., was read by the clerk. It stated that H.R a. the Prince of Wales, the executive president of the Com- mission, bad expressed his hearty concurrence with a pro- posal to afford the working classes of the United Kingdom opportunities for acquiring a more intimate acquaintance with the products and manufactures of the British colonies and the IndianZmpire, and hoped the members of the Local Board would be willing to co-operate with him by encouraging working-men from the district to visit the exhibition, by which course they could not but gain much valuable in- formation by witnessing the finest examples of the produc- tiens and manufactures of the British colonies, and in the case of India by studying the actual methods of workman- ship which would be expansively shown at the exhibition. It was proposed that the chairman (Mr. Gossage) should in

the first instance interest the manufacturers in the scheme' and establish clubs whereby for the payment of a mall sum weekly, as done in connection with the gteat exhib- tion of 1851, parties of working men could be sent up ta se, the exhibition. It was suggested that the w,ekly subscrip- tion shou!ci not be more than is, and in some cases &I. THE NEW JEPUSALEM CITURCH. Or Sunday evening Mr. It. (3 unton, of London, one of the missionaries of the New Jerusalem Church, gave a lec- ture in Calru,treet chord-room, V arrington, on the subject, "Where the millions who have died now dwell, mad whet they do." Tnere we a large attendance. Before delivering his discourse, Mr. Gunten read a passage of scrip' ore and offereu upe prayer. 'foe portion of scripture selected was part o: chapter f I ef lieveiations, and he ex- plamed that ney did nut inierprst that chapter in any metesial or literal sense. They did aut think the " holy city " there mentioned was a materiel city. The.dirnersisma I of the city were given, and it was se large thet it it were to ! come out of heaven this istated eeuld hot contain it. That "New Jerusalem" was representative of a new view of Christien principle, a revelution in a spiritual sense in which the elnech was to be suede new by new Perceptions of the Lord and the prinmple.s which rule in His Kingdom. The church was t,ew when it hid new sentiments. They did not think there we; e three persons in ems God ; there was nothine .eletut three persons in one God in the scrip- tures; rhea use ostler a oilman dogma. It was quite true the Father and Son was mentioned. ad the Holy Spirit, Out it did not say these were three persons. They held that the Christian Church had gone far away from the truth, and ceased to promote the work for which it was eeteblished. If the church was in full strength in their 'nide', did they teinla they would have all the distress which disgraced the natiou at ths present time ? This Was because they lad not A true church amongst thsm. From the top of society to the bottom the church had income a defaulter. Dealing with the subject of his even•rg's discourse, Fur. Gunton said that man was a dual being, that was, he had two sides to his nature. He had what they called the natural mind, or a natural degree of the mind and a spiritual mind or a spiritual degree of the mind. In that respect he diffe:•tal from all other s.ensDive beings. Animals had no spiritist side to their nature ; they were quite incapable of thinkine ef a supreme teeing or a life after death. Both animals and men are organisatisns, and the manifestation of life is ac- cording to the orgartisetion. Life is the same in all eases, the life of the tree and the animal is the same as the life of a human being. The difference is nor in the life, but in the organisation. The Almighty created this world thet out A its materials He might create hurnin bodice, end human bodies are created throuch the instruinentatey of that which we call the human soul. The human soul is a spiritual entity, a spiritual reality send substance, and ir clothed itsslf with the human body. Thetiumen soul existed before the child was berm and it clothed itself with the materials of the body. Having mentioned that they had a law of in- terpretation according to which every material thing mentioned in the scriptures represented something spiritual, Mr. Gueton went on to say that in the beginning Gest created heaven and earth, that was two worlds, a material wend and a spiritual world. Heaven is the spirituel world, the world of spiritual substances. There were millions and millions millions of angele dwelling in heaven, and these would go on increasing. Sometimes they felt a little difficulty in realising in their minds the eu!'seantiality and entity of spiritual things, but they must try to think of substances ef two kinds—a material substance and a spiritual szbstance. There was really a third substance, as God Almighty is a divine Being and not a material or a spiritual being, and in that sense be is not composed of the same sort of substance as angels or tbe bodies of men. When a man died, as they called it, he was to all intents and purposes a spiritual body. 'rho spirit, viddch was the essential quality of the man, went away, the wicked still being wicked and the good still good. When the spirit left man it was received by angels, as a child noway born was rrceived by nurser, and they would look after it in their beautiful world. If it ' could not bear their company, if while on the earth the man had not cultivated heavenly princiPles it would sink amongst spirits of a loWer quality until it found its level. Angels are "men in lighter habit clad." Sonic people had an idea that angels were different beings to themselves, but that was a mistake, becense angels were created men. The oh.. j,ct God had in creating men was to make them angels. The speaker then contended that the material bodies of human beings when once cast off were never again resumed, and, he said, the world in which the spiritual substances which had thrown off their material bodies dwelt was all round us. The good thoughts of men came from the good spirits and tbe bad thoughts from evil spirits. At the close of the lec- ture a nuallyl of pamphlets were distributed, and books eold,

PARR'S BANKING CO, LIMITED. , ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING. , An annual ordinary general meetirw of the shove com- pany was held at the Bank Premises, Warrington, yester- day, for the purpose of declaring a dividend, el-cting direc- tors and auditors, and coaducting the ordinary buairass of the company. Mr. J. C. Parr, the chairman of the com- pany, presided, and the other directors present were Messrs. N. Eckersley, Wigart ; 1). :iamble, Sr. Helens ; P. Stubs, Warrivaton ; E. Gr,enall, Urappeahall ; G. McCorqaodale, Newton ; H. Woodcock, Sues2x ; J. Pearson, Newton; A. Hewlett, Warwick; T. H. Dixoa, Gresford ; J. Thompson, Chester ; a. Turner, L:vetpoal ; H. W. Meede-Kinz, Liver- pool ; tied C. F. Parr; Northwich. 'nig DIRLC TORS' RRPORT. The fellowing report was submitted by the directbrs, , viz. :—The three ore, in submitting to the shareholders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to re- pott teat the positien and prospects of the business continue to be in every ‘57.5" satisfactory. Including £15.196 lOs 7d, brought from previous account, the net balance of profits, after providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five Frr cm, is et:lls 281 Os 46. ' Tne dist, Nolan of this sum, recemmended by the direc- tors, is as follows: Interim half-yearly dividend, at 15 per ' cent. per annum. declared 24th July, 1:42,000 ; dividend to be now paid at the rate of 15 per cent, per antuin, free of income tax, £42,000; bonus of lOs per share, free of income tax, £l4OOO ; to property account, £2,000; balance to next account, £15,281 Os 46. The directors who retire at this time by rotation are Mr. John Pearson, Mr. Alfred Turner, Mr. Henry Warren Meade-King, Mr. Cecil Francis Parr, Mr. Thomas Philip Parr, and Mr. Geo. afcCorquodale, all of whom are eligible and are recommended for re-election. Tire CIIAIRM&N, in moving the, adoption of fhe report, said the year that hadlust elapsed had been very like its imme- diate predecessor. There was very little that was fresh ta say about it. The same stagnation and depression hal existed, and perhaps had been even more accentuated, and especially in the agricultural interests. The average value of money had been lower, and the difficulty of employment ' and anrenaunerative rates for money had all exercised an adverse influence on their Profits, while at the same tiZIO l'iey had thought it prudent and good pol.iay not f 0 eiraltidg their rate of interest as low as the average bank rate might have entitled them to do. He felt quite cure, however, that the balance shirt the directors had the pleasure of bringing before them would meet with every satisfaction, and would be a source of pleasure and confidence not only to everar shareholder but to every one connected with the hana; (Hear, hear.) The bad debts for the past .year callci hr no remark; they were important neither in number nor amount. As long as banking was banking there would always be bad debts, and if bankers vvre exempt from lorses they would be unlike any other section of the trading community. The number of ac- counts had increased by nearly one thousand and that increase bad Lien pretty evenly Cita ibuted over all the area of tire bank. '1 he number of t: rella elders bad also increased by thirty-four. The money I, dge I had risen by the amount of .f. 0,000 which was a small amount com- pared with the total of £5,000,000, but still it was satisfac- tory as showing the benk was holding its own in that re- spec. They would notice an increase of English Gevern- ment consols which now amounted to £300,000, which was. also the amount of their reserve fund, and all these Govern- ment securities were held at considerably below their market value. Having referred to the strong position the bank held, the cheirman said the dividend and bonus they proposed to pay would make a total distriaution of 171 per cent. It would not have surprised him if, considering the circumstances of the past year, the result had not been quite so favourable. (Hear, bear ) Mr. ECKEIV.I..tir seconded the adoption of the report, and the proposal was agreed to.

This committee report,d mat during tae month fees were recommended to be paid in 27 cLses. Twenty persons had been cotvicted before the magistrates for contravention of the Education Act. On the recommendatio—n—olth—;-S.chool Management Cow- mitre, Miss VVorkmas was appointed head mistress of the infants' departmesa of the West ilink Schools (vice Miss ScwerOults resigned) at a salary of £94 per annum. GOTERNIIENT GRANTS.

The Rev. Fath;r7.-F-nTe—g-a-r;,- -c.:;;;;;;;,n of the School Management Committee, presented a report on the Govern- ment grants received by the schools during the year ended August 31, 1885 The average grant per child was 18s 11d, an ircreaee of 81 on the previous year. At West Bank the average grant earned per child was 18e 9d, an increase of 911 on 1884; at Warrington-road 17s 911, increase lid ; te• eel, Bank 18s 10.1, increase 4id. The total grant of the schools was £2,142 7s 4d, with an average attendance of 2354. In the previous year the gran. was £1,915 8e 4d, with in average attendance of 2,098. Out of 38 pupil teachers examined four pessed w 11 and 22 fairly, while 12 were marked in one or more subjects. • In 1884 14 passed well and 17 fairly. The result of the cookery classes was that 224 were examined, and a grant of £44 163 earned.— Mr. Deacon remarked that the poor results obtained by the pupil teachers at their exam:nation had been explained by the fact that the examination was held six months earlier. This he considered was only a pirtial explana- tion. The teaching with regard to pupil teachers was rather weak at present.—Father Finegan replied that the subject had received the attention of the c.ermnitree. The teachers could not be expected to pay the same attention to their own examinations wheu they had the trouble of bringing up the children for inspection at the same time. He was afraid ' the Inspector did not make allowance for the fact that the teachers had to do twelve months work in six months. Ha r 34, h9WeVerl in love with the present system ot teach- mg pupil teachers in the Board Schools, but they were Out prepared to made any change at present. The examina- tions were in April.—Mr. Davies said ,the future prosperity of the schools depended upon the proper teaching of the pupil teachers, and he urged the importance of the com- mittee taking up the subject as soon as possible. They would nor be successful until they had day classes for the teachers.—The Chairman : That means increasiug the staff very much.—Mr. Davies replied not so great as would ap- pear.—Mr. Glover argued that at present there was no- body responsible for the training of pupil teachers or for their passing or failures. Neither had they proper arrange- ments for the care of female pupil teechers la these clisses. The requirement that a mistress should be present on '64idb oulasion were allowed to go by, and these , night classes, too, led to an amount of ,liesipation.— The Chairman : You don't mean dissipation in its usual acceptation, Mr. Wove,: ?—Mr. Glover explained that he meant that there WAS not that discipline and order there ought to be.—Father Finegan observed that teachers were paid to instruct the pupil teachers, and if there was no re- sponsibility attached to them he thought the sooner they took the pay away and the better. He was glad the word dissipation had been explained.—The report was adopted,

Thomas Shaw Joseph Shaw, and J.4hn Shaw, brothers, and employed as Shaw, at Liverpool, were summoned to show cause why orders should not be made upon them to support their aged mother, at present chargeable to the common fund of the Present Union.--Tbe Bench erderea John to ptv is per week, Thomas is 6d per week, and Joseph 2e 6,1 'per week. • _ _

• • A SIMI:Min ASSAULT.—On Tuesday, at the Present Petty &,eesions. before Lieut.-Colonel F. W. Earle. Captain Willis, KO Mr. A. H. Gladstone, Joseph Holdcroft, labourer, of unsettled residence, was summoned for assault- ing William Mawdsley, a collier, on the 7th just —The defendant did not appear.—The complainant stated that he was returning from Prescot, when be met the defendant, who asked him for some tobacco. He told him be had none, whereupon the defendant struck him on the face with his fist, cutting his lip and making it Weed. He also thortip,d him and knocked him against a wall. In reply to the Bench, complainant added that he had known the defendant previously. de (complainant) bad bad no drink, but he thought the defendant had had\ a "sup."—P.S. Bull gave evidence that the complainant 'bad called at the police office, and complained of the assault. He was then bleeding from the mouth.—"uperintendent Barker informed the magistrates there was a long list of previous convictions against the defendant, who was one of the worst characters in the district.—The Bench remarked that the defendant appeared to be we:l known, as he had been 16 times pre- viously convicted. There did not seem to have been any cause for that assault, and the defendant would be committed to prison for two months, with hard labour.

Hay- wood, on the 25th December, at Little Leigh, 5s and costs ; Michael Dowd, 2nd January, at Appleton, 21 6,1 and costs; Thomas Hart, senr., en the 12th January, 5s and costs; Wm. Rustige, at Seveneake, on the 20th 'December, coats 2e 6d; and James Brannen, for having been drunk on the 17th January, at Whitley Inferior, was ordered to pay costs 4s 6d. STILAY CATTLE —James aWithingsbaw, for having al- lowed cattle to stray on the highway at Little Leigh, on the 17th January, was ordered to pay 5s 61 coats. ASSALZT ON BELL-RINGERS —Four young men named John Lee, Robert Dolan, John Dean, and Samuel Smith, were charged with baying, on the 4th January, assaulted Thos. Houghton, Peter Hamblet, David Wiihingshaw, James Ryder, and William Gill, at Preston-o'-th'-Hill, on the 4th January. It appeared from the statements of the prosecu- tors that they were a party of hand bell-ringers. On the evening of the 4th January they were at Preston Brook, and having called at the hotel there they left a few minutes be- fore ten o'clock for Daresbury. They were followed by the defendants, one of whom they heard say "Come on, let's have a b— row, and take the bells and muffles from these fellows." The defendants then came up to the party of bell-rine•ers and commenced to push them about, knocked their hats off, &c. No defence was offered by the defen- dants.—The Chairman (Mr. R. Pierpoint) said that had been a most disgraceful disturbance, although it seemed to have arieen more through foolish bear-play than anything else. The prosecutors were most respectable men belong- ing to a beneficial society of bell-ringers, and their behav- iour bad been most creditable to them, as the affair might have resulted in.a very serious disturbance. Each of the defendants would be fined 5s and costs. Mao Doos.—The Clerk said he bad recaivA a com- munication from the chairman of Quarter Sessions relative to precautionary measures being taken by the police with regard to mad dogs.—Superintendent Leah said he would communicate with the Chief Constable on the matter.

LIBERAL MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON. "THE RIGHTS AND WRONGS OF TAXATION."

During the present week several ward meetings of Liberals have been held in Warrington. That for the North-East Ward was held on Monday evening in the Brick-street Schoolroom, when an address on " The Rights and Wrongs of Taxation " was given by Mr. J. Hampden Jackson (editor of the "Financial Reformer"). The chair was taken by Ur. Z. Armi- tage, J.P , who was supported on the platform by Dr. Gornall, Councillor W. Pierpoint, Councillor H. Roberts, and Mr. H. Hankinson. There was a good attendance.

The .CHAIRMIN, who was received with applause, in the course of his introductory remarks, apologised for the ab- sence of Mr. J. Platt, who was confined to the house through illness, and also for Mr. Barker, from whom he had just re- ceived a note saying he was unable to be present. Sine - their last meeting in that room on the eve of the general election, they had passed tbreugh an experience that had not been altogether pleasant. They hid been defewed et the poll, but at the same time he thought they might feel con- fident that they had not been in any way disgraced. (Hear, heir). They fought a good fight, and they had had a can- didete who so gained their esteem as to ensure, if he elected to again centeet that constituency, their hearty co-operation. (Applause.) Mr. 11. ROBErrrs, who was received with applau,a,e re- ferring to the present representation of the borough, said that if he knew anything of the Liberals of• that ward, he knew that they did not mean to sit down to the present condition of things any longer than they could help. (Hear, bear.) When they remembered that their defeat was due to a combination which, to say nothing about its absurdity, was as illogical as any combinatien could pos-ibly be, and looking at tee feet that in the future there was no lieeli• hood of that combination repeating itself, he thouelot they bad good reason to believe that, if they made no their minds to let nO opportunity slip, they should reverse the present misrepresentation of the borough. (Hear hear.) If Ithe.y- were to do that they must have the strongest possible committees they could get—committees consisting of good and true men. They must have no black Sheep, for they had had some during the past election. (Hear, hear, ' and applause.) A ward committee having been elected. Mr. J. H. JAcS.S3N, who met with a very cordial recep- tion, gave his address. Most of them, he said, had a pretty ~keen appreciation of what taxition was when it reached themselves, but it surprised him the longer ha lived how very little the people of England, and even intelligent aim ' in the electoral body, knew how to choose between a right , principle and a wrong principle of taxvion. They always 'thought that a tax was wrong to some extent when it mode them feel, and the principle upon which most men acted was as to whether the tlx would touch them or not. (Hear, hear.) Those who bad read the " Financial Reform Al- manack "—(applause)—would know something of whet were the principles upon which they stood. They were principles which, at the foundation of their association in the year 1848. had the clear and decided approval of Richard Cobden and John Bright—(applause)—thev were the principles of free trade, and they said in the first place that it was a right principle of taxation that men should be taxed in proportion to their means. (Hear, hear.) They said that another right principle of taxation was that there should not be favouritism in the levying of texes, or in the assessment of the amount to be paid by different people. They said that it was a fundamental principle that industry should be left free ; they said that whatever taxes were levied they should be taxes • that would on the whole cost least in collecting, and that would discourage fraud as far as possible. (Applause.) Mr. Jackson then proceeded to contrast our present system of taxation with the principles just laid down, first, however, alluding to th a character of the pre-ient Parliament. In analysiug the list of members who had been returned to the new Parliament, ha foun4 that the number of great landowners, or the SOUR and heirs of great landowners, had been reduced from 277 to 190 (Applause.) This was satisfactory, as people always looked after their own interests no matter who sent them to Par- liament, and the landed class looked after the interest of the landed class. In the old Parliament they had 272 members , who were in some way related to peers, but in the new Par- liament they had only- 155 he was glad to say. (Hear, hear, and a Voice," And plenty, too.") In the old 'Parliament there were 168 members who were in same way connected with the fighting services of the country, but that number bad been reduced by 50, and there were only 118 who hAd in any way been connected with the fighting services in their lines. (Applause.) There were still articles left upon the customs tariff of this country, and this was contrary to their principle of taxation that no duty should be levied upon articles of consuption and of daily use. It was also according to their eerinciple that taxation should be levied upon the people in proportion to their means, and that the trade of the country should be set free in every direction. (Hear, hear.) There was nothing more common than the belief that a proper tax was easy to get. That was a most fallacious thing, as indirect taxes were often the means of freeing the rich, and particularly the landed classes, from their due share of taxation. The man who paid an indirect tax in the price of his beer and tobacco did not know what he was paying., and did not know what he was paying it tor. If they levied a direct tax a man was made to feel what he was paying, and such a man would he a fierce critic if his money was thrown away in Afghanistan, in Zululand, and Soudan campaigns. It would become more and more im- possible for the aristocratic class in this country to throw away money in foreign campaigns, and they would have to do more ler the people with the money they got from the people. (Heir, hear.) In a country like England they ought to raise their money honestly and go directly to the mass of the people of the country and cause them each to pay their due proportion. If to-morrow the working people realised in any degree how they were being "robbed and bamboozled "—these were Richard Cobdea's words—and how they had been robbed and bamboozled for ages by the intricate system of taxation,. they would refuse to pay another copper until the system was altered. (Hear, hear.) It was not that the working people of this country be- grudged to pay their fair share of taxation, as they were the most loyal of the people of the country, but there was reason to believe that they did not know how vast and dis- proportionate is the amount got from them as compared with the landed and wealthy classes. Referring to the waste in cennection with the commissariat department in the campaigns in Egypt, as revealed before Dr. Cameron's Com- mittee, and to the defective bayonets served out to the troops, Mr. Jackson said there would be nobody punished for these things, and even the names of those responsible would be kept back somehow or other, and the reason would probably be that they were sons or nephews or poor rela- tions of Lord Somebody or other. (Hear, hear, and laugh- ter.) Such things would be impossible under a direct system of taxation, if people would then see that their money was rightly spent. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the cost of collecting taxes, he said that in the collection of direct taxes the cost was £1 10 for every £lOO collected, but with regard to indirect taxation the cost was £8 103 for every £lOO. And this was not all, because it was esti- mated in the case of tobacco, that owing to the accumulat- ing profits which were required by the dealers on the duty of 3s 61 per pound that had to be paid when the leaf tobacco was imported, the price was augmented something like 500 per cent. With respect to the daties paid he pointed out that whiskey' which was very largely consumed by work- ing-men, the duty was I.Bs per dozen, while on champagne, which the working-men did not consume very largely, it was only 2a per dozen. Gin, the favourite beverage of the London poor, was taxed to the extent of 15s the dozen, while the port and sherry used at the Carlton and the Re- form Clubs only paid ss. These facts furnished cepitil guages as to what sort of Parliaments had been levying [taxes. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the death duties the i same favouritism existed. If a manufacturer who died left behind him mill property, machinery, and leasehold, which was called personality, to the value of £120,000, his execu- tors would have to pay 97,200 death duties; but if the owner of the freehold upon which the mill was erected died and left realty that was landed property to the value of £120,000 his executors would only have to pay £990, there' being a difference of £6,210 between the two individuals. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Jackson then referred to the assessments and the difference in the assessments of large mansions and other property. Chatsworth, he said, was a few veers ago, only assessed at £1,500 ; Hatfield, the residence of Ike Mar- psis of Salisbury, at £900; and Woburn Abbey at £7OO. With regard to the assessment of landed property, the land tax had never been revised since the time of William of Orange. Lord Derby, who owns the whole of Bootle and nearly the whole of 'Kirkdale, which are now the most valu- able districts about Liverpool, is paying land tax at this moment upon an assessment that was made in tile time of William of Orange, when all that district was A bowling sendhill with nothing on it but rabbits. (He rre hear, and laughter.) The Marquis of Bute has made a tremendous amount of money from the development of Cardiff and Swansea, but the land tax he is paying on his land in that nei,tie bourbon(' was made so far back- As the time of William and Mary. Tne Duke of Norfolk ,s paying en the same assessment, and so is Duke of Westminster, whose property in London is worth an almost fabulous amount. The Earl of Dudley had property which a few years back was de- ' veloped £700,000 in value in one year, and yet he paid lend tax on that property on an assessment made iu the time of William of Orange. He (Mr. Jackson) thought there was a good deal of wrong in taxation of that Rind. (Hear, , hear,) at the conclusion of his address Mr. Jackson was very loudly applauded. voAtefsteort ttwhoa noirs tt nh r e:Nrei Mr. Jackson questions haad ndbeenthe a e nhnasiwr me raend , ncronrudgi ,iellt the proceedings to a close. "FREE TRADE AND FAIR TRADE." . On Tuesday evening the meeting for tee North-west Ward was held in Wycliffe Hall. The chair was taken by Mr. F. Monks, J.P., and there were also on the platform Ald. J. Crosfield, J.P., Coancillor Roberts, and Mr. J. H. IJackson, the latter gentleman in the course of the evening

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 30. 1886
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 30. 1886

giving an address on "Free trade, fair trade, and depressed trade: A review of England's position." There was a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN, havirg mentioned that the first business , of the meeting woul:i be to appoint a committee for the ward, said they should strengthen themselves as much as possible for the work of tn election. He thought no man could look at the present position of the Tory party with- out feeling that were in great straits and without feeling that before very long they would have another general election with, he hoped, very much better results for the Liberal party. If that was to be the result it would have, so far as they were concerned to be brought about by hard work, and it would have to be done by sotne persuasive efforts being made in order to turn a majority of 776 against them into a majority in their favour. (Hear, bear, and ap- plause.) He thought they must all have oeeu disappointed, as he was disappointed at the last election, but it had not disheartened him one hit. It made him all the more in- cllned to say, as the Duke of Wellington said at Waterloo, "Up, lads, and at them.' (Hear, hear, and applause)

Mr. ROBE RTS said the ward committee would. be called to- gether for the parpuse of considerinc, the whole question of organisation of the ward. It had been felt for some time now that the ward was so large that it required sub-division, and the consideration of this matter would be left to the committee. (Hear, hear.) The ward committee was then elected.

Mr. JACKSON, who was received with loud applause, then gave his addreas. He said that the subject of his remarks that night partook very largely of the character of that of the previous night, which was" The rights and wrongs of taxation." For that great question of free trade serene fair trade really involved the same principles as to whether it was right or wrong, as to whether it was expedient or in- exoeilient, as to whether it was for the good or for the loss and detriment of the nation, to adopt any principle by which taxation should be levied upon the imports or barriers pat in the way of free trade between nations. It had been given to this nation to lead the way during the past 40 or 50 years in the adoption of the system of free trade, which he wished he could call a system of entire free trade, but which was more than in the case of any other European nation a system of nominal and almost entire free trade. They called their tariff system a system of tariffs for revenue purposes only. They had nominally discarded all idea of levying protective duties I upon imports. He was not laying down the thesis that their duties were not protective; but still it had been their proud position to lead the way in the adoption of free trade principles. There was a time, they knew, when tree trade was not the cuetona of England, orof the colonies of England. Why was it they had to drop tat system? Well, it was true that there had been in this co ntry for centuries a few wise people who saw that not only on moral grounds, but also upon econtonical grounds, it would be better for every- body that there should be a principle of free trade adopted, still these people were few in nutnber, and their influence did not extend S 9 widely as it would have been for the country's benefit it should have extended. They were really forced to adopt free trade by the ruin and the misery that the system of trotectien had brought upon this coantry. (Hear, hear.) All of them who read of those days of bitter suffering through tlse British islands would know that they were forced to the discussion of their fiscal position by that great agitation of Mr. Cobden and Mr. Bright to secure free trade in the article of corn. Between 1831 and 1839 Mr. Powlett Thompson, a Whig minister, knocked off 700 articles from their customs tariff, tied as a consequence during the next ten years the foreign commerce of the country increased to a great extent. It was next the privilege of Sir R. Peel in the year 1842 to set about abolishing the tariffs on a oreat number of articles until he reduced the list by about 730 articles. The consequence of this was that in the next ten years after that the foreign commerce of this country had been increased by a full half. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Then they came down to the year 1876, when Mr. Gladstone, the glorious leader of the Liberal party—(lend applause)—took up the work Sir R. Peel carried on until he had abolished every duty upon foreign manufactures im- ported into this cluntry- and until he had lowered the duty upon all raw material. What was the consequence of these fiscal reforms? In 20 years from that time the trade of the country had been doubled and more than doubled in extent. (Applause.) FOr every tax or fiscal hindrance they re- moved ;oat of the way they conferred a benefit upon them- selves just as much as the benefit they conferred on the , foreigner. He would clinch this argument by taking certain cases of import duties they had abolished. He would go back as far as the year 1607, and give them the history of one import duty. That was a time when the silk trade in this country was very flourishing. There was free trade in silk, and consequently there was a mannificent silk industry developed in these islands. Very shortly, however, the Government of this country thought, in those old unen- lightened days, that as the silk manufacture was growing rich they would make it grow richer by protecting it. But from the time when the Government 'protected the flourish- ing silk trade it began continuously to decline until in the year 1776 it was found that even then no less than 17,000 loans were idle, and the climax was reached when a law was passed to regulate wages and the number of ap- prentices employed in the silk mills. (Hear, hear.) They used to hear a good deal about the harm that had been done to the silk industry of this country by the Cobden treaty with France, but protection had been more ruinous to that trade than ever free trade had been. (Hear, bear.) As illustrating the beneficial effects free trade in any particular article had upon the country, he took the cases of glass and bricks. The import duties upon these articles were taken off in 1841, and in the ten years following the general in- Grease of population was 13 per cent., but the increase in the number of glass-makers was over 50 per cent., the in- crease of brick-makers was over 70 per cent., and all over the building trade, connected with glass and brick- making, the increase was over 40 per cent. That was a most remarkable fact which he hoped they would bear in mind. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With regard to the question of free trade Richard Cobden took a higher standpoint than most politicians were accus- tomed to take, for, when Sir Robert Peel had jnst carried the Corn Laws he wrote to him saying that free trade prin- ciples were applicable to every article as well as to corn and must be carried out in all our ports. He (the lecturer) asked them did not free trade principles commend themselves as principles that were right to be carried out and had the ap- proval of their common sense. We wanted people to come to our island shop to buy. Import duties, of whatever kind, crippled the buyers who had to go to that shop, and the buyers became poorer thereby and less able to purchase that which we bad got to sell. (Hear, hear.) We did not in this island grow enough food for our own people, nor could we produce enough raw material for our own manufac- tures, and that being so, if duties were put upon these things we must tax and fetter oriraelves. • The true theory was that every nation throughout the world should produce what it best could, and should be free to exchange the articles so produced. (Hear, hesrr.) The highest right of property, he was speaking now to political economists, was the right to exchange the.fruits of one's industry to others, no matter where they found them, unobstructed by the State. (Applause.) If A might trade with B, but might not trade with C without a penalty put by the Government in the shape of a treaty that was a form of slavery. If any trade or any set of eapitelists, landowners, or manufacturers, said that they could not earn an honest living without the mass of the people being taxed that was a form of pauper- ism. Those were the principles of the free trade movement. Upon these principles, as far as they had been carried out ia this country, they had flourished. If he ware to take the last ten years of what the Tory papers were accustomed to call unparalleled depression and show them the social state and condition of this country, by carefully-selected Government statistics, they would say with him "If this is what free trade is doing for the country do not let us have less, but more of it." (Applause.) In those ten years, despite the agricultural depression and the enormous amount of emigration, the population had increased by four millions of people. During that period the ex- ports had increased in value 10s per bead of every man of the population. The imports of the country had increased £2 4e per head for every person of the population. The consumption of articles like rice, sugar, and tea, generally used by the masses of the people, also had a great increase, and the pauperism returns, al- though they had increased in Ireland from exceptional circumstances, bad in Scotland gone down by 23,000, and in England and Wales by more than a quarter of a million. The convictions for crime in the United Kingdom.were 3,000 fewer than at the beginning of that period, and there were two millions more children at school. (Applause.) The savings of the people, take them altogether, were 50 per cent greater in amount, and the number of insolvencies was about half. During that period also we had paid about 35 millions of debt. The clearing-house returns were largely increased, the number of passengers travelling by railway had been doubled, and the receipts for traffic were 50 per cent greater. Since the adoption of free trade the general average of wages had gone up 50 per cent, the hours of work were less exacting, and in many respects besides the position of the working-man with a weekly wage had been improved. The duration of human life had been increased by four years and a half, and the bank de- posits of the country since we commenced free trade had risen from 70 millions until they were in excess of 930 millions. He would give some facts and figures relating to the time just before free trade. During the period of fair , trade, when foreign goods were taxed, they gave the land- owners, but no one else, a chance. In 1820 to 1836, under protection, there were no less than eight Parliamentary Commissions to inquire into agricultural distress alone. In 1817 there were 409 people out of 575 in one agricultural parish receiving poor relief, In the city of Ely, in the heart of the skgricultural district, one fourth of the people had to keep the other three-fourths ; in Huddersfield 13,000 people were reported as in a state of semi-starvation. Mr. Jackson then described at bands monopolies Instancing were Bf y the la rsgheo rant! theych ol tarhmnek,eed effectsw Ring monopolistshi pni monopolies, he referred to protection in America and the which raised the cost of the articles produced and ut wanted to see the disastrous effects of monopolies in this country the means to pave the way was to put on a few more import duties, which crushed down the small capitalists and gave

every advantage of combination to the great ones. Lord Palmerston in 1864 said : " A protected class puts on its night cap ana goes to sleep ; competition is required to stimulate the energies of trade; to make the men in it be- stir themselves and improve the calling to which they have devoted their mind and capital ;" and it was a fact that during the operation of free trade there had been a rapid increase of inventions and a rapid, improvement in menu- teetering processes in consequence of the stimulus given to men to bestir themselves. tele imagined that some fair trade manufacturers must want to shut out the inventions of 'foreign nations, and keep out the competition which com- pelled them to alter their machinery. Just in proportion as they shut out competition they would in spite of themselves create monopolies, which tended to the depreciation of the article supplied, as well as to the increase of its price. (applause.) Regarding depression, he argued that the trade of natisens was subject to periodical fluctua- tions, or cycles, coming at periods of about seven or ten years, and that being so it was unreasonable to expect that commerce, even under a system of free trade, would not be without its changes. If they looked at the especial circumstances they would see that there had been enough, and more than enough, to cause the depression the Tories talked of. There was a time when everything was too dear, they were making money too quick, when profits were too high, when ownys of mines were making more than they had a right to. and when bankers and capitalists were netting immense profits. They were going a bit too fast— sowing their wild oats—and a corresponding period of de- pression naturally followed. From 1872 to 1874 the people, flush of money, did foolish things with it. Money to the amount of 160 millions lent to bankrupt foreign nations turned out bad in one year, and in addition six successive bed harvests were experienced, and the farming classes alone were estimated to have lost more than 150 millions of money that used to he spent in home trade. There was also the sudden stop of the war indemnity to be considered. When the harvests were bad in England they were fruitful in other countries, and corn was brought from all qearters. Thinking this merry state of things would last for ever, shipbuilders and owners gave orders for more. ships and steamers, which had afterwards to be worked at unremu- nerative freights, and brought a glut of foreign goods into the country when the demand for corn bad been fulfilled. Mr. Jackson also condemned a large expenditure on Euro- pean armies and navies, and said that the time was come when men were beginning to think of the extravagance of spending 150 millions a year in the censumptinn of intoxi- cating drinks, and were retrenching in that direction. In this way a time of depression induced economy, and led to the prevention of national waste. (Applause.) Mr. GEORGE WALLINGTON, who proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, said that their interest in the subject dealt with had been revived in a strong manner. The more he heard of it and the more he was convinced of the advantages of free trade. (Heir, hear.) Mr. JOHN CROSVIELD seconded the resolution. He said that he had listened to the lecture with a great deal of pleasure, and had gained a deal of information. He quite believed, with the lecturer, that the depression that they had been suffering from during the last few veers had been more a depression in capital than among the working class. Hie opinion was that the working class were as well off, or perhaps better, than ever they were; but capital had been suffering from the fact that in 1872 and 1874 they were on the very top wave of prosperity., and every manufacturer in the country was making too much money. The iron works in Warrington were making 40, 50, 60, and 70 per cent, of profit, and what was the consequence? The manufacturers began to enlarge their works, with the consequence that there was toe great a power of production. They (Messrs. Crosfield) could make more soap than the people could use, and the consequence was that they had to sell it for less • than it cost to make it. (Laughter.) That was neither free trade, fair trade, or any other kind. FOf that they had themselves to blame; they were prosperous gnd thonat that it was going to last for ever. He asked them to re- member that if they put a duty upon anything coming into this country, it was they who would have to pay for it, for the cost of the article to the purchaser was increased. (Applause.)

• litr. JACKSON, in replying, said that the nations who had during the last 20 years considerably increased their tariffs were at this moment suffering more in proportion from de- pression than England was doing. He then gave statistics showing how in America, Germany, and France the fair trade system had resulted in loss of national wealth, low wages, and lack of employment. At present, in New York, there were 50 000 men out of work, in Boston 20,000, in Chicago 25,000, and ire St. Louis 15,000: while in Germany several millions were working for £2O a year-9s 7id a week. Since the introduction of protection in France the silk industry there had declined in value to the tune of 11 millions, and was half ruined. A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the proceed- ings to a close. "THE RESULT OF THE GENERAL ELECTION." LECTURE BY MR. kW VC,ES. On Thursday evening a crowded meeting of Liberals of South-East Ward was held in the old Wesleyan School- room, Buttermarket-street, when the chair was occupied by Alderman Burgess, and a lecture delivered by Mr. Joseph Howes, who took for his subject " The Result of the General Election."

The CHAinuaN, before introducing the lecturer, said that if there was one thing more than another that they should rejoice at it wae the fact that Mr. Gladstone still lived. What- ever difficuliies there might be in forming and carrying on a Government, if Mr. Gladstone was not equal to the work, no man was. He felt persuaded that Mr. Gladstone would conquer the difficulties in the way. (Applause.) He advised his audience to be careful how they allowed newspapers to be their guides. They might read the leading articles, but not for their political guidance. What did the editor of a newspaper know more than any man in that room? Why should he set himself up as a guide and teacher ? He knew some of them, and so did they, and they knew there were other callings in life as well as editing for which they were quite as well suited. He said it without any feeling of antagonism to the Press, but he believed that the press was prostituted by the people who had got control, especially in London. They must not be too much newspaper governed; but must judge for them- selves. Read everything they could and go by their own convictions, and it would be much better. It was likely that they might be called into action before the year was out, and he urged them, therefore, to be very careful in the selectien of ward officers. When the time came when the struggle should again take place, he hoped to see as grand a committee as fought in that ward on the last election, and, in his judgment gave as good and true an account of them- selves as could have been desired. (Applause.) Mr. Howas Pahl that at the last. election Warrington elected to io with the minority, and remained behind when Many other parts of the country were struggling for im- provement and reform. But he hoped sincerely that they would be with the winning party next time. Warrington was a constituency of too much importance to be on the Tory side—(applause)--and he thought that one thing that the general election proved was that a Tory Government was an impossibility in this country. They must hope that those who did not vote for the Liberal party might see their way to return to an old allegiance, or to break through the dark gloom of Toryism. The Liberal Government from 1880 to 1835 did good work. The Employers' Liability Act, Ground Game Act, Irish Land Act, the Corrupt Practices Act were good bills, but the crowning work of the session was the extension of the franchise, (Applause.) The true feeling of Liberalism was discovered throughout the land when the election came. If battle cries could have won a victory the Tory party would easily have gained the day. They had the cry of fair trade. They went to the rural voters and told them that the foreigner should not be allowed to send cheap grain into the country, and in the towns they advocated a tax upon manufactured goods. That was standing with one leg in one county and the other in another county. They Dad another cry and discovered that the Liberal party were trying to rob everybody because they bad' dared to suggest the advisability of distributing the land more equitably among the people by fair and legitimate means. The Liberals recommended that the proper solution of the land question would remove many difficulties, and the Tories thereupon raised the cry of three acres and a cow. They were only too willing to cast ridicule on any sugges- tion,rhat had a tendency to improve the people. During the last 50 years the land had been taken from the people by men who should never have been allowed to do so, taken legally, hut by the aid of bad laws, and therefore those laws should be repealed as soon as possible. The Radicals suggested that county government boards should be entrusted with the compulsory power of purchase, and that was what the Tories were afraid of. They did not like the power of compulsory purchase of the waste lands for the purpose of parcelling it out in allotments. But they should have known that that would only sharpen the appetites of the people for the very things they wanted to keep from them. The next cry was the Church in danger, and in the rural districts Hodge stood by and laughed and said "Church be no friend of mine." (Laughter.) It was a melancholy fact that the vicar, who should stand as the guardian of the poor, between the poor and injustice, al- most invariably stood with the rich man in the district, even when the rich man was oppressing the poor, and the farm labourer had disc,vered that if the Church was his mother Church, his mother had weaned him at a very ten- der age. There was also the cry of the Constitution in danger, and it was likely that next it would be the Empire in danger. (Laughter.) Since the last election a farmer's friend in the preen of '3lr. Arch had been welcomed to Par- liament, but not by a Tory. The Tories tried their best to keep him out, but they failed. Ee was sorry that the Irish party gave their support to the Tories. He believed they had secured 20 seats in that way, but what good had it,done thorn ? Despite all their battle cries the Tories were de- feated, and the result was that it was realised now that people were ready for disestablishment and disendowment, and that, no matter what number ofebattle cries might be raised, it was impossible far the Tory party to get a sufid- ciynt majority to carry out the affairs of the nation. The result of the election was a glorious triumph for Liberal principles. He advised them to look well after their organi- sation and work shoulder to shoulder together. (Ariplanse.) A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Howes on the motion of Mr. JOIIN CHALMERS, seconded by Mr. PILLINGER, and, the chairman having been thanked for his services, the pro- ceedings concluded.

PRESENTATION TO MR. W. CROSFIELD AT WARRINGTON. On Wednesday evening Mr. Wm. Crosfield, J.P., the Liberal candidate at -the recent. Parliamentary election in this borough, was presented with an address by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P., on behalf of the Liberals of Warrington. The meeting at which the presentation was made *was held in Wycliffe Mall, and was very largely attended by the Liberals of the town. The address was very handsomely bound in the form of an album and covered several pages, each of which was beautifully illuminated with original designs, and a large number of other similarly illuminated pages contained the signatures of the president, and other officers of the Liberal Association, and of the members of the Genet-0 Council, the number of signatures being about three hundred. The album, with the address in- scribed, was supplied by Messrs. John Walker and• Co., _Examiner Office, Warrington, and as a speci- mon of the bookbinder's and illuminator's art, was very generally admired, The following is the text of the address :

TO WILLIAM CROSFIELD, ESQ , J.P. SIR, The members; of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Asaociation desire to record their h-arty appreciation of the ability and devotion cisplayed by you in your recent candidature for the borough of Warrington. Throughout the contest your conduct was most honourable, and the zeal and earnestness wlfch always marked your ac- tions elicited our warmest admiration. We regret most deeply that in consequence mainly of a com- bloatiou of Interests, as novel as it was discreditable, our con- stituency has temp-warily receded fr rn the honourable Pxt- tion we have held during the past six years. We trust that in the enjoyment of good health you may be enabled for many years ta come to render to the great cause of Liberalism that hearty ano able support which has been so long the characteristic of the family whose honoured name you bear. At the meeting the chair was taken by Mr. S. Rigby, chairman of tbe Ltberal Association, and, in addition to Mr. W. Crosfield and Mr. J. G. McNlinnies, he was sup- ported on the platform by Alderman J. Crosfield, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P., Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P., Mr. F. Monks, J.P., Mr. W. Pierpoint, Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., Rev. J. Yonge, and Mr. H. Roberts. Mr. H. Roserers read the following letter of apology for non-atteudance from Mr. George Crosfield, viz. London, Jan. 18, 1886.—My dear sir.—ln answer to your note of the 16th inst., I find it necessary to avoid all trav- elling and exposure to the cold and variable weather that I can, and therefore I must ask to be excused coming down to Warrington on the 27th inst. I should have been glad to be present and publicly thank William Crosfield for his well-merited and unrewarded exertions. I believe that a very large number of voters already regret having voted for the Tories. (Hear, hear.) The so-called Fair Traders, the Irishmen, and the Roman Catholics, will soon find that the Tory party will do nothing for them, and have simply use them as toole to obtain their own selfish ends. I hope Mr. Gladstone will refuse to take office, and leave the Tory party to extricate themselves from the fraudulent mess they have got into, and I should be glad to see the Queen in a dilemma owing to her marked preference for a Tory Gevernment. (Hear hear, and laughter.)—Yours very truly, GEO. CROSFIELD. Mr. ROBERTS also mentioned that he had received letters of apology from Mr. F. A."Roherts, Mr. J. Platt, and Mr. C. 8: Burgess, who were prevented from attending by ill- health. The CHAIRMAN, who was cordially received, referring to the late election in Warrington, advised them to use their utmost exertions to remedy the defeat they had suffered. (Applause.) He knew that there had been various causes at work in Warrington. Some foolish persons who had not lived so long as h•e had began to talk about fair trade. If they had heard what had been said on that subject by men who had thought of it and made the subject their own he was quite sure they never would have been disturbed in their belief. Nothing was better for this country than cheep food and plenty of it. (Hear, bear.) He should like theni to consider that question, and disabuso their minds once for all. (Hear, hear.) eieferring to Mr. Crosfield, he said the more they were acquainted with him the more he would grow in their estimation, and the better they knew him the more they would appreciate the qualities he would have shown as a representative. (Applause.) A good worker, a conscientious man, a just man and true, a roan of increasing energy of purpose and of broad mind, what more did they want? (Hear, hear, and applause.) He asked them where if they were to have a man not resident in the town would they get a better? (Hear, hear, and loud ap- plause.)

Mr F. Monts said that he stood before them as a repre- sentative of the largest ward in the town, and all he could say was that if it be the wish of the electors to request Mr. Crosfield to fight the battle again he did not know where they could have a better man. (Hear, hear, and applause.) All he coald say was that they would promise to do what they could for his triumphant return. Mr. Rigby had asked how it was they were beaten at the last election. The fact was there were too many on the other side— (laughter)—and if the same influences were at work in the same cause there would be too many on the other side again. What they had to do was to use ttesir efforts with a view of turning a majority on the other side into a majority on their side. (Applause.) He did not care whether that majority was 776 or 76. (Hear, hear.) Before that con- test he never saw Mr. Crosfield, but the more they saw of him the better they like al him ; they felt that he had some backbone in him, and that was the sort of man they wanted as a member of Parliament. (Applause.) Mr. C. BRoADBENT said it was a great pleasure to him to be present that night. They had very momentous political news that morning. (Hear, hear.) Mr. George Crosfield ex- pressed the hope that Mr. Gladstone would not accept of office. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He (Mr. Broadbent) did not know whether Mr. George Crosfield would be right, but he thought that Mr. Gladstone would accept office, and at all events it seemed the most natural thing that when the majority of Englishmen are Liberals there should be a Liberal Government in office. (Hear, hear.) They could only hope to have a few years more of Mr. Gladstone's ser- vices, but be had the energy, power, and ability to still do great work for this ceuntry. (Applause.) He (Mr. Broad- bent) only hoped that those great powers would not be frittered away by senseless obstruction in Parliament. (Hear. hear.) With regard to the presentation of that even- ing Mr. Broadbent said he thought they were prepared to esteem Mr. W. Crosfield the first time he came among them, but every day he had been with them since they esteemed him more highly. (Loud applause.) Mr. WILLIAM PIERPOINT commented on the letter re- ceived frem Mr. George Crosfield. Mr. George Crosfield, he remarked, used the word unrewarded in reference to the efforts of Mr. W. Crosfield. Perhaps the efforts that that gentleman put forth in the late campaign entitled that he should have been successfel, but, at all events, he did not think Mr. Crosfield was unrewarded, for the simple fact that he had such a splendid gathering of his old friends to meet him there that night. There was another sentenc iin the letter that was rather apropos. It was the mention of the preference shown by the Queen towards the present and past Conservative Governments in personally assisting at the opening of Parliament. Perhaps it was a testimony of the extreme loyalty of the Conservative party to the cause of the Crown, but he ventured without fear of contradic- tion to say that the best loyalty to the Constitution and the Crown of this country was found in the Liberal ranks. He should like to say a few words of the high estimate he had formed of the character of Mr. Crosfield. He had not known him long, but the more he had seen of him the better he had liked him. He liked him as a politician and as a friend. They fought hard but were beaten by a peculiar combina- tion of circumstances as illogical as it was curious. There was the priest combined with the parson, and in addition there was the publican. It was not the first time, however, that they had seen the parson combined with the publican, and he did not think it would be the last. But he did not know how it was that with the priest, the publican, and the parson they found the Parnellites. Many of the Catholic Irishmen in Warrington whom he canvassed told him that it was the greatest wrench they had ever experienced, in deserting the Liberal petty and voting for those whom they had always considered their opponents. In addition there was the Roman Catholic voting with the Orangeman, and the Orangeman patting the Roman Catholic en the back. (Laughter.) He did not think that they would see that combination at the next election. It was illogical, in fact, people were right in saying that it was unholy. (Hear, hear.) How, he asked, was he at present represented, or misrepresented. Sir Gilbert Greenall- would naturally be in favour of non-interference in the affairs of the Estab- lished Church. He ',Mr. Pierpoint) was a Churchman, but Mr. Crosfield would have represented him thoroughly on the question of religious equality. There was also the question of the liquor traffic. He was not a teetotaller, but he was aware of the fact that the less a man I used in(oxicating drinks the better it was for him and his family. (Applause.) Their present representative must of necessity be pledged to maintain the present monopoly of the drink traffic. If Mr. Crosfield had been in Parliament he would have been in fav- our of any proper and fair temperance legislation. In Mr. Cros- field also they would have had one into would have been pre- pared to support an investigation the question of unfair incidence of taxation, and it was very possible he might have joheed Mr. Collings in voting against the enclosure of commons. In him, too, they would have had a strong de- fender of free trade. (Applause.) Mr. TANNER, a working man who hails from the Forest of Dean, spoke in eulogistic terms of Mr. Crosfield, and re- proached the Liberals of Warrington for not having used greater exertions in his favour than they had done. Mr. S. BARLOW thought, on the contrary, that the result of the late election was a great credit to them. No one would have gone through a candidature with so much credit to himself and the party as did Mr. Crosfield—(applause)— but no gentleman could have won the election in the Lib- eral interest under the then existime, circumstances. Mr. McMixterns, on rising to make the presentation, was received with loud cheering, He said that he had not had an opportunity of addressing any representative party of Liberals since the late election. A good dell had been said with which he agreed, but he thought that perhaps his duty would be best discharged if he presented that acknow- ledgment to Mr. William Crosfield of his abilities and the service he had rendered to the Liberal party. There was no doubt that at the last election they suffered a very heavy blow and great diseoutagement, and he thought .they all understood how it came about that a majority of 529 on their side was turned into a majority of 716 on the other side. It meant that 050 people joined the other party. He did not know that it was desirable that they should pursue that inquiry any further. They knew exactly how it hap.
