(Applause.) They would never again in that borough enter into a contest under circumstances so adverse as those they had to encounter during the last election. No candidate that they could have got could have won the battle, for circumstances were so much against them, but no candi date could have fought the battle more successfully than Mr. Crosfield did. His sincere desire was that they should have to fight another contest under Mr. Crosfield's auspices and under his banner. (Applause) Perhaps no one saw more of Mr. Crosfield during the contest than he did, but, those that saw most of him thought best of him. (Applause.) Day by day, as the contest advanced, he grew in favour with his party, and day by day they came to the conclusion that no man could have fought their contest better than Mr. Croefield did. He had great pleasure in presenting Mr. Crosfield with that testimonial from the Liberal party, and he joined most sincerely in the wish that he (Mr. Crosfield) might live for many years to come to render the great cause of Liberalism that hearty and able support which had been so long a characteristic of those bearing the honoured name of Crosfield. (Applause.) Mr. Wm. CROSTIELD, who met with a very enthusiastic reception, the applause being continued for some time, said they would readily believe him and he hoped his friends present would give him credit for the utmost sincerity when be said that he could have addressed them with far greater confidence on that occasion if there had been a spice of adverse criticism in the remarks to which they had been listening. If somebody would only have kindly attributed to him some single fault in the losing of the last election he thought he could have defended himself, but to prepare oneself for so much kindness required more nerve than it did to meet criticism, the more so because of the wording of that address, which was beautiful in its execution, and was more valuable still for the friendliness of its tone. It at- tributed to him virtues for which he certainly could not claim any monopoly. It spoke of the zeal and the earnest- ness with which they were good enough to say he conducted the late contest so far as it was his part to bear it. Zeal and earnastness were certainly not confined to their candidate for the zeal and earnestness of those who were most immediately around him, his managing committee, certainly was a thing to emulate and a thing to remember. He had suffered not one iota from the late contest. He believed that at the end of the contest he was better in health, though certainly not better in spirits, than when he began. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was sorry to say that the number of apolo- gies they had that night, and what one knew for oneself led one to fear that the exertions which in some instances were very much harder than anything he put forth, had hit considerably harder many of their own number, whose physical condition was worse that day that it was when they began the contest. (Hear, bear ) He only hoped that wherever his lot might be in the future, and whoever might in the future fight their battle, that they both might have as earnest supporters as he had had in the past. (Applause.) They spoke of the combination of in- terests by which they were defeated. During the later days of the late contest they who had the opportunity of seeing what was going on became aware that there were combina- tions against them which made it increasingly difficult for them to fight their battle, and he was bound to say that when the result of that election was announced to him be bad some feeling that there might have been a personal humiliation in the result of that unfortunate contest. (" No.") And as he went home to Liverpool that feeling grew upon him, and it was not till the early heurs of the following morning, when one became aware that the same thing that had happened to him was happening to infinitely better men, more particularly in this county. (Hear, hear.) He then began to feel that there was not a personal element in his defeat, and that he was only sharing a common lot. (Hear, hear:, They were defeated, as Mr. McMinnies had said, by temporary alliances, and, as Mr. Pierpoint had reminded them, special and particular interests. (Hear, hear.) It was not the first time that the Liberal party had been thrown out of office or kept out of office by the ...ecclesiastical system which has means of working which they could not countermine, and which, in spite of all their good intentions, again on that occasion had overtaken them. That system had defeated the Liberal party in times gone by. They had defeated it, he thought, as Mr. McMinnies had said, from conscientious motives, but it had turned out that the defeat had not ac- complished the benefits which it had been soueht to gain. (Hear, hear.) Whilst they had suffered or that ground in the past, he thought he was right in saying that that was the first occasion upon which they had to meet an organisa- tion similar to one which was a very material element in their opposition. It was the first time, he believed, that a very large section of the community had been twisted and turned from day to day in response to the will of a single individual—a single leader. He (Mr. Crosfield) might say that be looked forward to the future of politics with more dread since the election than he did before they had had that experience ; a dread that in the future that kind of element might show itself again, and that in future they might have large masses of electors turned, for selfish ends, at the will of some ether 'possibly less scrupulous individual. .(Hear, hear.) Mr. McMinnies had told them that they had been reviewing their position, and they hed bad many suggestions that evening as to the remedies which should be adopted. He was exceedingly glad they had made a good start that week in Warrington in the one particular direction which was the most valuable, and that was in the educational direction. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They were that week enjoying a series of lectures, which be hoped would have some beneficial effect on the minds of those who heard them. He thought that more of that kind of political education was wanted. tHear, hear.) The Liberal party depended upon the intelligence of the electors at large : it might do for the " stupid party " to come out when there was a heated contest going on, but the Liberal party, which is always advancing, must of necessity educate itself as it goes along. He hoped that process of education which they found so valimble would be adopted in all other constituencies, and that in the future candidates there and elsewhere might feel confidence in appealing directly to the individual intelligence and the individual oonscience of each elector, disregarding the leadership, of any particular individual (Hear, hear, and applause.) Referring to the general question of the politics of the day, he said the Conservative Government had given them the Queen's speech, many of the phrases of which looked ex- ceedingly plausible, and taking them on the surface one was inclined to think that after all we were going to have sonic good work even by a Conservative Ministry. But when an inkling of the details was got it was seen that the phrases were mere phrases, and were not likely to result in any very great benefit to the com- munity. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crosfield then criticised the pro- cedure proposals of the Government, which he said looked fairly ssatifactery, but were not nearly so satisfactory as they looked. One thing was wanted which the Government did not seem inclined to give, and that was some power to stop the torrent of talk which was always going on. (Hear, hear.) During the first few weeks of the late contest he bad occasion to remark that in the course of the few weeks the Conservative party had been in office they had got mixed up in tho wars, one in Eastern Rournelia and the other in Burmah. Since the Queen's speech was delivered, they had got mixed up in another broil, and the English fleet, it was said, had been ordered into Turkish waters, for what he thoifght to be the most lamentable object for which the British fleet could possibly be used—the support of that Dower which is least powerful of all the powers of Europe, and which had given England the most trouble during the last forty years of any power they had to do with. (Hear, hear, and applause.) And meanwhile the country for which they all had an admiration, and which had a great history, was left in the position which Lord Beaconsfield pointed out to her some seven years ago when he said that " Greece has a future, and she can afford to wait." Refer- ring to the defeat of the Government on the question of allotments he (Mr. Croafield) said they must all regret that many of those who might be regarded as thoroughly good Liberals, and whom they should hope to see in the next -Liberal eiovernmeet had not felt it their duty to support Mr. Jesse Collings. (Hear. hear.) But it was important to remark that they had voted against hint on a matter of detail rather than on a matter of principle. (Hear, mr.) Lord 'Remington conspicuously pointed out that he -esidered there was no necessity why he should permanently Fever himself from the Liberal party because he did not se, exactly the same on that par- ticular question, and he gave very broad hint that if some detail had been intreduced inte the amendment he would have found himself on the side of the majority. (Hear, hear.) Lord Hartington who had done such loyal work for the Liberal party had shown that he was still at heart a thorough Liberal as all his family bad ever been, and that he would still remain in the ranks which followed Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.) Having ridiculed the Irish policy of the Government, Mr. Crosfield concluded by saying that the recent contest in which they had been engaged together had left many pleasant reminiscences, and he felt ha had made friendships which he should treasure all the days of his life—(applause)—and whatever his political future might be fie should feel that his experience of Warrington during the year 1885 had been most valuable and to him most pleasant. (Loud applause). Mr. Jome CROSVIELD, wno was received with applause, moved a vote of thanks to the chairman Ho congratula- ted those present on that enthusiastic meeting and he re- joiced, he said, to see that in the Liberal party in Waning- ton in spite of the defeat there was a spirit of determina- tion to wipe it out. (Applause.) They were defeated by unfair and underhand means, and they would never rest until they had wiped out that stain. (Loud applause.) He bad p.orfect faith in the Liberal party. CONCERT. On Monday the congregation of S. Paul's Church. Warrington, celebrated their annual tea party 50C1 entertainment at the Public Hall in a very successful manner. At tea there were between 700 and 800 people present, and at the subsequent entertainment , an audience assembled that almost filled the built-11'2z- , In tbe absence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., who w3s expected to preside. the chair was occupied by The MAYOR t,Alderman Harrison) who, in openirg proceedings, said that he thought that if there was anyege entitled to occupy that position it was the vicar of Sti Paul's, Mr. Wilkinson. He felt he had greatness thn.24 upon him in being called upon to occupy that position. lc must be gratifying to their vicar to find that the annual tes• party connected with Sr. Paul's Church was alwaes pre- eminently sacctssful. Without throwing the slightest re- flection on other churches he might account for that bY saving, in the first place, that Mr. Wilkinson was the o'dest clergyman in the parish, not in years, but his church ranked next to the Parish Church. He had been longer amongst them, and althouab yet comparatively a young. man, he was the senior clergyman in Warriegton. He WO supported by a most amiable and excellent wite,Mrs. Wilkin- son. (Applause.) Long might their excellent Vicar con- tinue to preside ever the parish, and he hop?,d also that Mrs. Wilkinson might be spared in her sphere of usefulness for a long time to come. (Applause.) The Rev. S. WILKINSON thanked the Chairman for his kind remarks, and read a letter from Sir Gilbert Greenall stating that he could not be present to take the chair, as he must be in his place in the House of commons that even- ing. He (Mr. Wilkinson) sincerely thanked all their friends - for the assistance they bad rendered during the past year. From his heart he thanked those 200 men and women who helped them in various goods works in connection. with the parish of St. Paul's. He believed they regarded what they did as a labour of love. They had started during the past year a mission house In Hoyle-street, which was doing good work. They bad a large Sunday school, and they had about 200 children to service on Sunday, as well as a service on Friday evening. They had a Bible class. for women on the Monday, and various good works were carried on there, principally 17 lay people and by their mission woman, Miss Macleenzie, and Messrs. Smith and Lawless, who had worked indefatigably. (Applause) Their day schools and Sunday schools were in an excellent con- dition, and everything connected with the schools was flourishing. Another great work, the improvement of the churchyard, had also been going on. DEATH or A GIAN'N.—The decease is reported, on Sunda. at the City of London Infirmary„ of James Macdonald. the well-known Scotch giant. He was A native of Aberdeen- shire, stood 71t. 2in. high, and at the time of his death was fifty-six years of age. Macdonald, who like most giants was Of an arnlabls dispoiition, met with a serious accident in 1882, having been run over and had both his legs broken, since which he has always been ailing; but the imtradiate cause of death ,vas dropsy. The man who takes a hint is not necessarily a thief. AaTISTIC POINT.—A lady calls the little memorandum her butcher sends in with the meat "Pencillings by the weigh." "You never saw my hands as dirty as yours," said a tnother to her little girL "No, but grandma did !" was the prompt reply. THE B 11/IND.—Customer : Have yen some good Havana cigars ?—New boy: Not just now, sir; but we shall have some in in about an hoar. The printer round the corner is at work on the labels now. Bland election-canvasser during the late elections: My good woman, I understand your husband is not at home; but perhaps you may be able to tell me whether he intends to support Mr. Keith ?—Good woman: My certy ! Believe me, sir, I have seen better days." "So have I," said Lamb, handing the , poor creature a shilling—" so have I; it's a miserable day! I Good-bye!" CONSOLATION.—The other day a lady on one of the I Southern railways was watching with horror the process of putting a huge leather box directly over her head. "Oh, sir, what if it should fall?" she exclaimed tremblingly to the owner. "All right, madam," was the reply; "don't j you bother about the portmanteau. There is nothing in it that will break." BLACK HEN'S EGGS.—" Two dozen black hen's eggs," said an old woman, addressing a grocer. "Black hen's egga!" exclaimed he • "I don't know a black hen's egg , from any other colour;c1. citicken's." "Troth, then, I do," ; I said the woman. "Then go and pick them out yourself," he replied, p)inting to a large basket of eggs. The woman did so, and picked out two dozen of the largest eggs in the I basket. ABOUT A LOVING Srouss.—The death of a member of an old Boston family recalls the following incident connec- ted with him. A few years ago he was preparing to leave ; for Europe, and his wife, while packing his trunk, said, 1 " Hens is my picture ; shall I put it in with the other things ?" "Yes, certainly; for I should feel lost without 1 it. You know I take it with me wherever I go." "Yes," replied the wife," I know you do; but I don't believe you ever look at it !" "Indeed I do, every night of my life!" , rejoined the loving spouse. The little velvet case was put ; into the trunk as usual. When the husband returned and ! the trunk was being unpacked by the happy couple, the! wife found the case, and, taking it out, said, "Well, tell . me now—did you look at my picture whileyou were away?" "Look as it? Indeed I did, and it was the greatest corn-: fort to me!" The wife opened the empty case and showed him that she had taken the picture out and packed only the case; the likeness had remained at home in her own upper drawer! OILING A CRANK.—The palatial steamer Mary Powell , was on her daily trip up the Hudson. A number of pas- sengers had gathered around the open door of the engine- room, looking with interest at the movements of the pon- derous machinery. Among the passengers was Sam Foster, a New York gentleman, and a practical joker. He is a young ; man of means, and was elegantly dressed. He is, moreover, a very good amateur ventriloquist. "Now, boys," said Foster," let us have some fun with the engineer." A. creak- ing, squeaking noise was heard among the machinery. The i engineer was sometrhat startled, and with great industry 1 and an oil can he lubricated various and sundry parts of ' the machinery. The can contained half a pint of oil. Fos- ter nudged one of his companions in the ribs, and soon after- wards the machinery squeaked again. Once more the en- gineer calmed down a suspected piston by anointing it with his alleviator. The squeaking still continued, and Foster pointed out the place that in his opinion needed oiling. The 1 engineer toek up the alleviator, and, removing the cork, ' p )ured the contents down the back of the festive Fester and ; over his elegant suit of clothes. " There," said the en- 1 gineer—" I don't think that crank will equeak again in a I hurry." The most carefully-edited journal is fallible. On the I New York Herald proof-readers have been suspended for ; weeks. In spite of this severe discipline, the Herald once made the astonishing announcemeet that "a long line of scorpions' feathers filed into the church," instead of " sure 1 pliced fathers." A reporter on that paper had occasion to ! quote a verse from a familiar hymn in which the word "herald" occurred. The proof-reader dutifully underscored 1 the word, and the verse appeared, "Hark, The Herald ; angels sing !" It was in the New York World's report of a ! political meeting that the word " ehoate " was so ludicrously I misprinted as to make the blunder famous. "The snouts of ten thousand Democrats rent the air," read the report. " ThrOnes reeled," wrote the ImPami"e4 "•dath,.4 The next morning he saw in type. eeeledin The story is told that Ernest Henan once had oCusion to telegraph across the British Channel OA subject of a proposed Lecture of his in Westminster Abbey. The subject as written by him was "The Influence of Rome on the Formation of Christianity." It was pub- lished in England as "The Influence of Rum on the Diges- tion of Humanity."

WARRINGTON INFIRMAIN AND DISPENSARY. On Saturday afternoon a well-attended meeting of the representatives.who have been Appointed by the various works in the town to form the Workingmen's Infirmary Committee, was held in the Town Hall. There were also present the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) who presided, Alderman Pickmere, Alderman Davies, Major Litton, and Mr. Z. Armitage (bon. sec. of the Infirmary Committee.) —Mr. ARVITAGB presented a statement of accounts which showed that up to the present time a total subscription of £438 13s 6cl had been received, there being three subscrip- tions yet to come in which would probably amount tb £4O. Last year the total, including concert, was £4OO 120 10, while this year it would probably ameuet to £478 13s do. The expenditure had been £l4 16s 10p.—This report was adopted.--Mr. JOIIN ROBIIIITS moved that the list of subscriber-5 be printed and circulated as last year, and sug- gested that the firms who had not subscribed anything should also be named.—Mr. Forma seconded this propo- sal.—Mr. A. RATHRONB, in supporting the proposal,,said that in addition to publishing the list they might do what was done when the scheme that is now carried on in the various works of the town was originaVd. At that time they called together a number of men who were well known to have influence in the different works and laid the matter before them in order to ascertaia which would be the best method of working the subscriptions. As the result of that meeting meetings were called in various works, White. cross amongst the number, and a plan of subscribing then adopted. Ile suggested that something of the same sort should be done now and in this way try to induce some of the men engaged in the works from which no subscriptions had beee received to take steps similar to those taken at other works. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. ARYITAGA said that would be the work of the Workingmen's Executive Committee.—Mr. ROVERTS' proposal was then agreed to —A general committee and also an executive committee was then appointed, and Mr. JOHN HONERTS unani- mensly re-appointed chairman of the latt3r.—Aldere man DAVOS moved that the dates of sending in subscrip- tions be the end of May and the end of November, as last year. In doing so he contrasted the position the infirmary now held with that it held fifteen years ago when it was simply supported to the extent of £165 by the general in- habitants of the than. The management of the infirmary, he said, was carried on on exactly the same lines as in the case of similar institutions in other towns. They could not, however, please everybody, and the result ,wasghat there were one or two complaints. He held in his hand a letter from rt Mr. Charles •Connor, who, he was told, was col- lector for the London and Norta-Western Etailway Com- pany's employ loat Dallam, and he said, in reply to Mr. Z. Armitage's communication, "lii consequence of several of our men being insufficiently attended to in the ibfirmary it has been decided to subscribe no more, so no one is ap- pointed to attend the meeting of '''representatives in the Town Hall on January 23rd." With the exception of that and two other complaints, he (Aldermen Davies), was very happy to tell them the management of the heft- mary had been carried on without complaint. If there was any man to find fault it was Major Litton, and their thanks were due to him for the way he looked after the institu- tion and saw that everything was done that could be done. (Hear, hear.) He thought they might jest satisfied when they had only received three complaints that the institu- ion was carried on in a way satisfactory to the town. (Hear. hear.)—A Representative thought that the excuse for not contributing given by the railway employ4a at Dallarn was a very childish one, and be expressed the opinion that those men ought not to be treated at the infir- mary until they saw the advantage of subscribing.—The Mayon was afraid such a course as that would have a ten- dency to make the institution unpopular.—Mr. RAIHBONE said he thought such a course would be a great mistake. Their object was not to make enemies but to make friends. (Hear, hear.) With regard to complaints he believed that many were made that were not lodged with the committee, bet he was ot opinion that many of them had been made without due consideration of the difficulties the house ' and other surgeons had to contend with. (Hear, hear.)— Another Representative said that a young brotherofhis who had been in the hospital said that he thought the doc- tor rather brutal.—The MAYOR said he had always thought their present house surgeon was very humane and considerate, and solicitous fer the welfare of the poor people whom he came in contact with. He was sure, however, that the committee would pay the strictest attention to any com- plaint that came before them, as they were anxious the institution might be so conducted As to merit the confidence of the public in every respect.—Major Lie- TON said he visited the infirmary almost every Friday after- noon and spoke to nearly every patient and asked them if they were comfortable, and he had not had a single corn- pla.inte—The Representetive who last spoke, said the pa- tients did not care to complain whilst in the infirmery.—

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. Last Thursday the business of the new Parlia- ment was opened with all the pomp that accom- panies the presence of the sovereign. It is a signi- cant circumstance that on the two recent occasions when the Queen has lent to a Conservative Govern- ment the support of her presence at the open- ing of a session, the event has been followed by a crushing catastrophe. Eighteen hundred and 'eighty was the occasion previous to Thursday when the cream-coloured steeds were ordered out, and the 'Queen drove to Westminster. Within a couple of -months Parliament was dissolved, and the great 'Conservative majority scattered to the winds. Then -followed the five years' Government of Mr. Glad- stone, whose long spell of hard work was never 'cheered by the sunlight of the presence of majesty. Next comes the Government of the successor of Lord leaconsfield, and come again the cream-coloured 'steeds. This was last Thursday. To-day in the hall where seven days ago the Queen sat for a few minutes, Lord Salisbury admits that his attempt to govern the country has failed, and announces his resignation. The end came at an early hour yesterday morning, some forty-eight hours before it was expected. The week was hardly entered upon, but the vagaries of a, bewildered and desperate Government had already ex- cited the amusement of mankind. The Queen's Speech had disappointed the Conservatives by its vague and inconsequential references to coercive measures in Ireland. There had been so much tall talk, so much wagging of the head ins Conservative cicles before the Speech was published, that it was everywhere accepted as certain that very strong measures dealing with what Lord Salisbury called "the scandalous state of Ireland would be imme- diately forthcoming. It turned out that there was nothing but a weak reference to what might hap- pen in certtn contingencies, and thereupon the Government were attacked by their own followers and their organs in the press. The country was next startled by the announcement 'that Mr. IV. 11. Smith, the eminent bookstall proprietor, had at this 1 critical juncture been sent. over to Ireland to make I inquiry into its condition. Sir Henry Wolff's mis- sion to Egypt was a joke, but this was past a joke. If the Government were not possessed of the facts relating to the condition of Ireland, they had been terribly remiss in their duty. In any case the de- spatch of a Commissioner meant the indefinite de- ferment of action. If the Government knew through the ordinary channels of Ministerial information how things were in Ireland, there, was no need to send Mr. Smith. If they did not, it would be physi- cally impossible for him to acquire the. necessary information in a less period than a mouth or six weeks. Lord Salisbury maintained the situation with becoming gravity. Pressed for information upon Ministerial intentions in Ireland, he always answered " Wait till we hear from Mr. Smith." But the effect of this policy of Mr. Smith was more ' disastrous even than that which preceded it. The Liberals laughed with spontaneous merriment, whilst the Consei vatives muttered ominously among themselves. ".The policy of Mr. Smith" did not last more than two days. On Friday it was announced in Parliament, and on Monday night, almost before Mr. Smith had unpacked his portmanteau in Dub- lin, the Government had come to the conclusion to bring in forthwith a Coercion Bill, proclaiming the Land League and strengthening the hands of the executive in dealing with boycotting. Had this movement been firmly indicated in the speech from the Throne, the Government might at least hive fought the enemy on favourable ground, and died decently. But their shilly-shallying reduced -them to a condition of contempt, and on Tuesday night the majority of the House of Commons suddenly, and without prior notice, made up its mind to get rid of them forthwith, which they did, not on the Irish Question, but on a side issue raised by Mr. Collings, and having reference to agricultural hold-

ing Lord Salisbury, Lord Randolph Churchill, and the rest have already disappeared from the front of the stage, and all eyes are turned upon Mr. Gladstone. The question whether he should form a ministry has been anxiously put since the session opened. The difficulties that surround the task have con- siderably increased after the division on Mr. Jesse Collings's amendment. On that occasion Lord liar- tington, Sir Henry James, Mr. Courtney, and other Liberals went into the lobby against the Liberal chief. Sir Henry James and Mr. Courtney äo not count for much. But Lord Hartington's threatened secession is a very grave circumstance. This is the first time in his life he has ever found himself in the "no " lobby whilst Mr. Gladstone was in. the "aye." In taking this important step he was care- ful to modify its significance by limiting his differ- ence of opinion to the particular question at issue. Ile hoped, he said, in the future to generally co- operate with Mr. Gladstone as he had done in the past. There is no question of Lord Hartington's loyalty and his total absence of personal feeling. He will not. as Mr. Forster did when he felt it his duty to cut himself adrift from his colleagues, turn upon them as endeavour to the best of his ability to discredit them. Lord Hartington, if he cannot agree with the new Gladstone Ministry, will not stoop to earn Tory cheers by attacking them from his place in the House of Commons. But whether he will go beyond that and subordinate his pre- indices to their views is a matter anxiously debated .but not yet settled. One thing is quite clear. If Mr. Gladstone comes in it will be with the tacit pledge to deal with the question of local government in Ireland upon a broad basis. In voting upon Mr. Jesse Collings' -amendment, Liberals, like Irishmen, were really vot- ing against that system of coercion which has been frequently tried of late and has always failed. It .is time to try something new, and Mr. Gladstone, ji believe, is prepared to undertake the task, and has secured the collaberation of all his important col- leagues in the late Government, save Lord Harting- ton, and he may yet come round. When he meets Parliament as First Lord of the Treasury it will be necessary for Mr. Gladstone to formulate his views ,on the Home Rule question. That will be an oppor- tunity welcomed no less by him than by the coun- try. He will then be able to show that there is no basis for the fears that have been conjured up, and that in endeavouring to meet the wishes of the Irish people as expressed at the general election, he will be careful first and above all things to maintain the integrity of the British Empire. The directors of the Indian Village are just now in a state of some consternation. All the snakes are sickening of a vague disease, to which some have already succumbed. No one in the village was able to decide upon the nature, or trace the course, of the disease. In desperation, application • was made to Mr. Bartlett, of the Zoo., who was offered any reasonable fee to restore the snakes to convalescence, and Mr. Bartlett, having a shrewd suspicion of what was the matter, visited the interesting_ patients and speedily discovered a quite sufficient cause of their indisposition Their mouths were all sewn up and the wretched treatures were simply dying of starvation. This throws a weird light upon the accomplishments of the Indian snake charmers. In some cases the fangs are drawn, and the snake plays harmlessly around the fearless charmer. In other cases, as in respect of the snakes at the Indian Village, their mouths have been sewn up, and tiley are therefore helpless. At the same time it must be admitted that the mere feat of sewing is one that excels any- thing snake charmers do in the ordinary way of their business. The association recently started under the patron- . age of Lord Randolph Churchill for establishing a system of newspapers designed to educate the public mind has not prospered according to its merits. It was to supply all kinds of things for provincial papers, leaders, London letters, reviews, and selected paragraphs all warranted to be free fro. m Radical taint and subtilly impregnated with Conservative flavour. Th 6 newspapers .do not seem to have taken kindly to this sug- gestion, and now a fresh departure is made. The Association propose to issue what they call "Con- servative insides." This has not, as would apliear upon the face of it, anything to do with the in- ternal organisation of Conservative electors. It is the tecnical name for a newspaper sheet printed on one side, leaving the other side blank for the inser- tion of local news to be printed on the spot. The pity of it is that the association find themselves at the outset handicapped by serious competition. Cassell and Co. it seems supply these " insides " at the rate of 5s a hundred. The Conservative Associa- tion cannot supply them under 6s 6d. They ac- cordingly propose to raise more capital in order that they may at the loss of is 6d a hundred compete with Cassell and Co. This is a very remarkable commercial undertaking. The larger their business the quicker ruin to the shareholders. It The deputation of Belfast Loyalists which waited the other day upon Lord Hartington agreed to his lordship's suggestion that the proceedings should be strictly private. Members of Ihe press proposing to i eport the proceedings were politely nformed

that they could not enter. The representative of , one of the news agencies was, however, not to be done. He awaited the arrival of the deputation, , and then assuming with more or less success the appearance of a Belfast Loyalist, he walked in and was duly introduced to Lord Ilartington. If, like Mr. Marvin, he could have trusted to his memory, his strateg,em would have proved successful. But when he was observed to be taking notes the atten- tion of the deputies was attracted to him, the fraud was discovered, and the gentleman of the press was somewhat unceremoniously hustled off nu premises. Perhaps the best part of the story is that he never- theless wrote an account of the proceedings two columns long r

MR. JOHN BROOKS AND THE TENANT FARMERS. Sir.—l wormer what tbo tenant farmers in the Altrin- cham Divis,.m who voted for Mr. John Brooks in corre- quence of his pledges to support anythin% that would give them the utmost security for their capi-1 and improve- ments think now of his vote against Mr. Bar clay's amandment to the Address in reply to , the gAeen's Speech ? Mr. Barclay's amendment affirmea the principle of altering the conditions upon which agricultural land is held, so as to give better Lecurity to tenant farmers, and yet Mr. John Brooks, in the teeth of all his pledges, helped to defeat this first effort to assist the tenant farmer.—Yours, Lyinm. • THOMkS STELFOX

"THREE ACRES AND A COW." Sir,—Can any of your readers info, in one who is of an inquiring ttr.3 of inird what was the original founda'on of the term "Three Acres and a Cow," or when the words were first used. 1 have heard the term attributed to Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Coiltsgs, Mr. Arch, and °nets, and sul-ne msert that the tirst-nam.d politician made use of the words ' 4 Three acres" during his famous speech at Warringtc.n in the early part of the electoral campaign, but that lie forgot to mention the "cow." Surely someone will know the truth of the matter, whether the famous sentence has really a foundation in fact, or is merely the invention of Tory 1 genius.—Yours, &c., IGNORANT.

OUR PUBLIC LIBRARY. Sir,—l was pleased to see the letters of " Clifford Dix" anl " Visitor "in your late issues. Why can we net have a free lending library ? lam sure it would be a great boon to the large mass of the people of our town—particularly at the present time when so many men are out of work, and indeed to all pocr people lalhose means at the present time are very limited. lam given to understand that Warring- ten holds the un'que posit:on of being almost, if not abso- lutely, the only town of its size in •England that does not ,possess a Free Lending Library. At all events it is very far behind many towns of equal size and impJrtance. I was surprised, and at Erst irscred-tlous, when I heard that the realing-room is not supplied with the leading daily pip2rs. I wish to use mild language, but I cannot halo thinking that it is a disgrice to the town that we should be I so far behind the times. I was a subscriber to the Library for twelve months, and during the whole of that time I could not 'get a cata- logne. I had to stuely the one at the desk, and whenever I i asked for one I was always told they were being printed, and I believe they are being printed yet. homebody must have got a large order. - I shag be glad to see this matter taken up by others, and trust it may not be allowed to drop until we have a Free Library and a reading-room wo.,:hy of the town.—Yours, &c.. • JOHN GANDY, 23, Church-street, Warrington.

SOCIAL EQUALITY. Si-,—The general tone of " Jaques' " letter in your last issue I most cordially agree with, but must take exception to the following retnafe, "Not the unnatural equality of com- munism, but the equality of like opportunities of acquiring distinction and fortune " ; the preceding line states that, "What we now want to win is social equality." I would like ".Lques " to explain how there can be "social equal- ity " when certain members of society can attain " distinc- tion and fortune ? " The paragraph appears to me para- doxical. Suppose Ais the son of a landlord or capitalist, i land B the son of a workirg-man, how can the latter be said Ito have the s tme opportunity as the former to :-.cquire " dis- tinction and fortune? ' Clearly B is at a great d'sadrantage in the race, as all events at the atarting point. True, B may be the sharpest of the twain, but that does not enter into 1" Jacques' " argument. Will " Jaques " explain the da- -1 ferenct between a capitalist landlord and a capitalist trader? I Both may kiave attained either positions, or they may have I come to thorn by heirship. And most certainly both " ex- -1 tract a luxurious living from the poer " tihethe- of I-eiand ! or any other country; therefore in order that there may be, Ino "'perpetual pensioners living on the produce of other I 1 people's labour " the blow must be struck at capitalism all I round. Is " Jaqu es " prepared for such a course? Will " Jaques " also show how fortunes are or can be made by one or more individuals without a corresponding loss to a !larger number of other individtaals ? The question of Co.n- I muniim is a wide one, and I would ask "Jaquca" to give me his definition of what be calls "the unnatural social equality of Communism." I will then offer come remarks I thereon if you, Mr. Editor,,will kindly allow me to do so in • ! your valuable medium. W. H. CHAPMAN. 1 January 27, 1886.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES COUNCIL.

Sir,—As the case stated by Clifford Dix "in his letter Piot seek- may lead to a wrong impression being formed respecting the Trades Council, I should like, with yonr per- mission, to state why the body of men referred to by him should have been refused admission to the Council, me- dially as the •• short reports of the mere 'meetings " have lately stated that we were anxious for more societiee to join ns. In an ordinary case, if applied to by the secretary, or a delegate from a society, as to the steps necessary to be taken to .in the Council, I should not hesitate to instruct him to come prepared to join at our next meeting, but the following will show that it was an exceptional case. About Christmas last, I was waited Neon by Mr. H. Whitham and a gentleman whose name I am not acquainted with, stating. that they came as a deputation from the Warrington Wire- drawers' • ociety, which society was prepared to join the Council if I would tell them how they could do so. Now, as the Wiredrawers' Society is already represented by 200 members on the Council, and as the standing of the other society was unknown to me, I left it for the Council to de- cide the matter, and after hearing a statement from the wiredrawers' delegates present, they decided that under pre- nent circumstances it was not advisalele to receive them. Doubtless " a abort skrch of their proceedings would have been interesting to y6ur readers," especially to Mr. Whit barn, who would like to be the guiding star of the Council. But I venture to say that, in spite of the threat, or warning, or whatever else it may be intended for, which is given in the letter, the Trade Unionists of Warrington will be able to overcome their difficulties as they arise, and acquit them- selves as men. With respect to the rest of his letter, it is not my purpose to attempt to say anything, except that I heartily agree with many sentiments expres.;ed therein, and believe it will benefit workmen to think deeper, so that they may see further —Yours, &c., JONATHAN WILD, 20, Queen-street. Secretary to the Trades Council.

WARRINGTON. WARRINGTON GRAMMAR SCHOOL. The open mathematical scholarship at Exeter College, Oxford, has been awarded to Mr. 11. Worthington Curjel, Warrington Grammar School. The Scholarship is of the annual value of £BO, and is tenable for five years during residence and good conduct. Candi- dates were under the age of 19. THE MIKADO.— On Monday and Tuesday Mr. D'Oyly Carte's Opera company will present, at the Public Hall, Gilbert and Sullivan's latest and enor7

mously successful Japanese opera, "The Mikado." New and elaborate scenery will be brought from the , Savoy theatre, and we may hope to see the piece mounted in the style for which Mr. D'Oyly Carte is so famous. The plan of reserved seats is at Mr. Pigott's music warehouse. i WORKING MEN'S 'MISSION, BANK QUAY.—A band of hope entertainment was given in the above schoolroom, on Wednesday evening, by the Howley- lane Band of Hope friends, under the superintend- ence of Messrs. Roberts and Ford. A very interest- ing programme was gone through before a large and appreciative audience. There were glees by the choir, recitations by the children, and two dia- logues entitled "The Vacant Chair" and "New Brooms Sweep Clean." Mr. H. Pickersgill occupied the chair. PENNY READING AT LATCHFORD.—Another of a eeries of penny readings was held in Christ Church schoolroom, Latchford, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occu- pied by the Vicar, the Rev. B. B. Prescott, who apologised for the absence of Mr. Harold Broadbent and Mr. Longdin. The following was the prc • gramme.:—Pianoforte solo, Mrs H. Woods; recita- , tatiou, Mr. Burgess; duet, "Larboard watch," Mr. Monks and __Mr. Grounds; recitation, "Cure for
tooth-werch," (encored) Mr. J. Brierley ; song, "Our last waltz," Miss Rose Blackhurst ; _ reading,

Mr. Rupert Crossley ; song (encored), Mr. Fry; reading (encored), Mr. Guy Reynolds; song, "The midshipmite,". Mr. Monks ; song (encoied), Mr. Arthur Reynolds; song, Mr. T. Acton; song, Mr. Grounds; song, "The watchman and the child," Miss Rose Blackhurst ; recitation, Mr. Brierley ; song, Mr. Monks; song, Mr. Arthur Reynolds. A DISORDERLY PUBLIC-HOUSE.—At the Borough Court, on Monday. John Gordon, who holds tem- porary authority to sell crl the licensed premises, the Gun Inn,. Scotland-road, was summoned for permitting drunkenness there on the 16th inst, and for being himself drunk at the same time and place. Mary Stewart, John llines, and Martin Fleming, were charged with being drunk on the premises.—lnspector Berry said that when he visi- ted the house the landlord was drunk, was only partially dressed, and appeared more like an im- becile than anything else. There were thirty peo- ple in the house, of whom fourteen were females. —Mr. Fox, from the office of Messrs. Davies, Kirk 7 connell, and Co., appeared on behalf of Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co„ and said that the firm regfetted that the house had been so badly con- ducted; they would not allow Gordon to conduct it any longer.—The Bench fined Gordon 20s and costs, Fleming lOs and costs, and Stewart and Hines 5s each, including costs. THE SINGULAR FATALITY TO A CHILD.--An in- quest was held by Mr. T. Husband, deputy coroner, on Saturday, at the Unicorn Inn, Winwick-street, regarding the death of Mary Alice Bate, five months old, daugloter. of Peter Bate,. labourer at Dallam Forge, which occurred on the previous Thursday under circumstances reported in our last issue.— Mary Bate, mother of the child, gave evidence tol ! the effect that at about eight o'clock on the Thurs- day morning in question she was standing near the door of her house-18, Appleton-street—with the baby in her arms, when a quantity of spouting fell from the roof and, struck the child on the head. At the time she was stooping down to pick some wood from the ground, and the falling spoutl and snow only missed her by about three or four inches. The child died aboat an hour afterwards.—After the evidence had been completed, a juryman said that he and several others had examined the spouting, which was about 36 feet in length. It had only been held in its position by a few spout irons, which had no screws in them, and by two downspouts. The spouting that still remained was secured in a similar manner, and might at any time come down. Ile thought it .a shame that life should in that way be endangered, as he considered that there must have been negligence on the part of the builder of the property. Several other jurors assented in these remarks, and a verdict of. "Accidental death '• was then returned. DETERMINED ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.—On Monday night, as the 11-37 train for Liverpool was coming into the Central Station, a woman who had pre- viously taken a ticket for Liverpool was seen to go into the fourfoot, and lay herself down with her head on the metals. Two porters—Edward Hughes and Joseph Whalley—succeeded in lifting her into the sixfoot before the train reached her, and they had in doing so a narrow escape. The police were sent for, and Constable Baxendale, with the assis- tance of a porter, took her to the police station, where she remained until Tuesday morning, when she was brought before two of the borough magis- trates and Charged with attempting to commit suicide.—Chief Constable Hunt, in narrating the circumstances of the case, said that prisoner, whose name is Elizabeth Heves, was the wife of a person employed at the India Rubber works, who lived at 8, Rose and Crown-street. They had come from Salford to Warrington eight or ten months ago. It', appeared that between five and six 'o'clock on Mon- day evening the husband went home for his tea,, but it was not ready, and his wife had been drinking.. In consequence they had some words. A little after eleven o'clock the wife went to the Central Station and took a ticket for Liverpool, and as the 11-37 train was coming in deliberately lay down with her head on the metals. On her having been rescued it was found that she was under the influence of liquor and very much excited. A bottle that had contained whiskey was found in her pocket.— Edward Hughes, foreman porter, informed the , magistrates that the train was only ten or twelve yards away when prisoner jumped into the four- ; foot, covering her head with her shawl. Whalley, ! another porter, had a narrow escape of being killed. Prisoner could not have been saved had there becn an up-train in the station at the same time. On being taken away she said that it was her intention 'to be killed, and she would do it some other time. The prisoner's husband said that he had threatened to thrash her if she went drinking again, but he had no idea that she meant to attempt anything rash. She had never attempted such a thing be- fore.—The Magistrates dismissed prisoner on the husband being bound in the sum of £lO for her good future behaviour. COMMITTAL OF A BANKRUPT FOR CONTEMPT OF CURT.—At the Warrington County Court on Mon- day, Mr. Peter Philip Longshaw, who recently carried on business as a chemical manufacturer, at Sankey Bridges, came before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes on his adjourned examination in bank- ruptcy. Mr. Worsley, the Deputy Official Receiver, asked his Honour to commit the bankrupt to prison for contempt of court, on the ground that he had failed to comply with an order that was made upon him on the 11th of last month to file a complete list of his accounts. Mr. Worsley remarked that he had gone out of his way to explain to the debtor what would be the consequences of neglect, with a view to avoiding the then proceedings, but Mr. Longshaw had set at defiance both • the Official Receiver and the Court. The Official Receiver would never be able to carry out, his duties if such conduct were allowed. Mr. Longshaw informed the Judge that he had done all that he could to assist the Official Receiver. He had been endeav- ourino• to obtain the assistance of his late clerk, Mr. Sorter, cd that a complete list of his accounts might be preparo, but Mr. Worsley was not will- ing that Sorter should help him without he (the debtor) agreed to pay him .E 2 a week, which he !vas not able to do. Mr. Worsley said that the bankrupt already owed Sorter the sum of £34 18s 3d for wages. A discussion followed, and afterwards his Honour said that the bankrupt had not done a single thing that he had been ordered to do, which was a gross contempt of Court. The bankrupt had been utterly negligent of his duty, and he must commit him for contempt of Couit. He would have ,purged his contempt when he had complied with ! that order, but until then he would have to remain in gaol. At the, County Court, on Thursday, Mr. A. Browne; solicitor, applied to his Honour to release the bankrupt.—His Honour asked on what grounds the application was based.—Mr. Browne replied that the bankrupt was willing ta comply with the order of the Court, and asked that he should be released so that he could furnish the accounts u ragnes w hiser tn Mr. asked for.—His Honour said that Mr. Longsha mtdl, tinpw contempt Brownebef o,rew lhi en wasasasked eci ifreleased,the an official receiver would allow the bankrupt' to have s the books at the poi, said that he did not .know that, but a man from Wigan who was •in gaol for , contempt managed to file his accounts and. he dis- char.ged him.—Mr. Browne thanked his Honour for I the information.

RETURN OF THE COURT.
Preparations are being made at Windsor Castle for the return of the Court from Osborne, which, according to the present arrangement, will take place next week. THE RESIGNATION ACCEPTED.

TILE Sr. HELENS HAUSIEBS.—An introductory run in connection with the St. Helens Harriers Club took place on Saturday, the trail being laid by A. Loader anct J. Wood. The hares were despatched from head•quarters shortly after three o'clock, and the pack started five minu- tes later. The route was through Rainford and Crank, and an enjoy-Ale run was made, the bares arriving home about 4-20. The pack appeared 3-.1- minutes afterwards, the foremost being E. Lever, with H. Risby 2CO yards in his rear.

The Central News has the highelt authority for stating that Her Majesty has been pleased to accept the resignation of the Government, tendered to her by Lord Salisbury. Up to six o'clock last evening the Queen had not, however, sent for Mr. Gladstone. - -
The Fiatteenth Cent-ury contains an impnrtant article on the Irish question by Mr. H. 0. Arnold Forster, the son of the 11,ght Hon. W. E. Forster. It is a sweeping condemna- tion of the Trish race.

• GOODS POETERS' SUPPER.—The 41st annual supper of the porters and officials employed by the London and North-Western Railway Company at the St. Helens goads station; was held at the Fleece Hotel. Among the guests were Mr. Moss, Mr. Ashton, Mr. Bates, Mr. Merrill, Mr. Taylor, Mr. Matthewe, Mr. Prescott, Mr. Hughes. and Mr. Lucas. After an excellent repast had been enjoyed, Mr. Faulkner, goods agent, presided. Tile usual loyal toasts were duly honoured, after which Mr. Bates propoeed " Suc- cess of the London and North-Western Board of Dii4ctors." The Chairman, in responding, stated that he believed the board were actuated by the sincerest desire to do justice to everybody concerned in their undertaking, both the share- holders on the one hand and the public on the other. The toasts "Town and trade of St. Helens," "The donors," and "The hostess" were enthusiastically drunk and acknow- ledged. A selection of songs, ctc., were rendered by Messrs. J. Welsbv, R. Gray, J. Clarke, H. Merrill, G. Grime, J. Merrill, Ashton, A. T. Cox, J. Toyior, and W. Clarey.
The marriage of Miss Mary Glldst-me, daughter of Mr. and Mrs W. E. Gladstone, with the Rev. Harry Drew, curate of Hawarden, will take place in London on Tuesday next.

Damage to the amount of £25,000 was canspd by fire on Thursday at the carpet manufactory of Messrs. J, and J. S. Templeton, Glasgow. Snocsirso COLLIERY ACCIDENT: THREE MEN KILLED.— A fall of coal took place on Thursday morning, at Cwm Pit, one of the Cyfarthfa Collieries, Merthyr, and the result was that three men were killed. Their names are Tom Hughes, Thomas Harris, and John Harris. A fourth man named Foberts was also injured, and has been conveyed home Several others escaped.

THE BIRTH AND DEATH RATE OF WARRINGTON. —For week ending Saturday, Jan. 23rd, 188 G.—The mean temperature was 30.6 Fahr., and therefore 6.6 degrees colder than the preceding week. The maximum temperature 41 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 17th inst., and the minimum temperature. 11 Fahrenheit, on the 20th inst. The rainfall measured .Bin. The general direction of the wind was N.E. During the week, which was the 4th of the current year, 35 births and 33 deaths I were registered. The death rate from all causes

was equ-al to 37 per 1,000, against 256 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 26.3 the cor- responding week of last year. The deaths included 2 from diarrhcea, 2 from whooping cough, 2 from old age, 11 from lung disease, 6 from brain disease, 3 from liver disease, and 2 from heart disease. Six cases of whooping cough were reported under the ' requirements of the Act of Parliament —JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLT:I3.—A meeting of the committee was held at the White Bull -Inn, , Horsemarket-street, on Wednesday evening. Mr. J. Marsh presided. The principal business was to con- sider the present position qf the rent question— firstly as to how far short of the true merits of the case is the response made by landowners in the dis- trict to the memorials of the club, and secondly as to the Pe asons why the landowners' response is un- satisfactory and insufficient.—The Chairman referred

to the depression in agriculture. Being in a dairy district they were the last to feel it, but dairy far- mers were feeling the change.—Mr. T. Stelfox ured that rent reduction was necessary, as everything that a farmer had to turn out was reduced to from 30 to 40 per cent, under paying price.—Mr. Baguley thought it would not, perhaps, in a general sense, be advisable at present to agitate further for a rent reduction. He thought that if they spent their , energies in strengthening the hands of those- meal- hers of Parliament who Vould.help them in the legislature of the country they would be doing far more good, in a broad sense, by getting such altera- tion in the land laws as would be to ultimate advan- tage. If by any possibility they could get security of tenure, it would be a benefit for generations to come.—Mr. W. Darbyshire said that many felt dis- satisfied with what the landlords had done in answer to the rent memorial, but they could not have everything at once.—The Chairman said that there had been many remissions, but they were not the rule.—Mr. Darbyshire thought the response made by landlcrds fell short of what was requisite to meet the depressed state of agriculture.—The Secretary (Mr. J. L. Stelfox) said that the great de- pression in prices had occurred during the last ten years, and was it reasonable to expect them to pay the same rent now as then? It was said that land- lords were suffering equally with the tenant far- mers, but, after careful consideration, he had come to the conclusion that, so far as Lancashire and Cheshire were concerned, landowners were not suf- fering from agricultural depression, but were ac- quiring an enormously increased wealth by reason of the very agricultural depression which row. so intensely and severely affected the financial position of tenant farmers. A few of the landowners had made small reductions of 10 per cent., but in many eases no reduction at all had been made.—The Chair- man thought that as a rule the landlords had not met the tenants on a proper footing, but still there had been some who had paid attention to them.— Other members took part in the discussion.—Mr. Thomas Stelfox proposed a resolution to the effect that the best thanks of the club be accorded to Mr. Barclay, M.P., for the interest he manifested on be- half of the tenant farmers in Parliament on Monday night.—This was seconded by Mr. Warburton, and carried.

PR__ZITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, LEGII STREET.- -The special mission services held in this place of worship last week proved to be of an interesting character, and the conductors wore encouraged to continue them each evening during the present week. There have been large attend- ancee, and much attention was !manifested by the congrega- tions. The services have.been conducted by the Rev. F. Shimtnin, resident minister, assisted by I°oll preachers. LOWTON AND DISTRICT PLOUGHING SOCIETY The fourth annual competition in connection with the above society, which bad been postponed from the previous week,' owing to she frost, has been again postponed, the thaw which has recently set in not having taken place soon enough to enable the Secretary to communicate with the competitors. This is to be somewhat regretted, as the ground was in splendid condition for ploughing. The match will, however, take place next Tuesday, weather Der- mittinh, on land in the occupation of Mr. Henry Ratcliffe, Wood End Farm, Culchetb. R thrvseor ASSESSMENT AT ASHTON-IN-MAKERFIELD. —The hearing of the appeal case, London and North- Western Railway Company v. Wigan Union Assessment Committee was resumed on Friday at the Liverpool County Sessions. Sir William Forwood presiding. The appellants asked for the assessment of 53 chains of their line in the 1 township of Ashton-in-Makerfield to be reduced from a !rateable value of £1,560 to £984, as the traffic bad been greatly dinsinished by the opening of a loop line. After hearing several engineers and valuers, the court, after ten minutes' consultation in private, reduced the assessment to £1,285, without cot.• ! FATALITIES AT COLLINS GREEN.— On Tuesday morn- ing Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Pear Tree Inn, Collins Green, touching the death of Willana Yates, 18 years of age, residing at the New Cottages Collins , Green, who was killed in the four-foot ~seam of the Bold Colliery. He commenced work at six o'clock, and about eight a cross-bar in the roof fell without any warning, ,triking the deceased a very violent blow behind the head, killing him instantly. The deceased's father and Critchley were close by, and the deceased was taken to the top of the pit, and afterwards to hie home. The bar weighed about six hundredweight. The jury returned a verdict of "Acci- dental death."--Another fatality occurred at the same pis on Tuesday afternoon when Dominick Dalton, a browman, met with his death under shocking circumstances. He was eneaged pulling trucks from the cage, which jerked, and fearing he would be pulled to the ;rearing, jumped back. A truck fell upon and crushed him in such a shocking man- ner that he died an hour after being removed to his home at Collins Green. The poor fellow leaves a wife and six little children. THE LATE Ma. T. DixoN, OF GOLBORNE.—Last Sunday evening, a funeral sermon on the late Mr. Themes Dixon was preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Golborne, by Mr. Thomas Cook, of Lovrton. The preacher based his sermon upon the 4th chap. 2nd Timothy, 7,., and 8, and said there was nothing which could qualify a ' man for death so much as Christ, nothing which would en- able a man to face the season of departure from this life with resignation but the possession of principles of Christianity. Speaking of his departed friend, he said that he had known him from boyhood. Mr. Dixon was born a Primitive Methodist, and died a Primitive Methodist. He had travelled hundreds of miles to preach in various places for their principles, and be kept his faith to the end. Some men gave the church a great deal of anxiety and uneasiness through their unsteady habits; net so with Mr. Dixon, he caused the church no trouble: he was always steadfast and firm in his religion. He had travelled scores of miles with him, but never saw or heard anything contrary to his profession. Appropriate hymns were sung during the service, and at the concluson of the sermon, "Vital spark" was rendered by the choir. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT BAND OF HOPE UNION. —The annual meeting of the representatives of the seven temperance societies forming the Earlestown District Baud of Hope Union was held in the Good Templars' lodgeronm, Bridge-street, Earlestown, on Friday evening. There was a full attendance, and Mr. J. H. Graham (president of the Unions) occupied the chair. A report of the result of the recent festival at the Viaduct Institute and the financial statement for the past year were submitted by the secretary (Mr. It. Higgins), and, being considered satisfactory, were unanimously adopted. The election rif officers for the en- suing year afterwards took place, and the following were re-elected :—President, Mr J. H. Graham ; vice-president, Mr. John Taylor ; treasurer, Mr. George Clarke ; and secretary, Mr. R. Lbigg,ins. Meesrs. 0. Pickett and J. Barnard were appointed assishant-secretaries, and Messrs. William Pearson and John Judson auditors. The question of taking part in a forthcoming examinetien on alcohol under the 'auspices of the Lancashire and 4 heshire Band of Hope Union was considered, and it was decided to take part therein. The future work of the Union was briefly dis- cussed, after which tim meeting concluded with thanks to the chairman., SUPPOSED DEATH FROM VACClNATlON.—Considerable conversation has been occaelaned throuehout the Earles- town and Newton districts by a report that Annie Spelman, three months old; daughter of Peter Bpelman, a labourer at Lowtou, had died from the results of vaccination. Tbe de- ceased child was vaccinated on the 10th inst. by Dr. Seph- ton, of Culcheth, and seemed to recover all right for two daye. Her mother took her to bed on the night of the 21st ' inst., and slept until five o'clock on the following morning, when the child was screaming. The child had the breast, but immediately afterwards closed its Eyes and died. Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Traveller's Rest Inn, Lowton, on Monday afternoon, when the mother (Mrs. Spelman) gave evidence to the foregoing effect. She was closely questioned by the coroner and several of the jurors as to whether she believed that vaccination caused the child's death, but the reply she gave was that she did not know. A neighbour named Ann Littler deposed that she was called by the last witness when the child bad died. She aesisted in washing tbe body of the child, whom, she said, had been healthy from its birth. The body and cheek on the right side were discoloured, and the vaccination marks were on the right arm. The coroner asked the mother if she wished the inquest to be adjourned sn as to allow of a post-mortem exemination of the body, but the mother, in tears, replied that she did not wish her child to be cut up. The jury afterwards returned a verdict to the effect that the child died suddenly in its mother's arms, but from what cause the evidence did not show.
